title: bug: window ORDER BY returns garbage or panics with materialized CTE on multi-node
body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/issues) and found no similar issues.

### Version

`v1.2.935-nightly-6f473f1eb8(rust-1.94.0-nightly-2026-08-24T12:44:08.502801000Z)`

Reproduced on a local **3-node** query cluster.

### What's Wrong?

A simple window query returns wrong results, or panics.

The SQL only does:

1. a CTE referenced twice
2. `UNION ALL`
3. `sum(...) OVER (ORDER BY ts ...)` where `ts` is `TIMESTAMP NULL`

On a multi-node cluster, instead of getting `running = 1, 0`, you may get garbage values in the window output column, or the query crashes with:

```text
UnwindError / BadDataValueType:
failed to downcast column Opaque/Binary([...]) into ...CoreNumber<i64>
```

This is easy to hit with default settings. No special data setup is needed.

### How to Reproduce?

**Environment:** multi-node cluster is required.

On **single-node / standalone**, this usually does **not** reproduce, because the plan stays on `Sort(Single)`.

#### A. Wrong result

```sql
WITH
queries AS (
    SELECT
        CAST(to_timestamp('2026-01-01 00:00:01') AS TIMESTAMP NULL) AS start_time,
        CAST(to_timestamp('2026-01-01 00:00:02') AS TIMESTAMP NULL) AS end_time
),
timeline AS (
    SELECT start_time AS ts, 1 AS delta FROM queries
    UNION ALL
    SELECT end_time AS ts, -1 AS delta FROM queries
)
SELECT
    ts,
    delta,
    sum(delta) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS running
FROM timeline;
```

Actual:

```text
ts                          delta  running
2026-01-01 00:00:01.000000  1      822F4648470680010000000000000040
2026-01-01 00:00:02.000000  -1     C43E4648470680010000000000000080
```

Expected:

```text
ts                          delta  running
2026-01-01 00:00:01.000000  1      1
2026-01-01 00:00:02.000000  -1     0
```

#### B. Panic

```sql
WITH
queries AS (
    SELECT
        CAST(to_timestamp('2026-01-01 00:00:01') AS TIMESTAMP NULL) AS start_time,
        CAST(to_timestamp('2026-01-01 00:00:02') AS TIMESTAMP NULL) AS end_time
),
timeline AS (
    SELECT start_time AS ts, 1 AS delta FROM queries
    UNION ALL
    SELECT end_time AS ts, -1 AS delta FROM queries
)
SELECT
    max(running) AS max_concurrency,
    avg(running) AS avg_concurrency,
    count(*) AS event_points
FROM (
    SELECT
        sum(delta) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS running
    FROM (
        SELECT ts, sum(delta) AS delta
        FROM timeline
        GROUP BY ts
    )
);
```

Actual:

```text
UnwindError / BadDataValueType:
failed to downcast column Opaque/Binary([...]) into ...CoreNumber<i64>
```

#### How to check you hit the bad plan

```sql
EXPLAIN
-- use the SELECT in section A
```

Bad plan looks like:

```text
Sort(Final)
└── Sort(Partial)   -- Partial still outputs #_order_col
```

If you only see `Sort(Single)`, you are probably on single-node and will not reproduce.

#### Workaround

```sql
SET enable_auto_materialize_cte = 0;
```

Then rerun section A. Expected result comes back: `running = 1, 0`.

### Additional Context

What seems to happen:

1. Because the CTE is referenced twice, it is auto-materialized.
2. The constant CTE producer makes the plan serial, and Exchange is removed.
3. Window sort becomes `Sort(Partial) -> Sort(Final)` with no Exchange between them.
4. `#_order_col` is still present physically, but later operators assume it is already removed.
5. The window output column reads the leftover sort key instead of `sum(delta)`.
   - As a SELECT result: garbage / encoded bytes
   - Under outer aggregate: panic while downcasting that leftover column

Notes:

- Defaults are enough to reproduce on multi-node.
- `enable_auto_materialize_cte` is the setting that matters for this MRE.
- `enable_fixed_rows_sort` is not required; turning it off still fails, just with Binary instead of Opaque.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

- [ ] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

title: bug: materialized CTE fails when one consumer reaches LIMIT early
body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/issues) and found no similar issues.

### Version

`Databend Query v1.2.938-nightly-117f9e153d(rust-1.94.0-nightly-2026-09-07T09:41:48.684476000Z)`

Local build with the exchange-channel fix from #20450 applied; the compiled source corresponds to commit `ae540c435cb5b13bcf11607a3a6699a1acd0d0c3`. The embedded version uses the HEAD from before that fix was committed.

Environment: macOS arm64, three query nodes with two CPUs and a 2 GiB tracked-memory limit per node, isolated MinIO storage. The reproduction uses only `numbers()` and requires no tables or imported data.

### What's Wrong?

A valid query with two consumers of the same automatically materialized CTE fails when one consumer reaches `LIMIT` and closes early, while the other consumer needs the full CTE.

Actual result:

```text
Code: 1001
Failed to send blocks to materialized cte consumer
```

Expected: successful completion with two rows. The full-scan branch should return `499999500000`; the limited branch should return the value of its single selected row. That value is intentionally unspecified because there is no `ORDER BY`.

The early completion of one consumer must not abort another consumer of the same CTE. `enable_auto_materialize_cte` is enabled by default in the inspected source.

### How to Reproduce?

Run against a three-node cluster:

```sql
SET max_threads = 2;
SET max_block_size = 1024;
SET max_execute_time_in_seconds = 8;
SET enable_auto_materialize_cte = 1;

WITH t AS (
    SELECT number FROM numbers(1000000)
)
SELECT sum(number) FROM t
UNION ALL
SELECT sum(number) FROM (
    SELECT number FROM t LIMIT 1
);
```

`EXPLAIN` confirms a `MaterializedCTE: t` producer and two `MaterializeCTERef` consumers. The small block size allows consumer completion to overlap with ongoing production.

Rechecked on a freshly started cluster before opening this issue:

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| SQL above, rotating all three coordinator nodes | 12/12 failed with code 1001 and the message above |
| Same SQL with `enable_auto_materialize_cte = 0` | 3/3 succeeded |
| Materialization enabled, remove only `LIMIT 1` | 3/3 succeeded; both sums were `499999500000` |

The failure is an Internal error, not the eight-second execution deadline being reached. Both controls were checked for successful terminal state and valid results.

Likely cause:

- [`CTESource::event`](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/blob/ae540c435cb5b13bcf11607a3a6699a1acd0d0c3/src/query/service/src/pipelines/processors/transforms/materialized_cte.rs#L362-L365) closes the receiver when its downstream finishes.
- [`MaterializedCteSink::send_payload`](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/blob/ae540c435cb5b13bcf11607a3a6699a1acd0d0c3/src/query/service/src/pipelines/processors/transforms/materialized_cte.rs#L216-L220) continues sending to every consumer and turns any closed-channel send into an Internal error. It does not distinguish normal per-consumer completion from a query failure.

The producer should continue serving remaining consumers after one closes, and stop upstream when no consumers remain. Consumer cleanup should also release queued payloads.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

title: fix(planner): propagate UDF rewrite flags out of nested UDF definitions
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

A script/server UDF cannot be evaluated by the expression evaluator. It must be lifted into a separate `Udf` plan node by `UdfRewriter`, which only runs when `bind_context.have_udf_script` / `have_udf_server` is set.

`resolve_udf_definition` type-checks a Lambda/SQL scalar UDF body with a **fresh** `BindContext`, so a runtime UDF call inside that body recorded the flag on the inner context only. The flag was dropped on return, the rewrite was skipped, and the `UDFCall` stayed inline in `EvalScalar`/`Filter`. Lowering then turned it into a dummy column reference via `as_raw_expr()`, and the physical plan failed at `input_schema.index_of(&index.to_string())`:

```
Unable to get field named "18446744073709551611"
```

`18446744073709551611` is `usize::MAX - 4`, i.e. `Symbol::new_dummy_column(DummyColumnType::UDF)` — an internal sentinel, not corrupt data.

This also explains the reporter's observation that adding a direct call to the same UDF in the same `SELECT` made both work: the direct call set the flag on the *outer* context, so one rewrite pass then handled both calls.

Plan before the fix (no `UdfScript` node — the call is left inline):

```
EvalScalar
├── scalars: [wrap_add_one(add_one(t.a (#0))) AS (#2)]
└── Scan
```

After:

```
EvalScalar
├── scalars: [wrap_add_one(add_one(x) (#3)) AS (#2)]
└── UdfScript
    ├── scalars: [add_one(t.a (#0)) AS (#3)]
    └── ...
```

**Fix 1** (`type_check/udf.rs`): propagate `have_udf_script` / `have_udf_server` / `have_async_func` from the definition body back to the caller. `have_async_func` is included because async functions (`nextval`, `dict_get`) in a definition body lose their flag through the same path.

**Fix 2** (`type_check/lambda.rs`): while narrowing this down, a second path produced the identical error string — a script UDF inside a SQL lambda body, e.g. `SELECT array_transform([a], x -> add_one(x))`.

That one is **not** fixable by rewriting. A lambda body is compiled into a `RemoteExpr` and evaluated per element, while a runtime UDF needs a batched call to an external runtime, so `UdfRewriter` cannot lift it out. Rejecting it with a semantic error is the correct behavior instead of leaking an internal column id:

```
UDF \"add_one\" is not supported in the lambda body of array_transform,
because script and server UDFs are evaluated by a separate plan node
```

This also covers UDAF scripts, which construct `UDAFCall` directly in `udf.rs` and therefore bypass the existing \"aggregate functions can not be used in lambda function\" guard in `resolve_aggregate_function`. Pure-SQL lambda UDFs are inlined into plain function calls and remain allowed — there is a test pinning that.

Out of scope: #12922 / #12963 / #13057 report the same *symptom* with `usize::MAX` (window/aggregate sentinels). They share the dummy-column mechanism but leak at different sites and are not addressed here.

- fixes: #20497

## Tests

- [x] Unit Test
- [x] Logic Test
- [ ] Benchmark Test
- [ ] No Test - _Explain why_

New goldenfile `src/query/sql/tests/it/semantic/binder_nested_udf.txt` covers three rewrite paths (lambda UDF wrapper, SQL scalar UDF wrapper, wrapper in `WHERE`), three rejection paths (script UDF / lambda-wrapped script UDF / UDAF script in a lambda body), and one allow path (pure-SQL lambda UDF in a lambda body). The three rewrite cases and both script-UDF-in-lambda-body cases fail on `main` — the first three with no `UdfScript` node, the latter two with the raw sentinel error.

Verified locally:
- `cargo test -p databend-common-sql --test it` — 126 passed
- `databend-sqllogictests --run_file 03_0013_select_udf.test` — 88 passed, against a local standalone deployment
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets` clean

## Type of change

- [x] Bug Fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New Feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)
- [ ] B

title: feat(planner): validate column scope of the plan after every optimizer
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

A recurring class of planner bugs ends with the same opaque execution-time error:

```
Unable to get field named "14". Valid fields: ["0", "1", "9", "11", "12", "13"]
```

#20462 (correlated column in a join `ON` not decorrelated), #18073 (`UPDATE ... FROM` subquery scope) and #11831 (`prune unused columns` dropping lazy columns) all surfaced this way. The root cause is always the same invariant being broken somewhere in the binder or an optimizer rule: **an operator references a column that none of its inputs produces**. Today nothing checks that invariant; the physical plan builder trips over it much later, without saying which operator or which rule broke the plan.

This PR adds `SExpr::validate_column_scope` and runs it next to the existing `validate_types`, under `debug_assertions`, before the first optimizer and after each one. A violation fails immediately with the operator, the offending column(s) by name, the columns that were available, and the optimizer that produced the plan:

```
SExpr column scope violation in Filter: references [1 (b)] which no input produces;
available columns: [0 (a), 2 (c)] (after optimizer `RecursiveRuleOptimizer[...]`)
```

## Design

For every node, the columns referenced by its scalar expressions (`Operator::scalar_expr_iter`) must be a subset of:

- the output columns of its children,
- its own output columns when it is a leaf (a `Scan` references its columns in predicates),
- the enclosing scope: a correlated subquery embedded in a scalar expression is validated recursively with the enclosing node's available columns as ambient scope, and the right side of a `LATERAL` join gets the left outputs as ambient scope.

Plan conventions the validator understands rather than flags:

- a `Final` aggregate keeps the `Partial` aggregate's scalar items and reads the partial's *input* (looking through an `Exchange` in distributed plans);
- grouping sets produce `_grouping_id`, read by `grouping()`;
- `WindowGroup` evaluates its own scalar items before the window functions read them;
- a mark join converted to a semi join registers its marker as removed (`Metadata::is_removed_mark_index`), and the dead references left behind are tolerated, as `RuleEagerAggregation` already does.

## Two latent plan defects found by the validator

Running the `query`, `base`, `duckdb`, `crdb`, `tpch` and `mode/standalone` sqllogictest suites in debug mode against the validator flushed out two plans that referenced columns nothing produced. Both "worked" only because the physical plan builder prunes unused `EvalScalar` items:

1. `CacheScan` built for `LATERAL (VALUES ...)` reported an empty output column set although it produces the cached columns; the distinct `Aggregate` on top read them from nowhere. It now reports `cache_source.column_indices`.
2. Flattening a lateral `VALUES` projects every derived outer column as an identity `EvalScalar` item, but `construct_expression_scan` then prunes the cache columns the values do not use, leaving items like `a (#5) AS (#5)` over a child that no longer computes `#5`. Those items are now dropped when the scan is constructed.

Neither changes results; they make the plan honest so the invariant can be enforced.

## Tests

- [x] Unit Test
- [x] Logic Test
- [ ] Benchmark Test
- [ ] No Test - _Explain why_

- Unit tests for the validator (`column_scope_validator.rs`): accepts references produced by children, rejects a reference nothing produces (checks operator and column name in the message).
- Integration tests (`sql/tests/it/optimizer/column_scope.rs`): a bound plan whose `Scan` is mutated to drop a column that the `Filter` still references is rejected by `optimize_plan` with `column scope violation in Filter ... (b)`; correlated `EXISTS` with a join `ON`, `LATERAL VALUES`, and a scalar subquery in the select list are accepted.

title: fix: streaming mysql resultset
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://databend.rs/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

Currently, resultsets of MySQL handler are accumulated as a single data block in memory and then written back to the client.

If front-end users query a big table without limitation (by accident or intentionally), e.g. "select * from HUBGE_TABLE", the query node is likely to be killed by oom killer.

Therefore,  mysql handler SHOULD write back resultset in a streaming way:

- tweak `DFQueryResultWriter`
  write resultset back to the client in a streaming way  
- tweak `Procedure` interface
  adapt to the style of new-processor, so that procedure can scan data streamingly
-  tweak `system$fuse_snapshot`  and `system$fuse_segment`
  make them access snapshot history in a streaming way


---------

after these tweaks:

~~~
mysql> create table t as select * from numbers(1000000000);
mysql> select * from t;
~~~
memory usage of `databend-query` will not keep increasing.

NOTE:

by default, mysql client will keep all the resultset in memory before outputting them. 

`mysql -q ...` will let MySQL client output resultset streamingly (but ugly, since MySQL client can not figure out the best column width for printing, I guess)

-----------






@zhang2014, `InteractiveWorkerBase::exec_query` now returns a Stream (instead of a DataBlock), I am not sure if we should keep spawning a new task to construct the stream:

https://github.com/datafuselabs/databend/blob/1ab82f3a7eefd6d33074eb02693af6bde897532d/src/query/service/src/servers/mysql/mysql_interactive_worker.rs#L426-L460  
  

Fixes #issue

title: HTTP server: client disconnect should call `response.body?.cancel?.()`
body:
From the [spec](https://streams.spec.whatwg.org):

> Consumers also have the ability to cancel a readable stream, using its `cancel()` method. This indicates that the consumer has lost interest in the stream, and will immediately close the stream, throw away any queued chunks, and execute any cancellation mechanism of the underlying source.

When handling an incoming HTTP fetch event, when the client disconnects prematurely, perhaps it should `.cancel()` the response body stream, in addition to aborting `event.request.signal` (see #10829).

Example use case: I'm implementing a broadcaster that accepts multiple "event stream" connections and sends a message to all of them. Per Luca's [suggestion](https://github.com/denoland/deno_std/issues/950#issuecomment-853707043), it's done by responding (to each incoming `FetchEvent`) with a `ReadableStream` body, storing its controller / writer in the broadcaster. When a client disconnects, it should immediately call `.cancel()` on the response body stream, which allows the broadcaster to remove the write handle. Currently this doesn't seem to work.

Before any decision can be made, we should check how it's done in service workers. I'm not actually sure.

fix(ext/node): handle partial writes to process.stdout/stderr
body:
## Summary

- Fix silent data truncation when piping >64KB through `process.stdout` in Node compat mode
- The `_write` handler in `createWritableStdioStream` discarded the return value of `writer.writeSync()`, assuming all bytes were always written. When stdout is a pipe and the OS buffer is near capacity (~64KB), `writeSync` returns a short count and the remaining bytes were silently lost.
- The fix loops on partial writes until the entire buffer is flushed.

Closes #26784

## Test plan

- Added `stdoutPipePartialWriteNotTruncated`: verifies `fs.createReadStream().pipe(process.stdout)` with >64KB does not truncate
- Added `stdoutWriteMultipleChunksNotTruncated`: verifies multiple `process.stdout.write()` calls totaling >64KB are not lost
- `cargo test unit_node::child_process_test`

title: fix(ext/web): fix DecompressionStream failing on valid zlib data
body:
## Summary

`DecompressionStream("deflate")` was failing with `TypeError: failed to
write whole buffer` on valid zlib-compressed data that Node.js
decompresses fine.

**Root cause:** flate2's write-based decoders (`ZlibDecoder<W>`,
`DeflateDecoder<W>`, `GzDecoder<W>`) return `Ok(0)` from `write()`
when the compressed stream ends (zlib footer/end marker reached) but
there are still input bytes remaining (e.g., trailing data or padding).
`write_all()` treats `Ok(0)` as a `WriteZero` error and fails.

**Fix:** Use a custom `write_all_allowing_partial()` for all decoder
variants that stops gracefully when `write()` returns `Ok(0)` instead
of erroring. Encoders continue to use `write_all()` since they should
always consume all input.

Closes #29829

## Test plan
- [x] All 3 test files from the issue decompress correctly (1108, 2301, 6703 bytes)
- [x] `cargo test -p deno_web` passes
- [x] Node.js produces identical output

title: Deno throws unhandled exception, when streams used through H3 webserver are closed by client
body:
Version: deno 2.7.11

Originally, I wanted to run a Nuxt App on Deno and utilize both Deno KV and server-sent events to realize some real-time update capabilities. When implementing this functionality, I noticed that my webserver would crash, anytime a client closes the stream.
I tried to narrow the error down and found, that somehow the cancellation of H3 events, while using streams is not properly handled and results in an unhandled exception, that crashes the H3 server.
When executing the same code on node (in my case node v25.7.0), no exception is thrown on client disconnects.

Here is a full reproduction repo: [reproduction scenario](https://github.com/dyeske61283/repro-sse-with-h3-on-deno-bug)

I did not manage to find deeper details on what causes this, but here is the error stack trace I get:

perf(libs/core): drop libuv-style partial-read break to fix node:http p99
body:
## Summary

`poll_tcp_handle`'s read loop in `uv_compat` matches libuv's `uv__read` by breaking on partial reads (`n < buf.len`) to skip the predicted-EAGAIN syscall. That works for libuv's epoll loop, but it interacts badly with tokio: tokio's `TcpStream` readiness is edge-triggered and the internal "readable" bit is cleared only when `try_read` returns `WouldBlock`. Breaking on a partial read leaves the bit armed; the re-register block at the end of the function then sees `poll_read_ready == Ready` and `mark_ready()` puts the handle right back on the loop's ready queue and wakes `loop_waker`.

Under sustained HTTP keep-alive load with small responses every read is partial, so every tick re-queues every active connection. Tokio's current_thread runtime sees the deno task continuously awoken and never yields to its reactor (controlled by `event_interval`, default 61). New TCP readiness from the kernel piles up undelivered, and each connection waits a full event_interval window before its next request is processed.

The fix is to keep looping until `try_read` actually returns `WouldBlock`. That costs one extra `recv()` syscall when the read fully drains the socket buffer, but the syscall returns `WouldBlock`, clears tokio's readiness bit, and the handle drops out of the ready queue cleanly so the reactor is free to deliver fresh wakes.

This was easy to confirm with `DENO_TOKIO_EVENT_INTERVAL=1`, which forces tokio to check the reactor every poll and made p99 drop from 33 ms to 3 ms even without the source change.

## Reproducer

\`\`\`js
// server.mjs
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? "8004");

createServer((_req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/plain" });
  res.end("Hello, World!");
}).listen(port, "127.0.0.1");
\`\`\`

\`\`\`
oha -c 100 -z 20s --no-tui http://127.0.0.1:8004/
\`\`\`

## Results (release-lite, 100 connections, 20 s)

|        | node     | deno before | deno after |
| ------ | -------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| p50    | 1.26 ms  | 0.96 ms     | 1.58 ms    |
| p99    | 2.56 ms  | 33.4 ms     | 3.14 ms    |
| p99.9  | 4.26 ms  | 60.7 ms     | 6.34 ms    |
| p99.99 | 7.28 ms  | 68.0 ms     | 8.28 ms    |

\`Deno.serve\` p99 is unchanged at 1.31 ms (no regression on the hyper path).

## Test plan

- [x] Bench `node:http` hello-world at `c=100`, confirm p99 drops from ~30 ms to ~3 ms
- [x] Bench `Deno.serve` hello-world at `c=100`, confirm no regression
- [x] CI green

title: fix(jupyter): keep kernel alive across transient peer disconnects
body:
## Summary

When a Jupyter client briefly disconnects between sending a request and the kernel sending its reply, `KernelShellConnection::send` fails with `ZmqError::Other("Destination client not found by identity")` (see [zmq.rs router.rs](https://github.com/zeromq/zmq.rs/blob/v0.5.0/src/router.rs#L100)). That error propagated through `handle_shell_message` and `handle_shell` via `?`, ending the spawned shell task. From the user's perspective, the kernel just hangs — no future shell request gets a reply. The same hang could happen on the control channel and when publishing iopub status/output if a subscriber dropped briefly. This matches the symptoms described in #20542 where "Client disconnected PeerIdentity(…)" is logged and the kernel stops responding.

- Make `handle_shell` and `handle_control` resilient: read errors and per-message handler errors are logged and the loop continues so the kernel keeps accepting requests. The peer will re-issue the request after reconnecting.
- Make `send_iopub` swallow transport errors. IoPub is a fire-and-forget broadcast and its failures must not abort the shell-reply path the client is waiting on.
- Harden the stdin and heartbeat loops the same way; the heartbeat now yields on errors to avoid a tight spin if the socket is in a bad state.

Refactored `handle_control`'s message handling into a small `handle_control_message` helper so its errors can be caught per-message without losing the existing dispatch logic.

Fixes #20542.

Closes denoland/orchid#298

## Test plan

- [ ] `cargo check --bin deno` (passes locally)
- [ ] `./tools/lint.js` (passes locally)
- [ ] `./tools/format.js` (no diff)
- [ ] Manual: start `deno jupyter --kernel` from a Jupyter frontend, verify the kernel survives the first-launch disconnect that previously caused it to hang

title: perf(ext/http): coalesce chunked response writes into a single write
body:
## Summary

`Deno.serve` responses whose body is a `ReadableStream` (sent `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`) regressed in throughput when the HTTP/1 layer was rewritten: the chunked path emits the head, each body chunk, and the terminating `0\r\n\r\n` as **three separate `write` syscalls**, where it previously coalesced them into one. The fixed/`Content-Length` path was unaffected (it already coalesces head+body into a single write), so the regression is specific to streamed/chunked responses — which is what shows up as "streaming got slower" in the runtime benchmarks (a header-mutating Hono middleware re-emits the response as a `ReadableStream`, so it rides this path).

Measured with a `write`/`sendto` interposer, 30k requests, 100-byte body:

| path | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| chunked (`ReadableStream`) | **3 sendto/req** | **1 sendto/req** |
| fixed (`Content-Length`) | 1 sendto/req | 1 sendto/req |

## Fix

Buffer a chunked response into the connection's existing per-request scratch buffer (`SharedScratch::write_buf`) and flush it once, instead of writing each piece straight to the socket:

- `poll_start_chunked_response_with` leaves the head in `write_buf` (deferred) for `Chunked` responses. `NoBody` / `CloseDelimited` (HTTP/1.0) still flush the head immediately, since they have no chunk framing to coalesce behind.
- `poll_write_response_chunk_with` appends each chunk's framing to `write_buf`, flushing only once it crosses `CHUNKED_FLUSH_THRESHOLD` (64 KiB) so memory stays bounded for large/long-lived bodies.
- `poll_finish_response_with` appends the terminator, flushes once, then shrinks `write_buf` back to its default capacity so a connection that served one large response doesn't retain an oversized buffer.
- The streaming drivers flush the buffer when the body source has nothing ready (`Poll::Pending`), so incremental/SSE responses are still delivered promptly; only chunks that are available synchronously coalesce.

No new per-connection allocation — it reuses the buffer that already exists for building response frames.

## Results

`oha -c 100 --disable-compression`, `--profile=release-lite`, same build for both columns:

| | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| chunked stream rps | 75,643 | **102,024** (+35%) |
| fixed rps | ~145k | ~145k (unchanged) |
| stream RSS @ 400 rps | 60 MB | 60 MB (unchanged) |

## Tests

- `deno_http_h1` unit tests (which assert byte-exact chunked output, including partial/fragmented writes and trailers) pass.
- `unit::serve_test` and `unit::http_test` pass.

title: feat(lint): type-aware linting via tsgolint
body:
This adds type-aware lint rules (no-floating-promises and friends) to
`deno lint`. Type-aware rules need TypeScript type information, which
deno_lint on its own does not have, so the rules are produced by
tsgolint, the Go binary (built on typescript-go) that the
typescript-eslint / oxc projects use for the same purpose.

Rather than running tsgolint through oxlint, Deno drives it directly and
stays the host: file discovery, configuration, output formatting and the
`// deno-lint-ignore` directive all remain owned by Deno. tsgolint is run
once over the whole batch of files (it builds one TypeScript program per
tsconfig, so per-file invocation would be far too slow), and its
diagnostics are returned through deno_lint's existing external-linter
path. That means `// deno-lint-ignore`, `ban-unused-ignore` and
diagnostic sorting apply to type-aware diagnostics for free, with no
separate suppression logic.

Type-aware linting runs as part of `deno lint` by default. The tsgolint
binary is downloaded automatically: on first use the platform binary is
fetched from npm (`@oxlint-tsgolint/<platform>`) into `DENO_DIR` and
cached for subsequent runs, exactly the way `deno bundle` fetches
esbuild. The download is installed atomically (copy to a temp file, then
rename into place) so concurrent `deno lint` processes never execute a
half-written binary. Setting `DENO_TSGOLINT_BIN` overrides the resolved
path with an explicit binary.

Obtaining the binary is best-effort and never fails the lint: on a
platform with no tsgolint binary it is skipped quietly, and if the
download fails Deno warns and continues with the regular (non-type-aware)
lint. `deno lint --no-type` turns type-aware linting off entirely (and
skips the download).

tsgolint's headless protocol has no field for an explicit tsconfig or
inline compiler options; it discovers a `tsconfig.json` by walking up
from each file, and any file without one is still linted under a built-in
"inferred project" (ESNext + bundler resolution + strict null checks).
So type-aware linting works out of the box for Deno projects that only
have a `deno.json`. Feeding Deno's own compiler options through to
tsgolint, autofix pass-through (`deno lint --fix`) and LSP wiring are
intended as follow-ups.

title: fix(ext/node): apply backpressure to http2 stream writes
body:
## Summary

- keep the JS `WriteWrap` in a per-stream queue and complete it only once nghttp2 has framed its bytes, so `Http2Stream.write()` reports backpressure
- cancel queued writes with `ECANCELED` when a stream is destroyed

## Motivation

Node-compatible HTTP/2 writes completed synchronously even when nghttp2 flow control prevented pending DATA from draining, so a stream that kept producing could accumulate arbitrary native pending data.

This PR originally capped that at 16 MiB per stream and failed further writes with `ENOBUFS`. As @bartlomieju [pointed out](https://github.com/denoland/deno/pull/36044#pullrequestreview-3928820676), that treats the symptom: it diverges from Node (which never raises `ENOBUFS` here) and turns unbounded growth into a hard error for a legitimate producer. The real bug is that Deno completes these writes synchronously and so never signals backpressure. This PR does the "right long-term fix" from that review instead.

## Approach

Mirror Node's `src/node_http2.cc`:

- `Http2Stream::DoWrite` hands the `WriteWrap` to the stream's queue and returns without completing it, so the write is asynchronous (`kLastWriteWasAsync = 1`).
- `Http2Session::ClearOutgoing` completes the wraps once the bytes have been framed.

`writeBuffer` / `writeUtf8String` now keep the `WriteWrap` in a per-stream queue keyed by a cumulative byte offset, and its `oncomplete` runs when nghttp2 has framed those bytes — which only happens as the peer's flow-control window allows. `writableLength` therefore stays up while the window is shut, `write()` returns false, and the producer waits for `'drain'`.

A well-behaved producer now bounds `pending_data` at the stream's `highWaterMark`; one that ignores backpressure buffers exactly as it would on Node. No cap, no `ENOBUFS`.

Details worth flagging for review:

- The nghttp2 callbacks that drain `pending_data` must not re-enter JS, so completions are parked on the session and flushed by `send_pending_data` once `mem_send` is done — the same placement as `ClearOutgoing`. Both transports are covered: the libuv `consume_stream` path and the JS `getOutgoingChunk`/`sendPending` path.
- Queued writes are failed with `UV_ECANCELED` on stream destroy, as `Http2Stream::Destroy` does, so a producer waiting on a write callback isn't left hanging.
- Zero-length writes contribute no bytes for the data provider to drain, so they complete as soon as everything queued ahead of them has been framed. Without this `res.write('')` stalls the Writable (caught by `test-http2-res-writable-properties.js`).

## Validation

- `sequential/test-http2-large-file.js` **stays enabled and passes**. The earlier cap forced it to be disabled; it chains 100 MB of 1 MB writes through the write callback, which is exactly the pattern backpressure is meant to pace.
- http2 `node_compat` is at parity with `main`: `parallel::test-http2` 4 failures on both (`compat-write-information`, `compat-write-early-hints-invalid-header`, `client-session-close-before-stream-close`, `session-cleanup-on-nghttp2-goaway`), `sequential::test-http2` 3 failures on both (`timeout-large-write`, `max-session-memory`, `timeout-large-write-file`). All pre-existing.
- New `tests/unit_node/http2_test.ts` case asserts a write stays outstanding while the peer isn't reading and completes once it resumes. Verified it fails without this change (restoring synchronous completion trips `write completed even though the peer never read`).
- `cargo test --test unit_node http2`, `cargo test -p deno_node --lib`, `./tools/format.js`, `./tools/lint.js`.

title: `deno bundle` silently deadlocks with its esbuild service under CPU starvation (both at 0% CPU forever)
body:
> [!NOTE]
> Generated with Fable 5 as part of troubleshooting hanging builds

Version: Deno 2.9.1 (also inspected 2.9.4 — no relevant change), esbuild 0.25.5, `esbuild_client` 0.7.1 (`src/lib.rs` identical on its `main` as of `a49e43d1`)

## Symptom

A `deno bundle` invocation and the esbuild service child it spawns both drop to **0% CPU and stay there indefinitely**. Nothing is printed, neither process exits, and the state never resolves on its own (observed wedges of 33+ minutes locally and 60–74 minutes on CI before being killed).

Command that wedges (a browser bundle of ~2,500 modules):

```
deno bundle --platform=browser --minify --packages=bundle \
  --node-modules-dir=manual --no-remote --frozen \
  --output out.js packages/web/client/main.tsx
```

It only happens under concurrent load: our CI job that runs a full test battery concurrently on 4 vCPU hit it on 2 of 2 runs (`ubuntu-latest`); a 10-core macOS arm64 machine hits it in roughly 1 in 4 battery runs. The same suite run standalone has never wedged.

## Analysis: a two-channel deadlock in `esbuild_client`'s protocol loop

`protocol_task` (esbuild_client `src/lib.rs`) is a single `tokio::select!` loop that both writes the service's stdin and reads its stdout, and it forwards each decoded incoming packet with `packet_tx.send(packet).await` — a **bounded mpsc (capacity 100)** — *inside the read arm* (lib.rs:121 via `handle_read`). While that send is parked, the loop neither reads stdout nor drains `response_rx`.

The packet-handler task drains `packet_rx`. `on-resolve`/`on-load` hooks are spawned as separate tasks, but **`ping` and `on-start` responses are sent inline** with `response_tx.send().await` (lib.rs:712–720, 750–760) — the other bounded mpsc (capacity 100), which only `protocol_task` drains.

Every module load round-trips through the plugin hooks, and `--ping` keepalives arrive periodically. The client runs on a single-threaded runtime while the service is a multi-threaded Go process that keeps producing while the client is off-CPU. Under scheduler starvation the incoming flood backs both channels up, and the system can reach:

- `protocol_task` parked in `packet_tx.send().await` → needs the handler to drain;
- the handler parked in `response_tx.send().await` for a ping/on-start response → needs `protocol_task` to drain.

Neither can proceed; the spawned hook tasks pile up parked on the same full `response_tx`. The service ends up blocked writing its stdout (pipe full) with its goroutines waiting for hook responses that will never be written. There is no timeout anywhere in the protocol, so the deadlock is silent and permanent.

## Evidence from a live wedge (macOS arm64)

Parent `deno bundle` and its own `esbuild-darwin-arm64 --service=0.25.5 --ping` child, both 0.0% CPU for 15+ minutes:

- `sample` of the deno process: main thread in `kevent` (event loop idle), V8 workers in `psynch_cvwait`;
- `sample` of esbuild: every thread in `psynch_cvwait` — all goroutines parked;
- no read/write syscall in flight on either side;
- `lsof` shows the pair's stdio pipes intact, and exactly **one** esbuild service existed on the machine (the stuck bundle's own child), ruling out interference from a stale service.

Happy to attach the full `sample`/`lsof` captures.

## Reproduction notes

No minimal reproducer yet — the trigger is genuine scheduler starvation. Reliable recipe: repeatedly run a large `deno bundle` concurrently with a load that oversubscribes all cores (for us: a test battery of ~9 concurrent commands). Pure CPU-spinner load against an un-niced bundle did not reproduce it in ~200 attempts, and SIGSTOP/SIGCONT duty-cycling the whole deno process did not either (stopping all of deno also gates the service's flood through pipe backpressure) — the wedged instances we caught were running niced (`SN`) alongside a busy machine, i.e. asymmetric starvation of the client while its service keeps producing.

perf(ext/node): write UTF-16LE buffers with V8
body:
Fixes #36803.

### What and why

`Buffer.from(text, "utf16le")` currently converts the string through a JS per-code-unit loop into a temporary Uint8Array, then copies that into the Buffer. This is slower than a straightforward DataView loop on medium/large inputs.

This change adds a native op using V8's UTF-16 string write API and routes the normal `ucs2Write` path through it:

- Aligned little-endian destinations are written directly, avoiding the temporary allocation and copy.
- Unaligned destinations use a bounded 2 KiB stack buffer. The same fallback emits little-endian bytes on big-endian targets.
- Raw UTF-16 code units are preserved, including lone surrogates and a surrogate pair split by a byte limit. There is no lossy UTF-8 intermediate.
- Writes stop at complete code units and respect the destination view and requested length. This also fixes writing a partial code unit with an odd byte limit: `Buffer.alloc(3).write("A", 0, 1, "utf16le")` now returns 0, matching Node.
- Non-standard direct-call arguments retain the existing JS fallback. The helper remains available for its other callers.

Related: #35182 also ports internal binding helpers to Rust. This PR is narrower: direct destination writes for Buffer UTF-16LE encoding, with focused compatibility tests and benchmarks. It is based on current main, not that branch.

### Benchmarks

Apple M2 Max, macOS ARM64, Deno 2.9.6 / V8 15.0.245.2-rusty. Baseline: `336da420f4343cbb1dcbd5eed9d075ff555ed6ee`. Both baseline and candidate were built locally with Rust 1.95.0 using the same `release-lite` profile, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`, and `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LITE_DEBUG=0`.

Ran the committed `tests/bench/buffer_utf16le.js` unchanged on both binaries, three times each, sequentially in alternating order (baseline/candidate, candidate/baseline, baseline/candidate), after builds/lint finished. Each value below is the **median of three Deno.bench run averages**, not a latency percentile. Sizes are UTF-16LE output bytes.

| Corpus | Output size | Before (µs) | After (µs) | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| ascii | 64 bytes | 0.489 | 0.104 | 4.7× |
| ascii | 4096 bytes | 15.227 | 0.610 | 25.0× |
| ascii | 65536 bytes | 233.401 | 2.401 | 97.2× |
| latin1 | 64 bytes | 0.490 | 0.103 | 4.7× |
| latin1 | 4096 bytes | 15.344 | 0.601 | 25.5× |
| latin1 | 65536 bytes | 232.680 | 2.411 | 96.5× |
| utf16 | 64 bytes | 0.487 | 0.102 | 4.8× |
| utf16 | 4096 bytes | 15.333 | 0.620 | 24.7× |
| utf16 | 65536 bytes | 232.900 | 2.584 | 90.1× |

For the 64 KiB mixed UTF-16 case:

- The DataView control stayed approximately flat: 78.684 → 79.207 µs.
- Aligned `Buffer.write` into a reused destination: 232.054 → 1.440 µs (~161×).
- Unaligned `Buffer.write`: 232.153 → 72.349 µs (~3.2×).
- The three `Buffer.from` run averages were 232.900 / 231.448 / 233.129 µs before and 2.554 / 2.584 / 2.657 µs after.

These are warm, encoding-only microbenchmarks, **not application-wide speedups**. Full output equality is checked before timing. Timed `Buffer.from` cases allocate output and consume a byte; write-only cases reuse a destination and consume the returned byte count. Performance for other string representations, architectures, and sizes may differ.

Reproduce on baseline and candidate binaries:

```sh
deno bench --no-check --json tests/bench/buffer_utf16le.js
```

- `cargo build --locked --profile release-lite -p test_server --bin test_server`
- `cargo test --locked --profile release-lite -p unit_node_tests --test unit_node -- buffer_test`

- `git diff --check`

title: Conn.write() order guaranteed?
body:
Trying to debug a problem in my application where I am queueing a number of writes to a connection. The writes in a benchmark type situation initiate writes of 8K or a few bytes more. In some cases to allow more liveliness, a smaller write (6 bytes) is inserted which will trigger data coming back on the read channel of the socket.

The module is not waiting for a pending write to complete before a new write is possibly initiated. I am noticing that on the remote server, it seems to be possible for a smaller write to interleave with a bigger write - this makes it so that a partial write from the 8K buffer is followed by the 6-byte sentinel. 

Is the order of the write promises guaranteed in any way? Documentation doesn't make any notices of this not being supported, so perhaps incorrectly assuming that multiple writes are not processed in the order they were scheduled.

My code is not reusing buffers.

title: Catch errors on file_server response.send. Fixes #5624
body:
This PR simply logs errors thrown from `response.send` to the console:

```
2020-06-13 21:13:28] "GET /large.txt HTTP/1.1" 200
Broken pipe (os error 32)
```

I'm not sure if this is actually useful info for users (at least not in the case of #5624). I quickly looked at python's `http.server`, Go's. `FileServer`, nginx and http-party/http-server, and none of them seem to log any info when the client closes connection early.

Is it worth considering changing the `server.ts` api to better communicate when the client closes the connection? (instead of throwing an os error on write). In node, `http.ClientRequest` sends a `close` event when the client disconnects, using `response.write` after that is actually allowed and does not throw an error (last part is also not ideal imho).

title: fix: atomically write files in $DENO_DIR
body: This tries to fix an issue where files in the $DENO_DIR could be in an undermined state, where they are empty, only half written, or otherwise not correct. This issue may arise when multiple Deno processes try to cache the same file simultaneously. We should also consider adding integrity hashes to the files, so we can check if they are are valid when reading them from $DENO_DIR.

title: feat(tonic-xds): implement xds resource cache with watch-based notifications
body:
## Motivation

Ref: #2444

Add XdsCache as the shared store between the xDS resource manager (writer) and Tower service layers (readers).

## Solution

The cache bridges the xDS resource manager (future PR) and the Tower service layers:

- **Route config**: single `watch` channel (1:1 LDS→RDS per gRPC A27 spec)
- **Clusters/Endpoints**: `WatchMap<T>` (keyed `DashMap` of watch channels, lazily
   initialized)
- **Readiness**: `Option` semantics — `None` = not ready, `Some` = ready.

Consumers use `rx.wait_for(|v| v.is_some())` to gate on resource availability, eliminating the need for a separate readiness tracking mechanism.

Consumers subscribe to notifications but own their own read-side state (e.g. the routing layer will maintain its own `ArcSwap` for lock-free per-request lookups).

## Next Steps

- **PR 4 — Endpoint management**: EDS diffing and `Change` stream generation from `EndpointsResource` updates
- **PR 5 — Resource manager**: `tokio::select!` loop over LDS→RDS→CDS→EDS watchers, writing into `XdsCache`
- **PR 6 — Builder wiring + E2E**: connect the resource manager and cache to the Tower service layers, replacing `todo!()` stubs

title: fix: make encode_item panic/error-safe so it never exposes uninitialized header bytes
body:
## Motivation

`encode_item` in `tonic/src/codec/encode.rs` reserves a 5-byte frame header via `buf.reserve(HEADER_SIZE)` and advances the buffer length over those bytes *before* the message payload is encoded. If encoding then fails, either by returning an error or by panicking inside a user-supplied `Encoder`/compression codec, the `BytesMut` is left with its length advanced over header bytes that were never written. Those bytes hold whatever was previously in the buffer's spare capacity. On the error path the frame is abandoned; on an unwinding panic that a caller catches (or that crosses a `catch_unwind` boundary in a surrounding runtime) the buffer can subsequently be observed with a partially-formed frame whose header is uninitialized leftover memory.

Closes #2720.

## Solution

Wrap the header reservation and payload encoding in a drop guard that records the buffer's original length up front and truncates back to it unless `encode_item` reaches its normal return. On the success path the guard is disarmed and the fully-framed buffer is preserved; on any early return or unwinding panic the guard's `Drop` restores the buffer to exactly the bytes that were present before the call, so no half-written frame or uninitialized header is ever left behind.

Regression tests cover the five relevant paths: successful framing (header + payload written), encoder error, `finish_encoding`/framing error raised late, encoder panic (buffer restored after unwinding), and compressed-encoder failure with the `gzip` feature enabled. `cargo test -p tonic codec::encode` passes with default features (4 tests) and with `--features gzip` (5 tests); `cargo fmt --check` and `git diff --check` are clean.

title: tonic/client: support immediate cancellation of streams without sending End-of-Stream
body:
## Motivation

Tonic's client streaming and bidirectional (bidi) streaming APIs do not currently support immediate request cancellation. Because outbound request streams are infallible, completing them automatically transmits a `DATA` frame with an `End-of-Stream (EOS)` flag, which signals a normal, graceful termination. An `RST_STREAM` frame is only sent by the client after the request stream terminates and the corresponding response stream is subsequently dropped. 

This delayed teardown creates a problem: the server may interpret the `EOS` flag as a graceful finish and process or commit incomplete payloads before it ever receives the `RST_STREAM` frame. To prevent potential data corruption, Tonic requires a mechanism to abort and tear down the HTTP/2 stream immediately without sending a misleading `EOS` flag.

## Solution

Introduce a paired `CancellationHandle` to coordinate immediate, client-side cancellation of outbound request streams.

### Core Changes

*   `CancellationHandle` (User-Facing): Users can create a handle by calling `request.cancellation_handle()`. Invoking `.cancel()` on this handle triggers an immediate, non-graceful abort.
*   The `CancellationHandle` wraps a `CancellationToken` which is extracted from the request extensions by Tonic's client dispatcher to actively track the cancellation state of the active stream.
* Immediate Abort in Encoder : `EncodeBody::poll_frame` actively checks the `CancellationListener`. If cancellation is flagged, it immediately returns an error mapped with `H2Reason::CANCEL`. This bypasses the empty `DATA` frame with `EOS` and immediately triggers an HTTP/2 level `RST_STREAM`.


## Alternative
Use the Encoder API to inject an error causing hyper to cancel the stream: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-rust/pull/2788

This seems like a mis-use of the codec API and causes the RST_STREAM code to be `internal`.

title: Deadlock with tokio 1.7.0
Avoid flushing h2 socket while holding stream locks
body:
# Avoid flushing h2 socket while holding stream locks

Related: #531

There is also an active broader draft refactor in #917. This PR is intentionally smaller: it targets the specific path discussed in #531 where `Streams::poll_complete` can hold stream/send-buffer locks while the codec flush path reaches the socket.

## Summary

This change splits HTTP/2 stream draining into two phases so the connection task no longer holds the shared stream-state and send-buffer mutexes while flushing or polling writes on the underlying socket.

Previously, `Streams::poll_complete` held `Inner` and `SendBuffer` locks while `Prioritize::poll_complete` could call into `Codec::poll_ready` / `Codec::flush`, which can reach `poll_write_buf` on the socket. Under high write concurrency on one HTTP/2 connection, stream producer tasks contend with the connection task while the connection task is doing I/O progress.

The new flow is:

- ensure codec/socket write readiness before taking stream locks
- lock stream state and buffer pending frames only while the codec has local buffer capacity
- release the locks
- flush the codec/socket
- briefly re-lock to reclaim partially/fully written DATA frames and requeue as needed

The patch also adds a targeted write-contention benchmark that sends many response body chunks concurrently over a single HTTP/2 connection. It can be run with:

```sh
H2_BENCH=write-contention cargo bench --bench main
```

The benchmark is configurable:

```sh
H2_WRITE_CONTENTION_STREAMS=512
H2_WRITE_CONTENTION_CHUNKS_PER_STREAM=128
H2_WRITE_CONTENTION_CHUNK_SIZE=16384
H2_WRITE_CONTENTION_WORKER_THREADS=4
```

## Benchmark

Run environment:

- WSL Ubuntu 24.04
- Rust 1.96.1 stable
- workload: 512 streams x 128 chunks x 16 KiB = 1 GiB over one HTTP/2 connection

Median elapsed time over 3 alternating runs per worker-thread count:

| Worker threads | Baseline median | Patched median | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 336 ms | 337 ms | roughly flat |
| 2 | 358 ms | 238 ms | 33.5% faster |
| 4 | 382 ms | 337 ms | 11.8% faster |
| 8 | 407 ms | 340 ms | 16.5% faster |

Median throughput:

| Worker threads | Baseline | Patched |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 3043 MiB/s | 3038 MiB/s |
| 2 | 2853 MiB/s | 4294 MiB/s |
| 4 | 2679 MiB/s | 3037 MiB/s |
| 8 | 2513 MiB/s | 3004 MiB/s |

The one-worker case is effectively flat, as expected: there is little cross-thread lock contention. The multi-worker runs show the intended effect.

## Testing

```sh
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo check
cargo test -p h2-tests reserved_capacity_assigned_in_multi_window_updates -- --exact --nocapture
cargo test -p h2-tests small_data_frames_reclaimed_before_buffering_next -- --exact
```

The new `small_data_frames_reclaimed_before_buffering_next` regression test fails on the pre-fix PR commit (`3a42547`) with the `in_flight_data_frame` assertion, and passes after reclaiming the DATA frame before buffering another frame.

The write-contention benchmark was run before/after this change in WSL Ubuntu 24.04. On this Windows machine, checking the benchmark target currently stops in the existing `tokio-rustls` dev-dependency chain because `aws-lc-sys` needs additional native build tools (`cmake`/NASM) before it reaches h2 code.

CMD cargo run --example broken-pipe --features full
```
2. Build the docker image: `docker build . -t broken-pipe`
3. Create some fake data: `head -c 5MB /dev/urandom > payload`
4. From one terminal: `docker run -it -p 44309:44309 broken-pipe`
5. From another terminal: `curl -v -Fdata=@payload http://127.0.0.1:44309/`

### Workaround:

Note that if the body of the request is used, the `Broken pipe` error is no longer encountered.
[If you modify the `broken-pipe` cargo example](https://github.com/mitchhentges/hyper/commit/30ce9f6f0b34f6a57ab9a3af3a62faad9783052b#diff-5f721ef6a99881030412f0b7f528124672f081ca3c1d14555bef13444b621e51R16-R17), you can work around the error.

title: Composable pool: coalesced Singleton waiters are canceled when the maker bounces to the fallback leg
body:
### Version

hyper-util:0.1.20

### Platform

macos aarch64

### Summary

## Summary

In hyper-util 0.1.20's composable pool layers (`hyper_util::client::pool::{negotiate, singleton}`), concurrent same-authority requests through the eager `Negotiate` stack coalesce on the `Singleton` upgrade leg. When the maker discovers the connection is not h2 and returns `UseOther` to bounce to the H1 fallback, its error path resets the Singleton state and drops the coalesced waiters' oneshot senders. Each waiter resolves `Err(SingletonError)` with source `"singleton connection canceled"` instead of obtaining a connection. Exactly one caller (the maker) succeeds; all other concurrent callers to that authority fail spuriously.

## Mechanism

1. `Negotiate::call` starts in `Eager` state and polls the upgrade (`Singleton`) leg first.
2. Concurrent calls to clones of the same `Negotiate` (sharing `Arc<Mutex<State>>`) coalesce in the `Singleton`: the first becomes the maker (`State::Making`), the rest become waiters holding `oneshot::Receiver`s, with their senders stored in the `Making` waiter `Vec`.
3. The maker's inner future finds the slot empty (no h2 negotiation occurred) and returns `Err(UseOther)`.
4. In `SingletonFuture`, the maker's `Driving` arm hits the error branch (`singleton.rs:243-250`): it replaces the shared state with `State::Empty`, dropping the `State::Making(waiters)` value and thereby every waiter sender.
5. Each waiter's `Waiting` arm polls its `oneshot::Receiver`, which resolves `Err(Canceled)`, and returns `Err(SingletonError(Canceled.into()))` (`singleton.rs:255`).
6. The maker's `UseOther` propagates up to its own `Negotiate`, which bounces to the fallback leg and succeeds. The waiters have no equivalent path and are orphaned.

`DitchGuard::drop` resets state the same way when the maker future is dropped or cancelled before resolving (the path exercised by the existing `cancel_driver_cancels_all` test).

## Context

`singleton.rs` test `cancel_driver_cancels_all` currently asserts this cancel behavior and carries a `// TODO: this should be able to be improved with a cooperative baton refactor` comment, indicating the orphaning is acknowledged.

## Environment

- hyper-util 0.1.20 (crates.io release)
- Features: `client`, `client-pool`
- `tokio` `multi_thread` runtime (deterministic; does not surface on `current_thread`)


### Code Sample

```rust
## Reproduction

Minimal standalone crate: https://github.com/aajtodd/repro-hyper-util-singleton-cancel


cargo test -- --nocapture


Observed:


BUG REPRODUCED: 1/8 succeeded, 7/8 got SingletonError(Canceled)


The repro builds an eager `negotiate` stack with a `Singleton` upgrade leg, an identity fallback leg, and an `inspect` closure that always reports not-h2. It readies N clones of the negotiate service, calls all N synchronously, then polls the returned futures together on a `multi_thread` runtime.
```

### Expected Behavior

Expected: every coalesced caller obtains a connection — either the maker's established connection or its own via the fallback leg.


### Actual Behavior

Observed: the maker succeeds; all coalesced waiters resolve `Err(SingletonError)` with source `"singleton connection canceled"`.

Impact: any consumer issuing concurrent requests to the same authority through the composable pool with the eager negotiate stack sees most concurrent same-authority requests fail spuriously under load rather than reusing or falling back.

Additionally there is no typed error to key off of for this. 

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: Scrapers do not work in OSS
Configuration option to ignore infinity value metrics
body:
__Proposal:__
I'd like to have an InfluxDB config option that lets influxDB fully ignore points with +-infinity value. 

__Current behavior:__
Currently, InfluxDB can't handle float/double infinity values. There is an ongoing work to implement that functionality https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/issues/4089 , https://github.com/influxdata/flux/issues/1040 , but this seems to be rather complicated and is an option issue since almost 4 years. 

When I currently send an infinity double value to InfluxDB (e.g. via InfluxDB java client), an unparseable error is returned (invalid number) and the point is not stored. When sending a batch, I receive a partial write error. 

__Desired behavior:__
I'd like to have a config option like "IGNORE_INFINITY_VALUES" which when turned on, just don't writes those points without throwing an exception. When not set (default), the current behavior with throwing an exception should be running. 

__Alternatives considered:__
1. Implement proper handling for +-infinity values. This helps InfluxDB to become more compliant with prometheus and extends functinality. However, by the time the ticket is already opened, it lets me think that this will take much more time and is much harder to implement, as support for those values needs to be carefully implemented in all influxDB functions (How do agregations work, etc.).

2. Extend InfluxDB client functionality to prefilter infinity values and don't send them to InfluxDB at all. (Also via a config option). This is a solution suggested by Flink: https://github.com/apache/flink/pull/8513 However, you don't always have full control over all clients, which lets me think that an option within InfluxDB would solve the problem in a better way. More about this point in the usecase. 

__Use case:__
I currently try to setup InfluxDB as monitoring database for a big data application. I push metrics from Apache Flink, Apache Spark, various microservices and telegraf (Apache Solr, Apache Kafka, system metrics, Jolokia, influxdb_listener, statsd). 

A lot of metric components, which I can't influence directly, report infinity values, especially Apache Kafka, but also Apache Flink itself. Within my Flink application, I receive like 20 warnings/errors every 10 seconds, which pollutes my logs in an unreadable way. ( https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/FLINK-12579 ).

The microservices I monitor report a prometheus compatible /metrics endpoint due to historic reasons. They also report inifinty values regularly which also pollutes the telegraf logs with warnings due to telegraf being responsible to scrape prometheus and push to InfluxDB. 

In the end, InfluxDB can't handle infinity values right now and won't store them either way. In the monitoring setup (Which is a quite common InfluxDB usage purpose), the best thing to do is also to ignore those values as long as InfluxDB can't treat them. So I'm well aware in my situation, that I can't have infinity values and don't want all my logs to be polluted with warnings/errors especially for components I don't have in my control (telegraf, Flink).

title: Improve semantics of the `influxdb3 write` CLI for partial write behaviour
body:
### Problem statement

The semantics of the `influxdb3 write` CLI are confusing with respect to the `--accept-partial` flag. That there is an `--accept-partial` flag implies that the default behaviour is to _not_ accept partial writes.

However, the default behaviour _is_ to accept partial writes, so when the `--accept-partial` arg is not provided, partial writes _will_ be accepted and this can be confusing for users.

### Proposed solution

Replace the `--accept-partial` flag with the following: `--deny-partial-writes`, whose behaviour is as follows:
* Is a flag, i.e., does not require a `true` or `false` to be passed as an argument
* When included as a flag in the CLI command, passes `accept_partial: false` in the API request to make the write.
* Update the CLI docs to describe this new behaviour
* Add tests to verify the new behaviour in the [`cli` test suite](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/blob/624e67e95cdb84bced121ba8b9ac69f37889c7bd/influxdb3/tests/server/cli.rs)

The default behaviour, as is the case in the underlying `/api/v3/write_lp` API is to accept partial writes.

### Alternatives considered

N/A

### Additional context

The CLI is implemented here: https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/blob/624e67e95cdb84bced121ba8b9ac69f37889c7bd/influxdb3/src/commands/write.rs#L34-L38

Slack thread ([link](https://influxdata.slack.com/archives/C084G9LR2HL/p1736791230954149?thread_ts=1736730381.381219&cid=C084G9LR2HL)).

title: partial write of line protocol occurred with no detail on which line is rejected
body:
# Summary:
We are running a monitoring pipeline where customer-side Telegraf agents send line protocol data to a central Telegraf bastion server, which forwards to InfluxDB 2. This setup has been working without any issues.
We recently set up a parallel InfluxDB 3 Core pipeline: customer-side Telegraf agents now send data to both the existing bastion (for InfluxDB 2) and a new OCI load balancer (weighted round robin) in front of two new Telegraf bastion servers, which forward to InfluxDB 3 Core via the influxdb_v3 output plugin.
The client-side Telegraf agents show no errors. Data is visible and queryable in Grafana on both pipelines. However, the new InfluxDB 3 Core bastions consistently produce partial write of line protocol occurred errors every minute.
The core issue is not the error itself but the lack of detail in the response — InfluxDB 2 logged the offending line directly, making it straightforward to diagnose. InfluxDB 3 Core returns only a generic message with no indication of which line, field, or measurement caused the rejection.

1. Set up Telegraf 1.38.4 with influxdb_v2_listener input and influxdb_v3 output
2. Send line protocol data from customer-side Telegraf agents via a load balancer to the bastion Telegraf instances
3. Bastion Telegraf forwards data to InfluxDB 3 Core using influxdb_v3 output plugin
4. Observe 400 Bad Request errors in Telegraf logs every minute

Write succeeds, or if rejected, the error response contains the specific line(s) that failed parsing so the client can identify and fix the issue.
Actual behaviour:
InfluxDB 3 Core returns 400 Bad Request with only partial write of line protocol occurred — no line number, no field name, no further detail. Some lines in the batch are written successfully, others are silently dropped. The Telegraf log shows:

title: InfluxDB should do a partial write on mismatched type errors
body:
### Bug report

When a point is written with a mismatched type, it is handled differently than a malformed point. 

With a malformed point, a partial write is done of all well-formed points that are provided in the batch, and a "partial write" error is returned.

With a mismatched point, no points are written and a "mismatched type" error is returned.

both cases return http status code 400.

I think that we should treat mismatched types the same as malformed points, performing a partial write of the well-formed and valid points in the batch.

__System info:__ [Include InfluxDB version, operating system name, and other relevant details]

InfluxDB master, commit 8c2cfd1 (master some ways after 1.1.0)

__Steps to reproduce:__

1. write a metric called `test` as a float:
```
curl -i "http://localhost:8086/write?db=telegraf" --data-binary "test value=1"
```
2. write a batch of two metrics, first with `test` as an integer and then a new metric called `test2`:
```
curl -i "http://localhost:8086/write?db=telegraf" --data-binary "test value=1i
test2 value=1
"
```
3. Observe that the `test2` metric does not get created, even though it is valid.
4. Now write a batch of two metrics, first with `test` completely malformed and then a new metric called `test2`:
```
curl -i "http://localhost:8086/write?db=telegraf" --data-binary "test value
test2 value=1
"
```
5. Now observe that `test2` does get created, though a 400 status code and "partial write" is still returned.

Not sure, but this might be a dupe of #4856

title: Add "integral" function to InfluxQL
body:
The integral function is an aggregator that returns the area under the curve. The integral function also accepts an optional second argument as a time duration to determine the unit of the returned values. The default time duration is `1s` (similar to `derivative()`).

The area under the curve can also be grouped into buckets, but integral acts slightly differently than other aggregates. First, integral does not support `FILL()` and will ignore any `FILL()` function on the query. Second, the area under the curve will automatically interpolate the area under the curve using a point in the next interval if it exists. So if you group every 20 seconds and record metrics every 10 seconds, the point at 20 seconds will be used to find the area under the curve between 10s and 20s. If you record a point every 15 seconds and group every 20 seconds, then the point at 30 seconds will be used to interpolate the area under the curve between 15 and 20 seconds and the point at 15 seconds will be used to interpolate the area under the curve between 20 and 30 seconds.

Unlike `derivative()`, you cannot use a function inside of `integral()`. If you wish to perform a query like that, subqueries are the easiest way.

If there are multiple points at the same time, this is considered a vertical line. Vertical lines do not add anything to the area under the curve, but they do change the line so the next point will be calculated based on the last point at a timestamp rather than just being completely ignored. This behavior differs from the traditional behavior of just ignoring duplicate points in a stream.

Example queries:

```
SELECT integral(value) FROM cpu
SELECT integral(value, 1m) FROM cpu
SELECT integral(value) FROM cpu GROUP BY time(20s)
SELECT integral(value, 1m) FROM cpu GROUP BY time(20s)
SELECT integral(mean) FROM (SELECT mean(value) FROM cpu GROUP BY time(10s)) GROUP BY time(1m)
```

title: Close TSMReaders from FileStore.Close after releasing FileStore mutex
body:
More work to properly fix #9786

Confirmed that `DROP SHARD X` works properly when the service is loaded with 10 concurrent select sum(f) style queries. Files are deleted, and file descriptors are closed. So #9792 is WAI.

Looking at RP more closely:

- created a 1 minute RP (one-line local code modification)
- set 10 second RP check interval (config file setting)
- loaded the service with the same queries mentioned above
- watched the oldest shard (89) disappear from `SHOW SHARDS`
- shard 89's files never deleted from the filesystem
- shard 89's file descriptors never closed
- waited 30 minutes, then killed the query load

Discovered that a RP event and exactly one query were deadlocked. RP was blocking here:
```
// Close closes the TSMReader.
func (t *TSMReader) Close() error {
	t.refsWG.Wait()  // blocked forever
```

Hung query discovered here (duration reached as high as 1h, never returned):
```
> show queries
qid  query                   database duration status
---  -----                   -------- -------- ------
8216 SHOW QUERIES            rain     38µs     running
8158 SELECT sum(rand) FROM m rain     1m10s    killed
```

The deadlock happens because
1. the RP event holds the FileStore mutex (write) while waiting for a TSMReader WaitGroup
2. a query waits for the FileStore mutex (read) in order to done the TSMReader WaitGroup

This change closes FileStore (clears the object members so that it looks closed) under write lock **then releases the write lock** before closing the underlying files.

To test this change:
- set 1 minute RP
- write random points with 100k cardinality, in an infinite loop
- `select sum(field) from m` in 5 concurrent infinite loops
- observe RP deadlocks and hung queries

Before this change, the test fails within 1-3 RP cycles, even deadlocking 3 of 5 queries in one case. After the change, the test has not failed after 200 RP cycles (about 2.5 hours).

title: [multistream-select] Reduce roundtrips in protocol negotiation.
body:
## Overview & Motivation

This is another attempt at https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/issues/659, superseding https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/pull/1121 and sitting on top of https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/pull/1203. The following are the main conceptual changes:

  1. The multistream-select header is always sent together with the first negotiation message.

  2. Enable 0-RTT: If the dialer only supports a single protocol, it can send protocol data (e.g. the actual application request) together with the multistream-select header and protocol proposal. Similarly, if the listener supports a proposed protocol, it can send protocol data (e.g. the actual application response) together with the multistream-select header and protocol confirmation.
    
  3. In general, the dialer "settles on" an expected protocol as soon as it runs out of alternatives. Furthermore, both dialer and listener do not immediately flush the final protocol confirmation, allowing it to be sent together with application protocol data. Attempts to read from an incompletely negotiated I/O stream implicitly flushes any pending data.
    
  4. A clean / graceful shutdown of an I/O stream always tries to complete protocol negotiation, so even if a request does not expect a response, as long as the I/O stream is shut down cleanly, an error will occur if the remote did not support the expected protocol after all.

  5. If desired in specific cases, it is possible to explicitly wait for full completion of the negotiation before sending or receiving data by waiting on the future returned by `Negotiated::complete()`.

Overall, the hope is that this especially improves the situation for the substream-per-request scenario.
 
The public API of multistream-select changed slightly, requiring both `AsyncRead` and `AsyncWrite` bounds for async reading and writing due to the implicit buffering and "lazy" negotiation. The error types have also been changed, but they were not previously fully exported anyway.
    
This implementation comes with some general refactoring and simplifications and some more tests, e.g. there was an edge case relating to a possible ambiguity when parsing multistream-select protocol messages.

## Examples

### 0-RTT Negotiation

Logs of a 0-RTT negotiation; The dialer supports a single protocol also supported by the listener:
```
[2019-07-26T09:06:24Z DEBUG multistream_select::dialer_select] Dialer: Proposed protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:06:24Z DEBUG multistream_select::dialer_select] Dialer: Expecting proposed protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:06:24Z DEBUG multistream_select::listener_select] Listener: confirming protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:06:24Z DEBUG multistream_select::listener_select] Listener: sent confirmed protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:06:24Z DEBUG multistream_select::negotiated] Negotiated: Received confirmation for protocol: /proto2
```


A corresponding packet exchange excerpt (Wireshark) of 0-RTT negotiation where `ping` and `pong` are "application protocol data" and e:
```
> /multistream/1.0.0
> /proto2
> ping
< /multistream/1.0.0
< /proto2
< pong
```
### Other Examples

Logs from a 1-RTT negotiation;  The dialer supports two protocols, the second of which is supported by the listener.
```
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::dialer_select] Dialer: Proposed protocol: /proto3
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::listener_select] Listener: rejecting protocol: /proto3
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::dialer_select] Dialer: Received rejection of protocol: /proto3
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::dialer_select] Dialer: Proposed protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::dialer_select] Dialer: Expecting proposed protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::listener_select] Listener: confirming protocol: /proto2
[2019-07-26T09:15:01Z DEBUG multistream_select::listener_sele

title: QUIC support
body:
I am using the latest quinn git master.  While I could backport to the latest release, I would prefer to get the existing code working first.

Current approach:

* Use `quinn-proto` (the bare state machine)
* Each connection has a pair of `HashMap`s to store wakers, one for readers and one for writers.  When I/O on a stream becomes possible, the corresponding waker is awoken.
* The mutable state is protected with mutexes, so `libp2p-quic` is thread-safe.
* The state machine is only advanced on a background task.
* Channels are used for incoming connections (to an endpoint) and incoming streams (to a connection).  They are also used to send packets generated by a connection to the background task for transmission.
* Strict mutex aquisition ordering is upheld to prevent deadlocks.  Specifically, if both the mutex protecting the endpoint and the mutex protecting a connection need to be taken, the mutex protecting the endpoint must be taken first.

What I would like feedback on:

* Should I be using channels in places where I am currently using mutexes?
* To avoid potential memory exhaustion denial of service attacks, I am using a bounded channel for outgoing packets.  If it fills up, packets are dropped.  Since QUIC is a reliable protocol, I expect that these will be retransmitted, which is much better than having to buffer an unlimited amount of data.
* How should I handle the case where a connection arrives, but we are not ready for it?  We can’t buffer an unlimited number of them, so at some point we will need to impose backpressure.  The current plan is to rely on quinn-proto limiting the number of connections that it returns but have not yet been accepted.

### Edit

The code is now essentially complete and is ready for review.

feat(kad): Implement ability to acknowledge `AddProvider` before reading further messages from substream
body:
## Description

The goal is to make it possible for `AddProvider` to be processed asynchronously. It is a special case in Kademlia because there is no response expected.

While it works fine with in-memory storage, disk-based and other kinds of storage present challenges here and it might be desirable to do it asynchronously, but this is a challenge because Kademlia implementation before this PR will simply move on and will accept ever growing announcements, which may result in DoS.

The approach here is to process `AddProvider` with events (`KademliaStoreInserts::FilterBoth`) and keep introduced event guard alive for corresponding event as long as necessary. As long as guard is not dropped, corresponding incoming stream will be in pending state and will not receive new incoming messages from sender. Once guard is dropped incoming stream will continue working normally.

## Notes

This could have been implemented with an additional message passing, but I find it more cumbersome to implement and to use, thus prefer RAII whenever possible for these things.

Opening as draft for now since due to lack of stream reuse this resurrects following error in my environment:
```
New inbound substream to PeerId("X") exceeds inbound substream limit. No older substream waiting to be reused. Dropping new substream.
```

It was partially mitigated in https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/pull/3287, but never resolved fully and we acknowledged back then that there is a small chance it might still happen. Here chance is 100% under right conditions because incoming streams will be in pending state indefinitely, while sender will assume stream is closed already because they did it already.

This is fixed by stream reuse implemented in https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/pull/3474.

Note that we don't HAVE TO expose `Arc<InboundStreamEventGuard>` publicly, we could make it anonymous with `Arc<dyn Any + Send + Sync + 'static>`, but it looked not as nice to me, so I decided to leave it exposed.

## Links to any relevant issues

Primarily https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/discussions/3411

title: WebRTC listener always closes when any browser client disconnects
body:
## Summary **Issue**: When I start a libp2p server with **WebRTC** transport, then connect with a few browser clients, when any of the clients drop off, the swarm listener is closed instead of remaining open to handle remaining or subsequent browser connections. **Background**: When I was creating a long lived WebRTC server using `ping` and `keep_alive`, every time I closed the browser, libp2p would also close the WebRTC listener. [Discussion](https://discuss.libp2p.io/t/does-keep-alive-behaviour-work-with-webrtc-transport/1849/1) - Trying to work through whether this is a bug or intended behaviour... [Reproducable Example: https://github.com/DougAnderson444/webrtc-ping](https://github.com/DougAnderson444/webrtc-ping) - A simple ping server and web client ## Expected behaviour I expected the WebRTC server listener to keep listening as browser clients come and go. As an aside, I originally expected the `keep_alive` behaviour to ensure the Transport listener kept listening, but after investigation I realize the `keep_alive` behaviour was not preventing the `webrtc::tokio::Tranport` listener from closing in the event of a Mux Error. ## Actual behaviour When a browser client disappears (refresh, browser closes, doesn't matter) the WebRTC server receives a `UDPMuxEvent::Error` which closes the listener. The Transport closes the listener on any `UDPMuxEvent::Error`, even if we want to keep listening.

title: feat(swarm): make stream uprade errors more ergonomic
body:
## Description

The currently provided `ConnectionHandlerUpgrErr` is very hard to use. Not only does it have a long name, it also features 3 levels of nesting which results in a lot of boilerplate. Last but not least, it exposes `multistream-select` as a dependency to all protocols.

We fix all of the above by renaming the type to `StreamUpgradeError` and flattening out its interface. Unrecoverable errors during protocol selection are hidden within the `Io` variant.

Related: #3759.
