title: Shard snapshot transfer cancellation can leave source-side transfer snapshots behind
body:
## Root Cause

In the legacy/non-streaming shard snapshot transfer path, the source peer creates
and stores a named shard snapshot before the transfer code owns any cleanup guard
for that final snapshot path.

After `create_shard_snapshot(...).await?.await?` succeeds, `transfer_snapshot`
awaits `get_shard_snapshot_path(...)` and only then wraps the snapshot and
checksum paths in `TempPath`. If the transfer future is cancelled in that
handoff window, the future is dropped after the snapshot has been persisted but
before cleanup ownership is registered.

The source already has a TODO for this exact window:

https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/44ad62f8cd69642be5afa6441612525e24a0d063/lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/snapshot.rs#L213-L231

## Current Behavior

Cancelling a snapshot-based shard transfer can leave the transfer-created source
snapshot and checksum in the normal shard snapshot namespace.

The cancellation path reverts the queue proxy, but it does not delete the
transfer-created source snapshot if cancellation wins before `TempPath` cleanup
guards are pushed:

https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/44ad62f8cd69642be5afa6441612525e24a0d063/lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/driver.rs#L243-L273

The leftover artifact remains in the normal shard snapshot namespace and is
visible to operators through the existing shard snapshot listing API. Cleanup
appears to require manual deletion through the existing shard snapshot deletion
API:

https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/44ad62f8cd69642be5afa6441612525e24a0d063/src/actix/api/snapshot_api.rs#L379-L392

https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/44ad62f8cd69642be5afa6441612525e24a0d063/src/actix/api/snapshot_api.rs#L612-L628

The impact appears to be storage growth and shard snapshot namespace pollution
on the source peer. I do not think this finding implies transferred shard data
corruption.

## Steps to Reproduce

A minimal source-level scenario is:

1. Use snapshot shard transfer with a target peer that does not use the streaming endpoint, so the sender enters the legacy stored-snapshot branch.
2. Let `transfer_snapshot(...)` complete `create_shard_snapshot(...).await?.await?`.
3. Stop polling or cancel the transfer future before `get_shard_snapshot_path(...).await` returns and before `TempPath::try_from_path(...)` is called.
4. Observe that the generated `.snapshot` and `.snapshot.checksum` files remain in `snapshots_path/shards/<shard_id>/`.

The following whitebox unit test demonstrates the issue without sleeps. It adds a test-only hook immediately after `create_shard_snapshot(...).await?.await?` returns and before cleanup ownership is registered, cancels through the same `cancel::future::cancel_on_token(...)` mechanism used by transfer tasks, and then asserts that both the snapshot and checksum remain on disk.

Apply this patch to `lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/snapshot.rs`:

```diff
diff --git a/lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/snapshot.rs b/lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/snapshot.rs
index 6b66e5f37..b1e11442c 100644
--- a/lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/snapshot.rs
+++ b/lib/collection/src/shards/transfer/snapshot.rs
@@ -17,6 +17,30 @@ use crate::shards::replica_set::replica_set_state::ReplicaState;
 use crate::shards::shard::ShardId;
 use crate::shards::shard_holder::SharedShardHolder;

+#[cfg(test)]
+type SnapshotTransferAfterCreateHook = (
+    tokio::sync::oneshot::Sender<()>,
+    tokio::sync::oneshot::Receiver<()>,
+);
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+static SNAPSHOT_TRANSFER_AFTER_CREATE_HOOK: std::sync::Mutex<
+    Option<SnapshotTransferAfterCreateHook>,
+> = std::sync::Mutex::new(None);
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+async fn notify_snapshot_transfer_after_create() {
+    let hook = SNAPSHOT_TRANSFER_AFTER_CREATE_HOOK
+        .lock()
+        .unwrap()
+        .take();
+
+    if let Some((reached, release)) = hook {
+        let _ = reached.send(());
+        let _ = release.await;
+    }
+}
+

 /// This is called on the sender

title: Fix `SetRepicaState(Dead)`/`Transfer::Abort`/`Resharding::Abort`
body:
Follow up to #9695
Fixes <https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/9656>

This PR refactors `set_replica_state`, `abort_transfer` and `abort_resharding`, so that each operation is idempotent and partial-failure safe.

`set_replica_state`, `abort_transfer` and `abort_resharding` each might do all three things:
- `set_replica_state(Dead)` might abort transfers and/or resharding
- `abort_transfer` might abort resharding and set replica state to `Dead`
- and `abort_resharding` might abort transfer(s) and/or change replica state

To make each operation partial-failure safe, we need to ensure that each operation writes its own state **last**:
- `set_replica_state(Dead)` should abort transfers and resharding *before* it writes `replica_state.json`
- `abort_transfer` should abort resharding and set replica state to `Dead` *before* it writes `shard_transfers`
- `abort_resharding` should abort transfers and change replica states *before* it writes `resharding_state.json`

This ensures, that if we crash and re-apply operation after restart, we would retry each step of an operation, and only mark it "completed" by final write.

This is what PR does. We restructure all three operations, so that they "hook" into each other correctly, without accidentally updating state that should not be written yet.

Code changes are not _too bad, 2/3 of the PR are documentation/comments and tests.

title: Add early return in RecvStream::drop when all data read is true
docs(quinn): document cancellation safety for accept_uni, accept_bi and read_datagram
body:
Closes #2247 

For these 3 methods, if they consume a stream or datagram (in poll_accept or ReadDatagram::poll), they will definitely return Poll::Ready in this poll; if a Poll::Pending is returned, no intermediate states are stored so it's safe to drop it. As a result they are cancellation safe.

title: CONNECTION_CLOSE is never sent when close() is called while congestion-blocked; peer hangs until idle timeout
Send CONNECTION_CLOSE even when congestion blocked
body:
Fixes #2785.

Calling `close()` while the congestion window is full never gets CONNECTION_CLOSE onto
the wire. The gate in `poll_transmit` classifies the packet by the stream frames still
pending in the space, but a closing connection will never send those — the packet it
actually builds is just ACKs + CONNECTION_CLOSE. And once closed nothing can reopen the
gate: incoming ACKs aren't processed anymore so in-flight bytes never drain, and
`close_common()` stopped the loss timers so the `loss_probes` bypass never fires. The
peer just sits there until its idle timeout.

We hit this cancelling a bulk sender mid-transfer — captures showed zero close datagrams
leaving, every time the cancel landed on a saturated window.

Fix is to exempt close packets from the gate, same idea as the existing tail-loss-probe
exemption on the line above: the close packet isn't congestion controlled, and blocking
it can deadlock.

The new test saturates the window with unacked data, closes, and checks the peer sees
the right close code/reason within a few PTOs instead of idle-timing out. Fails on main,
passes with the change.

Enable discovery of aborted Connections
body:
This will allow connection managers like bb8 to drop async Connections
when the Future that owned them was dropped.
See: https://github.com/djc/bb8/blob/main/redis/src/lib.rs#L78-L80

Futures drop synchronously, so there's no practical way to block them
until their response from Redis has been fully hydrated. Instead,
this change _only_ seeks to make such a situation knowable to a
ConnectionManager so it can make a choice as to what to do with the
connection.

The impact of reusing a connection in this state has no upper bound;
it violates privacy of unrelated values. This change addresses this
by adding an IO error in the Connection under ConnectionLike such
that if the connection is in some partial & unknown state it will
refuse to execute the requested commands.

By using IoError as the ErrorKind, it is believed that other pools
will be able to make a good choice about what to do when they find
a Connection in this state, no matter how it got there.

Relates to: https://github.com/redis-rs/redis-rs/issues/325

title: fix(batch): pass the cancel token into batch executors
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

This PR fixes the problem that some batch queries can't be cancelled. Fix #10769.

### The problem

Currently this query can be cancelled:
```sql
dev=> select * from generate_series(1, 10000) as t1, generate_series(1, 10000) as t2;
^C
ERROR:  QueryError: Canceled by user
```

but this query can not:
```sql
dev=> select count(*) from generate_series(1, 500000000);
^C^C
```

The reason is that the shutdown channel is unconnected in both local mode and distributed mode:

https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/blob/24c6e7de987653460b85e29a2b362cdb49387b55/src/frontend/src/scheduler/local.rs#L114-L116
https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/blob/24c6e7de987653460b85e29a2b362cdb49387b55/src/frontend/src/scheduler/distributed/stage.rs#L568-L570

Therefore, executors can't be notified and exit themselves. So the second query will be blocking. But why there's no problem in the first query? Because we have a `select(executor, shutdown_channel)` on the outside. The join executor will constantly yield chunks, which gives the control back to the frontend. So there's a chance to stop running from the outside.

### The solution

The biggest challenge is that the types of shutdown channel in different places are not uniform. The current status can be shown as below:
```
<local>                                     <distributed>
Tripwire<Result<DataChunk, BoxedError>>     oneshot::Receiver<StageMessage>
   |                                            |
   x disconnected                               x disconnected
   +----------- <batch executor> ---------------+
                Option<watch::Receiver<ShutdownMsg>>
```



In order to connect these channels, this PR first unify these types into one `ShutdownToken`, basically a wrapper over `watch::Receiver<ShutdownMsg>`. Then we refactor all related usages.

After this PR the query can be cancelled in both local and distributed mode.

```sql
dev=> select count(*) from generate_series(1, 500000000);
^C
ERROR:  QueryError: Cancelled by user
dev=> set query_mode to local;
SET_VARIABLE
dev=> select count(*) from generate_series(1, 500000000);
^C
ERROR:  QueryError: Cancelled by user
```

title: Improve Union's stream key derivation
A complicated lateral join unsupported case
body:
As mentioned in the issue, `a, b` and `a join b` behaves differently before this PR:
* `a, b` reports `column arr not found`, due to the lack of `try_mark_lateral_as_visible` added in this PR. This is the "support lateral" half of the PR.
* `a cross join b` panics because `arr` was mistakenly accessible in the **current** context (`Unnest($1)` without a child plan node) rather than in lateral or upper context. It is now changed to upper context with `push_context` in `bind_table_function`. This is the "fix panic" half of the PR.

This inspired me to find a trickier case:
```
create table a (a1 int); insert into a values (3), (2);
create table b (b1 varchar); insert into b values ('x'), ('y');
select * from a, b cross join regexp_matches(repeat(b1, a1), '.', 'g');
```
Or similarly:
```
select * from a cross join (b cross join regexp_matches(repeat(b1, a1), '.', 'g'));
```

This issue applies to our lateral support in #11780 as well:
```
select * from a, b cross join lateral (select regexp_matches(repeat(b1, a1), '.', 'g')) z;
```

title: refactor(barrier): explicitly maintain database barrier state separately in local barrier manager
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

To simplify the implementation to support database failure isolation, we should isolate different databases for fields in local barrier worker. Previously, we isolate the barrier injection and collection of different partial graphs. Ideally, it will be great to isolate the fields of local barrier worker by partial graph, so that the local barrier worker won't be aware of the concept of database. 

However, after some efforts, I found it complicated to directly support isolation in different partial graphs. In snapshot backfill, during the stage of backfill, the streaming job has its own partial graph, but after the backfill finishes, its own partial graph will be merged to the global partial graph, along with its actors migrating from the own partial graph to the global partial graph. In this case, partial graphs are not completely isolated between each other. If we change to not merging the partial graph and assume that actors always belong to a fixed partial graph, we can easily support isolation in partial graphs, but the related code in global barrier manager will be unnecessarily complicated. In either way, it will be complicated to isolate different partial graphs.

Therefore, in this PR, we will let local barrier worker be aware of the concept of database. Fields in local barrier manager will be maintained mostly in the way of `HashMap<DatabaseId, T>`. In this way, the logic of database isolation can be easily implemented. Changes are mostly as followed:
* the original `ManagedBarrierState` is renamed to `DatabaseManagedBarrierState`, to store the barrier state per database. In the streaming control bidi-stream, we will specify the `database_id` in each request to specify the database_id to operate on.
* The `LocalBarrierManager`, which holds two channel tx for actors to report barrier event of actor error, will become per-database, so that the barrier event or actor error can be reported independently. It is previously stored in the `SharedContext`. In this PR, we change to store it separately out of `SharedContext`.
* The `SharedContext`, which is used to store pending exchange channels, will also become per-database. This is based on the assumption that there won't be exchange channel between two different databases. In exchange service, to get the exchange channel, we need to specify the current database_id to locate the correct `SharedContext`.

title: fix(meta): unregister aborted initial job tables
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).



## What's changed and what's your intention?

- Related to #25466
- Split from #25592

This PR is scoped to **DDL abort cleanup for creating streaming jobs**. It does not change per-database dirty-job recovery cleanup; that path is fixed separately in #25592.

Bug:

- When creating a streaming job fails, `create_streaming_job_inner` tries to abort the creating job with `AbortCreatingStreamingJobReason::CreateFailed`.
- `DROP/CANCEL` of an `Initial` job also tries to abort through the same catalog helper with `AbortCreatingStreamingJobReason::Cancelled`.
- Before this PR, these DDL abort callers could delete catalog rows without running the existing dropped-table cleanup path, so Hummock table ids that had already been registered could remain stale.
- The stale-id cleanup responsibility is in the DDL abort path after the create is actually aborted, independent of the mechanism that caused the foreground create to fail.

Fix:

- Split abort input reason from abort outcome:
  - `AbortCreatingStreamingJobReason` records why the abort is requested: `Cancelled` or `CreateFailed`.
  - `AbortCreatingStreamingJobResult` records what happened: `Aborted { state_table_ids, .. }` or `LeftForRecovery`.
- Collect cleanup table ids from the catalog table rows deleted by the abort path: internal table catalogs plus the MV table catalog.
- Route DDL create failure and `DROP/CANCEL` of `Initial` jobs through `try_abort_creating_streaming_job_and_cleanup`, so Hummock unregister and Hummock/compactor notification happen through the existing dropped-table cleanup path only when the catalog abort actually happens.
- Keep replace-job abort handling and live `Background/Creating` recovery unchanged.

Not covered by this PR:

- Dirty creating-job cleanup during per-database recovery. That is #25592.

### Testing

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `git diff --check`
- `cargo check -p risingwave_meta --lib`
- `cargo test -p risingwave_meta test_abort_initial_materialized_views_unregister_hummock --lib -- --nocapture`
- `./risedev sit-test test_snapshot_backfill_failed_foreground_ddl_unregisters_table_ids --no-capture`

The unit test is a focused meta-layer regression test: it uses the real `HummockManager`, `CatalogController`, and `cleanup_dropped_streaming_jobs` path, manually builds the minimal `Initial` MV catalog state, registers the MV table id into Hummock, then verifies abort cleanup unregisters it.

The simulation test updates the existing recovery case to match the intended invariant: when a foreground snapshot-backfill DDL is interrupted by database recovery and aborts, the created state tables are removed from Hummock member tables instead of being kept as dangling table ids.

title: fix(cdc): keep TOAST replacement path active on tables without downstream
body:
## Problem

PR #21577 added the Debezium unchanged-TOAST placeholder replacement path inside `MaterializeCache::handle_inner`: when an UPDATE event for a PG CDC row carries the placeholder for an unchanged TOAST column (varchar / jsonb / bytea / List, and after #25863 also \`vector\`), the cache fetches the previous row from state and swaps the placeholder back.

However, `MaterializeExecutor::execute_inner` contains an *unrelated* performance optimization in [materialize.rs:481](src/stream/src/executor/mview/materialize.rs#L481):

```

let optimized_conflict_behavior = if let ConflictBehavior::Overwrite = self.conflict_behavior
    && !self.state_table.is_consistent_op()
    && !self.cleaned_by_ttl_watermark
    && self.version_column_indices.is_empty()
{
    ConflictBehavior::NoCheck   // skip MaterializeCache, write_chunk straight to state
} else {
    self.conflict_behavior
};

```

This runtime demotion skips \`MaterializeCache\` entirely and writes the chunk straight into the state table. For PG CDC tables **without a downstream subscriber**, all four conditions are satisfied, so:

* the placeholder bytes land in state untouched
* a subsequent \`SELECT\` returns \`__debezium_unavailable_value\` for varchar / jsonb / bytea, the all-\`f32::MAX\` sentinel for vector, and so on

The construction-time invariant inside [\`MaterializeCache::new\`](src/stream/src/executor/mview/cache.rs#L88):


```
ConflictBehavior::NoCheck => {
    assert!(toastable_column_indices.is_none(), \"when there are toastable columns, conflict handling must be enabled\");
    return None;
}

```

only sees the original \`conflict_behavior\` passed at construction; the runtime demotion lives one level up, so this assert can never fire on the affected tables and the gap stays silent.

## Fix

Mirror \`toastable_column_indices\` on \`MaterializeExecutor\` itself and add it to the demotion guard:

\`\`\`rust
let optimized_conflict_behavior = if let ConflictBehavior::Overwrite = self.conflict_behavior
    && !self.state_table.is_consistent_op()
    && !self.cleaned_by_ttl_watermark
    && self.version_column_indices.is_empty()
    && self.toastable_column_indices.is_none()   // new
{
    ConflictBehavior::NoCheck
} else {
    self.conflict_behavior
};
\`\`\`

## Why this is exact, no over-correction

\`toastable_column_indices\` is populated inside [materialize.rs:241](src/stream/src/executor/mview/materialize.rs#L241) only when:

1. \`table_catalog.cdc_table_type() == Postgres\`, **and**
2. the table has at least one column whose \`DataType\` is in the TOAST-able whitelist (\`Varchar | List(_) | Bytea | Jsonb | Vector(_)\`).

For every other table — non-CDC tables, MySQL / SQL Server / MongoDB CDC, PG CDC tables that only carry int / bool / numeric / etc. — the field is \`None\` and the demotion to \`NoCheck\` continues to fire unchanged. Only the narrow class \"PG CDC table with at least one TOAST-able column and no downstream subscriber\" stays on the cache path. Those tables exchange a per-row LRU lookup for correctness; they are typically metadata / config / embedding tables with modest update frequency, and after the initial \`fetch_keys\` batch the LRU absorbs repeated UPDATEs on the same key with no extra IO.

## Cross-connector check

* MySQL / SQL Server / MongoDB CDC: \`toastable_column_indices\` is always \`None\`, behavior unchanged.
* Non-CDC streaming tables / MVs: \`cdc_table_type\` is \`Unspecified\`, \`toastable_column_indices\` is \`None\`, behavior unchanged.

## Tested manually

PG CDC table

\`\`\`sql
CREATE TABLE t (id int PRIMARY KEY, payload jsonb, ts timestamp);
ALTER TABLE t REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT;
\`\`\`

with a large \`payload\` (forced into TOAST), no downstream MV on the RW side.

* Before this PR: \`UPDATE t SET ts = now() WHERE id = ...\` leaves \`payload = '__debezium_unavailable_value'\` in the downstream table.
* After this PR: the same UPD

title: feat(sink): support LanceDB sink
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).



## What's changed and what's your intention?

This PR adds a new **LanceDB sink connector** that writes streaming data from RisingWave into [LanceDB](https://lancedb.com/) tables.

This is a fresh PR for the work from #25186, which was closed as stale.

### Architecture

The sink follows the **writer/coordinator pattern** with low-level write/commit separation:

- **Writer** (`LanceDbSinkWriter`): Converts each incoming `StreamChunk` to an Arrow `RecordBatch` and sends it through a bounded channel to a Lance fragment-writing task. `FileFragment::create_fragments()` consumes this stream incrementally, so the writer applies backpressure without buffering an entire fragment in RisingWave memory. At a checkpoint, the writer closes the stream, waits for the data files to finish, and returns lightweight `Fragment` metadata (file paths and row counts), not the data payload.
- **Coordinator** (`LanceDbSinkCommitter`): Collects `Fragment` metadata from all writers and atomically appends it through the Lance dataset transaction path. No data flows through the coordinator.

The sink supports both commit modes:

- **Two-phase commit** is the default (`is_exactly_once = true` or omitted). It stores both the stable `risingwave.sink_id` and monotonically increasing `risingwave.epoch` in Lance transaction properties. Retry detection scans transaction history from newest to oldest, ignores transactions from other sinks, and stops cleanly at the retained-history boundary. Because replacing a sink changes its catalog sink ID, `REPLACE SINK` rejects exactly-once sinks; set `is_exactly_once = false` to use replacement.
- **Single-phase commit** is available by setting `is_exactly_once = false`.

This design keeps memory bounded, avoids routing data through the coordinator, and makes replayed two-phase commits idempotent.

### Changes

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Cargo.toml` | Add workspace dependencies for LanceDB 0.29 and Lance 6.0 |
| `src/connector/Cargo.toml` | Add the `sink-lancedb` feature gate |
| `src/common/src/array/arrow/arrow_lancedb.rs` | Add Arrow type conversion for the Lance dependency stack |
| `src/connector/src/sink/lancedb.rs` | Add validation, streaming fragment writer, and single-/two-phase coordinators |
| `src/connector/src/sink/mod.rs` | Register the LanceDB sink |
| `e2e_test/sink/lancedb/` | Add the LanceDB sink end-to-end test |
| `ci/scripts/e2e-lancedb-sink-test.sh` | Add the CI test runner |
| `ci/workflows/pull-request.yml` | Add the label-gated `ci/run-e2e-lancedb-sink-tests` step |
| `ci/workflows/main-cron.yml` | Add the LanceDB sink main-cron step |

### Sink properties

```sql
CREATE SINK s AS SELECT * FROM mv
WITH (
    connector = 'lancedb',
    type = 'append-only',
    force_append_only = 'true',
    lancedb.uri = '/path/to/db',
    lancedb.table = 'my_table',
    is_exactly_once = 'true' -- optional, defaults to true
);
```

- Only **append-only** mode is supported.
- The LanceDB table must be pre-created with a compatible schema.
- `commit_checkpoint_interval` is configurable and defaults to 10.
- `is_exactly_once` controls the commit mode and defaults to `true`.

- Related to #25149
- Replaces #25186

title: feat(stream): evaluate project chunks concurrently
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt). ## What's changed and what's your intention? This PR lets `ProjectExecutor` evaluate multiple scalar projection chunks concurrently while preserving the original stream message order. The executor now keeps ordered in-flight projection futures with `FuturesOrdered`. It reads upstream input and polls the next projected chunk concurrently with `futures::future::select`, stops reading when `streaming.developer.project_expr_concurrency` is full, and drains all earlier projected chunks before processing watermarks and barriers. The new streaming developer config is: - `streaming.developer.project_expr_concurrency = 1` by default, preserving the previous sequential behavior. - `0` means unlimited in-flight chunk projection. - Values above `1` allow multiple chunk projection futures to be driven cooperatively in the executor task. The projection futures do not use `tokio::spawn`; they borrow shared projection expressions through an `Arc` and are polled by the executor task. Watermark state for nondecreasing expressions is still updated when projected chunks are emitted, so barrier-time watermarks include all chunks before the barrier. Tests cover: - concurrent chunk projection with a blocking async expression; - preserving chunk output order and draining chunks before a barrier; - job-level config alterability through `rw_streaming_job_config`. ## Checklist - [ ] I have written necessary rustdoc comments. - [x] I have added necessary unit tests and integration tests. - [ ] I have added test labels as necessary. - [ ] I have added fuzzing tests or opened an issue to track them. - [ ] My PR contains breaking changes. - [ ] My PR changes performance-critical code, so I will run (micro) benchmarks and present the results. - [x] I have checked the [Release Timeline](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/rw-commits-history/blob/main/release_timeline.md) and [Currently Supported Versions](https://docs.risingwave.com/changelog/release-support-policy#support-end-dates-for-recent-releases) to determine which release branches I need to cherry-pick this PR into. ## Documentation - [ ] My PR needs documentation updates.

title: bug(frontend): cancel_all_scheduled_tasks panics on task with location=None
body:
## Describe the bug

In distributed batch scheduling, when a query is cancelled (e.g. by `statement_timeout`), the frontend iterates every entry in `self.tasks` and unwraps the task's worker address. If a task was created but never successfully assigned to a worker (its `location` is still `None`), the `expect()` panics and the whole frontend process restarts. In single-frontend deployments every Postgres client session drops with `SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly` and the cluster is unreachable until the pod is back.

## Affected versions

Reproduced on v2.8.1 (commit `f49ef55`). Code path is still present on `main` and on v2.8.4 — only an unrelated hummock-IDs backport landed in `src/frontend/src/scheduler/` between v2.8.1 and v2.8.4.

## Suspected root cause / pointers

`src/frontend/src/scheduler/distributed/stage.rs:895` (function `cancel_all_scheduled_tasks`):

```rust
let loc = &task_status.get_status().location;
let addr = loc.as_ref().expect("Get address should not fail");
```

A task is inserted into `self.tasks` before its location is set; `location` is only filled to `Some(worker_node_addr)` after `schedule_task` successfully RPCs the chosen worker. If scheduling for that task did not yet complete (e.g. the chosen serving worker was masked via `mask_failed_serving_worker` / `mask_worker_temporary_secs`, or the upstream wedge prevents the per-task schedule call from completing), the entry remains with `location: None`. When cancellation later iterates **every** task — including not-yet-scheduled ones — the `expect()` is hit.

## Reproduction

1. Single frontend, distributed mode (default `query_mode`).
2. Run a sequence of heavy `INSERT INTO <table> SELECT … FROM <s3 parquet source>` bulk loads with `ALTER TABLE … SET PARALLELISM TO ADAPTIVE` toggled per load. After ~25 min one of the queries wedges (batch_task_num goes to 0, no event-log entries) — the distributed batch scheduler stops scheduling new tasks.
3. Wait for `statement_timeout` (default 3600s) to fire on the wedged query.
4. Frontend panics at `stage.rs:896:37` with `Get address should not fail` and restarts.

## Logs

```
WARN  Query QueryId { id: "<redacted-query-id>" } timeout after 3600 seconds, sending cancel message.
INFO  Send cancel request to query-QueryId { id: "<redacted-query-id>" }
thread 'rw-batch-local' (41) panicked at src/frontend/src/scheduler/distributed/stage.rs:896:37:
Get address should not fail
  23: risingwave_frontend::scheduler::distributed::stage::StageRunner::cancel_all_scheduled_tasks
      at /risingwave/src/frontend/src/scheduler/distributed/stage.rs:896:37
  24: StageRunner::schedule_tasks                       at stage.rs:611:47
  25: StageRunner::schedule_tasks_for_all               at stage.rs:728:60
  26: StageRunner::run                                  at stage.rs:314:66
```

## Expected behaviour

The cancel path must tolerate tasks whose `location` is still `None` (i.e. tasks that were never successfully scheduled to a worker). Skip the cancel RPC for those tasks instead of unwrapping the address. The frontend must not panic and restart when a distributed batch query is cancelled.

## Actual behaviour

Frontend process panics on the unwrap and is restarted by the supervisor; every client session is dropped with `SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly` and the cluster is briefly unreachable.

## Impact

- Severity: high — entire frontend process dies on a routine cancel path (statement timeout, explicit `pg_cancel_backend`, or any cancellation that races a partially-scheduled distributed query).
- In single-frontend BYOC/standalone deployments (which is the default for many customer setups), this means a cluster-wide outage for all batch and serving sessions until the frontend pod is back.
- Reproduced in production during bulk bootstrap loads; user-facing error is `SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly` / `E_UPSTREAM_UNREACHABLE`.

title: bug(cdc/postgres): zombie walsender process locking postgres replication slot
body:
## Summary

`DbzCdcEngineRunner.stop()` is non-blocking. When the coordinator thread is stuck in
uninterruptible native JDBC I/O, stop signals are ignored, the keep-alive thread
continues sending `StandbyStatusUpdate` to Postgres every 10 s, and the replication slot
stays locked indefinitely — `wal_sender_timeout` cannot fire.

---

## Root cause

### 1. `stop()` does not wait for thread termination

```java
// DbzCdcEngineRunner.java
public void stop() throws Exception {
    if (isRunning()) {
        engine.stop();   // sets stop flag, returns after internal timeout
        cleanUp();
        LOG.info("engine#{} terminated", engine.getId()); // premature: threads still running
    }
}

private void cleanUp() {
    running.set(false);
    executor.shutdownNow();  // Thread.interrupt() only — no awaitTermination()
}
```

`executor.shutdownNow()` interrupts the runner thread (`rw-dbz-engine-runner-N`). The
coordinator and keep-alive threads run in their own `ExecutorService` instances created
inside Debezium; they are not owned by this executor and are unaffected.

### 2. The coordinator is blocked in non-interruptible native JDBC I/O

```java
// PostgresStreamingChangeEventSource.java — processMessages(), every loop iteration
connection.commit();  // regular JDBC connection — Thread.interrupt() does not unblock this
```

When `connection.commit()` blocks (e.g. on a transient database-side condition),
`Thread.interrupt()` sets the interrupt flag but does not unblock the native socket call.
`context.isRunning()` is never re-checked. `execute()` never returns.

### 3. The keep-alive thread is never stopped

```java
// PostgresStreamingChangeEventSource.java:221-225
stream.startKeepAlive(
    Threads.newSingleThreadExecutor(
        PostgresConnector.class, connectorConfig.getLogicalName(), "keep-alive"));
```

`stopKeepAlive()` is called only in `cleanUpStreamingOnStop()` inside the `finally` block
of `execute()`. Because `execute()` never returns, `stopKeepAlive()` is never called.

**Result:** every call to `runner.stop()` (on restarts, rescheduling, or meta recovery)
logs `"engine terminated"` while the coordinator and keep-alive threads remain alive.
The keep-alive thread keeps the walsender alive indefinitely. New engine instances fail
to acquire the slot:
```
PSQLException: ERROR: replication slot "..." is active for PID <zombie>
```

---

## Observed in production

The following was observed on a PostgreSQL 15 Aurora cluster with `wal_sender_timeout = 1min`.

The zombie walsender survived **7 h 46 min** without triggering `wal_sender_timeout`.
`pg_stat_replication` across three measurements taken over ~7 minutes showed:

| Column | Value |
|--------|-------|
| `state` | `streaming` |
| `write_lsn` | non-null (one initial status update was sent at connect time) |
| `flush_lsn` | **NULL throughout** — coordinator never committed a single offset |
| `reply_time` | **advancing** (+20 ms in 21 s wall clock, +430 ms in 438 s) |
| `confirmed_flush_lsn` | **frozen** — identical value across all three measurements |

`reply_time` advancing proves Aurora was actively receiving `StandbyStatusUpdate` messages
from the JVM — a transparent TCP proxy cannot synthesise replication protocol messages, so
the keep-alive thread was demonstrably alive and sending. With `wal_sender_timeout = 1min`,
a connection that receives a keepalive every 10 s will never be timed out regardless of how
long the coordinator has been stuck.

WAL accumulated ~3.2 GB over the zombie's lifetime with no sign of self-healing.

Every new engine startup produced the following in the connector-node logs, then exhausted
its retry budget and cycled:

```
WARN  Failed to start replication stream at LSN{...}, attempt number 2 over 6
      thread="debezium-postgresconnector-<source-id>-change-event-source-coordinator"
      error="PSQLException: ERROR: replication slot \"...\" is active for PID <zombie>"
```

title: stream: actor failure notification (recovery trigger) is delayed seconds by backtrace symbolization in exit logging
body:
## Describe the bug

When an actor exits with an error, the failure notification that triggers recovery is sent only **after** the error is logged:

```rust
// src/stream/src/task/actor_manager.rs (two call sites)
tracing::error!(%actor_id, error = ?err.as_report(), "actor exit with error");
barrier_manager.notify_failure(actor_id, err);   // <- this is what triggers recovery
```

`?err.as_report()` Debug-formats the error report **including backtrace symbolization**. Symbolization is lazy in Rust: capture (at error creation) is cheap, but the first symbolization in a process must load and parse the binary's debug info. For a RisingWave dev/ci-dev build this is huge (locally: 1.6 GB binary, 7.3M symbols, `split-debuginfo=unpacked` OSO references into a 128 GB `target/debug/deps`), so the first symbolization takes **seconds**, and the recovery signal is stuck behind it.

Measured with an instrumented build (12-core M-series Mac, dev profile), splitting the cost into `format!("{:?}", err.as_report())` vs log write vs `notify_failure`:

| scenario | symbolization | log write | notify_failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| first backtrace in CN process, idle machine | **0.92 s** | 1–5 ms | µs |
| second backtrace, same process, heavy load | 1–5 ms | ms | µs |
| first backtrace in fresh CN process, heavy CPU+IO load | **7.31 s** | ms–0.1 s | µs |

The cost is dominated by first-time (per-process) cold loading of debug info, which is IO-heavy — so a loaded/IO-contended machine (i.e. CI) amplifies it dramatically.

## Consequences

1. **Recovery latency**: after an actor dies, the graph keeps running for seconds as if nothing happened. Recovery may instead be triggered later by a lower-quality signal — e.g. the next barrier failing to inject into the dead actor — with `failed_actor=None` and a less useful root cause.
2. **The late notification can be silently lost**: once the partial graph is suspended via that other path, `PartialGraphStatus::poll_next_event` no longer polls `actor_failure_rx` (returns `Pending` for `Suspended`), and `notify_failure` ignores send errors (`let _ = ...send(...)`). The real root-cause error then never reaches the barrier worker.

This was observed in CI (see linked flaky-test issue): 4 sink actors exited intentionally at `07:19:27.408` (the process's **first** backtrace — the "actor exit with error" lines are the first `Backtrace:` blocks in the whole CN log), yet no `recv actor failure` suspension ever happened; the graph was only suspended at `07:19:33.180` by a barrier-injection failure (≥5.77 s later), on a machine loaded enough that concurrent minio writes were hitting 5 s IO timeouts. The event loop polls the failure channel with top priority (`select! biased`), so the channel was provably still empty at that point — the notification was still stuck behind symbolization.

## Suggested fix

- Call `notify_failure` **before** the `error!` log at both call sites in `actor_manager.rs` (one-line reorder; the log can keep the backtrace).
- Optionally: also drain `actor_failure_rx` for suspended graphs (it is already consulted during reset via `try_find_root_actor_failure`) so late notifications still contribute to root-cause scoring.

## Error message/log

```
2026-07-02T07:19:27.408 ERROR risingwave_stream::task::actor_manager: actor exit with error actor_id=1072 error=Executor error: Sink error: sink_id=299, error: This is not an actual error condition. The system is intentionally triggering recovery procedures to ensure ALTER SINK CONFIG are fully applied.
(followed by full symbolized Backtrace:, the first in this process)
...5.77 s of silence...
2026-07-02T07:19:33.180 ERROR risingwave_stream::task::barrier_worker: suspend partial graph on error partial_graph_id=8589934591 failed_actor=None failed to inject barrier err=Failed to send barrier with epoch 10862039377248256 to actor 1073: failed to send to registered sender
```

title: time travel: epoch-row vacuum deletes a stalled stream's newest mappings, permanently breaking in-retention time-travel reads
body:
### Describe the bug

Follow-up to #26380 / #26390. #26390 fixed the version-threshold inference, but the epoch-**row** deletion in `truncate_time_travel_metadata` is unchanged:

```
DELETE FROM hummock_epoch_to_version WHERE epoch < epoch_watermark   -- only pinned snapshot rows exempted
```

There is no per-table exemption. A row `(e, T, v)` serves every query epoch in `[e, T's next row's epoch)` — so a table's **newest row below the watermark** still serves the whole retention window, and serves it forever if the table's stream has stopped committing. When a stream stalls for longer than `time_travel_retention_ms` (compute nodes down, a database stuck in recovery — the recovering-database scenario raised in [this discussion](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26377#discussion_r3627613152)), all of its tables' mapping rows age below the watermark and get deleted. Afterward, a time-travel read at a timestamp that is both **inside the stall window** and **within retention** fails at the epoch→version row lookup — permanently, since the rows are gone.

A second instance: a creating job's fake-epoch rows (`new_fake_barrier` epochs, always below any real watermark) are wiped within one vacuum round while the job is still running, breaking the CN `get_time_travel_version` fallback for those epochs after a recovery evicts `recent_versions`.

### Blast radius

Only reads that resolve an old epoch through `hummock_epoch_to_version` are affected: `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` queries, re-resolution of old snapshot epochs past the `recent_versions` window, and the internal fake-epoch fallback above. Ordinary current-epoch queries and streaming are structurally unaffected: the live version is propagated and persisted by a separate mechanism, every new version carries a stalled table's `state_table_info` and SST references forward, and vacuum's SST deletion exempts everything referenced by `latest_valid_version`. The damage is loss of in-retention history, not of current data or availability.

### Reproduced on `main` @ 668df343b7 (includes #26390)

Fresh cluster (`time_travel_retention_ms=600000`), `create table t` + inserts (1009 rows, last commit 12:13:47), control read `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF now() - '2' second` OK. Then `kill -9` the compute node at 12:14:57 (meta/frontend stay up) and wait 12.5 min.

Once the watermark passed the stall point, vacuum deleted all pre-stall mapping rows:

```
12:23:10  Delete 16 rows from hummock_epoch_to_version. epoch_watermark=10977620169719808
12:23:40  Delete 30 rows from hummock_epoch_to_version. ...
12:24:10  Delete 36 rows from hummock_epoch_to_version. ...
12:24:40  Delete 30 rows from hummock_epoch_to_version. ...
12:25:10  Delete 15 rows from hummock_epoch_to_version. ...
```

while #26390 correctly preserved the versions in the same rounds:

```
12:24:10  Deleted 1 rows from hummock_time_travel_version.  latest_valid_version_id=56
12:25:10  Deleted 0 rows from hummock_time_travel_version.  latest_valid_version_id=56
```

After restarting the compute node (data intact, `select count(*) from t` → 1009):

```
select count(*) from t for system_time as of now() - '8' minute;
-- target 12:26:25: inside the stall window, well within the 600s retention
ERROR:  Failed to run the query
Caused by:
  Storage error: Hummock error: Time-travel version expired: table 7, epoch 10977670922240000
```

Re-running a minute later fails identically — the version metadata exists (preserved by #26390) but no row maps the in-stall epochs to it.

Reproduction caveats (both produce false negatives if ignored):
- The CN `recent_versions` cache (default 60 versions) serves any epoch ≥ the recovery version's `committed_epoch` from memory without consulting time travel; the failure only surfaces for target epochs below that floor (or ~60 checkpoints after restart).
- The CN `simple_time_travel_version_cache` masks the failure for any timestamp queried before the vacuum; use a fresh timestamp.

title: No-op ALTER SINK can restart KV log reader without rewind and panic
body:
### Version

RisingWave v3.0.1.

### Symptom

Issuing an unchanged `ALTER SINK ... CONNECTOR WITH (...)` against an active commit-decoupled sink can panic a compute node:

```text
src/stream/src/common/log_store_impl/kv_log_store/reader.rs:252:13
future state is not Reset
```

The stack reaches `KvLogStoreReader::start_from` through `DecoupleCheckpointLogSinker::consume_log_and_sink` and the sink executor.

### Suspected control flow

In `src/stream/src/executor/sink.rs`, the `select!` branch receives `RebuildSinkMessage::UpdateConfig`. Even when `sink_config_has_changes(...)` is false, selecting that branch cancels the active `consume_log_and_sink` future. The unchanged-properties branch logs `skip alter sink config because properties are unchanged` and returns `Ok(())` without calling `log_reader.rewind()`.

The outer loop then creates another log sinker. `DecoupleCheckpointLogSinker::consume_log_and_sink` immediately calls `log_reader.start_from(None)`, but the KV reader is still in its prior future state instead of `Reset`, triggering the panic assertion.

### Expected behavior

A no-op connector-property notification should not panic or restart a KV reader from a non-reset state. If cancellation of the consumer is unavoidable, the decoupled reader should be rewound before the outer loop starts a new consumer.

### Operational mitigation

We removed repeated no-op connector ALTERs from our idempotent deployment SQL and now set `commit_checkpoint_interval` only in `CREATE SINK`. This prevents the known trigger but does not harden the engine against another unchanged config notification.

I can prepare a focused regression test/patch if the expected behavior of the unchanged-config branch is confirmed.

title: fix(stream): keep consuming on a no-op sink config update
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

A sink config notification cancels the in-flight consumer through `select!`. Restarting it requires a rewound log reader, and when the log reader cannot rewind (`sink_decouple = false`, in-memory log store) the only way back is recovery. Since #26412 that price is paid even when the incoming properties already equal the current ones.

So an `ALTER SINK ... CONNECTOR` that changes nothing:

- drags the whole database through a recovery, restarting every streaming job in it;
- panics meta where recovery is disabled — `database N failure reported from M but recovery not enabled` (`barrier/worker.rs:763`). That is what CI runs, so `end-to-end clickhouse sink test` and `end-to-end starrocks sink test` have been red on `main` since 2026-07-24.

This PR detects the no-op **before** the consumer is dropped and keeps it running — no cancellation, no rewind, no recovery. Everything reaching the handler now really did change, so the branches there no longer repeat the check. #26409's fix is preserved: a real change on a rewind-capable reader still rewinds.

The consumer future is `Box::pin`ned so `drop` releases its borrows on `log_reader` / `sink` before the change path mutates them.

### Why exactly those two e2e tests

Both start with `set sink_decouple = false` and then run `ALTER SINK s6 CONNECTOR WITH (commit_checkpoint_interval = '1')`. `set_default_commit_checkpoint_interval` already persisted `commit_checkpoint_interval = 1` at CREATE time, so the ALTER is a pure no-op — they only ever passed because of the pre-#26412 short-circuit.

### Tests

The two existing `test_no_op_*` tests encoded the old semantics and are rewritten; the two "config actually changed" cases they were missing are added.

- `test_no_op_sink_config_update_keeps_consuming_{with,without}_rewind` — consumer survives, no rewind. Liveness is asserted deterministically: a following `RebuildSink` gets acknowledged, no sleeps.
- `test_sink_config_update_rewinds_log_reader` — a real change still rewinds and restarts (regression guard for #26409).
- `test_sink_config_update_triggers_recovery_without_rewind` — a real change without rewind still errors to trigger recovery.

`./risedev check` clean; `./risedev test executor::sink` 12/12.

### Limitation

A *real* `ALTER SINK ... CONNECTOR` on a non-decoupled sink still forces recovery and therefore still cannot run under `disable_recovery`. Unchanged here.

- Closes #26483

title: feat(connector): support WebSocket source connector
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).


## What's changed and what's your intention?

**Summary**

This PR adds a new `websocket` source connector that lets RisingWave ingest messages directly from a WebSocket server (e.g. an IoT sensor telemetry feed, an event stream, or a subscribe-style push API), in both plain `ws://` and TLS `wss://` modes.

**How it works**

- A `websocket` source/table is configured with a `url` (`ws://...` or `wss://...`, scheme validated at creation time) plus optional connection options. It has exactly one split: a WebSocket connection is a single ordered, non-partitionable, non-replayable message stream.
- The reader connects with `tokio-tungstenite` (TLS via `rustls` + native root CAs), streams `text`/`binary` frames, skips empty keep-alive frames, and feeds each message through the standard parsing pipeline (`format plain`, `encode json` / `protobuf` / `bytes`).
- **Reconnection**: WebSocket servers routinely drop long-lived connections, so the reader transparently reconnects with a capped exponential backoff (1s up to 60s) instead of erroring out. The optional `init.message` (e.g. a subscribe request) is re-sent on every (re)connect.
- **Keep-alive**: `ping.interval.secs` (default `30`, set to `0` to disable) sends WebSocket pings; pong handling is done by `tungstenite`.
- **Stale-subscription guard**: `idle.timeout.secs` forces a reconnect (and re-subscribe) when no data message arrives for the given period. This covers servers that silently expire subscriptions while keeping the transport (and ping/pong) alive. Disabled by default.
- **Offset semantics**: because a WebSocket stream cannot be replayed, the message offset is a per-reader sequence counter used for observability only (exposed via `INCLUDE offset`); it is not persisted, and on recovery the reader reconnects and consumes from that point on.

**New connector options**

| option                | required | default | description |
|-----------------------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `url`                 | yes      | –       | server URL, must be `ws://` or `wss://` |
| `init.message`        | no       | –       | text sent right after (re)connect, e.g. subscribe request |
| `headers`             | no       | –       | JSON object of string pairs added to the handshake, e.g. `{"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}`. Enforced as a `SECRET` on RisingWave Cloud (`enforce_secret`). |
| `ping.interval.secs`  | no       | `30`    | keep-alive ping interval; `0` disables |
| `idle.timeout.secs`   | no       | –       | reconnect if no data message arrives in this many seconds |

**Tests**

- Unit tests: connector properties parsing/validation, split JSON round-trip, and reader behavior against a real in-process server — text/binary ingestion and empty-frame skipping, `init.message` re-sent across reconnects, keep-alive pings, idle-timeout reconnect + re-subscribe, custom handshake headers.
- End-to-end: `e2e_test/source_inline/websocket/websocket_source.slt.serial` runs against a local `ws_server.py` fixture, covering basic ingestion, creation-time validation, bearer-auth headers, and `INCLUDE offset`.

**Limitations**

- WebSocket is not replayable: messages the server sends while the connection is down are lost (inherent to the protocol; no offset-based recovery).
- A single split — no partitioning.
- TLS uses system-trusted native root CAs; no custom CA/client-cert options in this PR.



Closes issue https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/21555

title: cherry-pick fix(stream): keep consuming on a no-op sink config update (#26484) to release-3.0
body:
Cherry-picks the fix for [#26409](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/26409) to `release-3.0`.

## Why

On `release-3.0`, an `ALTER SINK ... CONNECTOR WITH (...)` whose properties are **unchanged** aborts the compute node:

```
thread 'rw-streaming' panicked at src/stream/src/common/log_store_impl/kv_log_store/reader.rs:252:13:
future state is not Reset
```

```
KvLogStoreReader::start_from            reader.rs:252
TruncateBarrierLogReader::start_from    connector/src/sink/log_store.rs:317
CoordinatedLogSinker::consume_log_and_sink  connector/src/sink/coordinate.rs:93
```

The `UpdateConfig` branch on `release-3.0` logs `skip alter sink config because properties are unchanged` and returns `Ok(())` without rewinding, but selecting that branch has already cancelled the active `consume_log_and_sink` future. The outer loop then builds a new log sinker, which calls `start_from` on a reader that is no longer in `Reset` — hitting the assertion.

This is reachable from plain user SQL and it aborts the process rather than returning an error, so a deployment pipeline that idempotently re-issues sink `ALTER`s will restart-loop compute nodes.

Observed on a v3.0.2 cluster: two compute nodes aborted simultaneously (exit 133), the barrier could not be collected, the `AlterConnectorProps` call failed with `failed to collect barrier`, and the affected database stalled until recovery completed. It repeated on the next `ALTER`.

## What is included

Two commits, in order:

| Commit | PR | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `e459ee3` | [#26412](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26412) | rewind the log reader on a no-op sink config update |
| `645cd2f` | [#26484](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26484) | keep consuming instead — do not drop the consumer at all |

[#26484](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26484) supersedes [#26412](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26412), but its pre-image assumes [#26412](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26412) is applied. Cherry-picking [#26484](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26484) alone conflicts throughout `src/stream/src/executor/sink.rs`; with [#26412](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/26412) first, the only remaining conflict is the one-hunk test-ordering collision described below.

title: fix(stream): make remote input recovery resilient
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Large streaming graphs currently fail actor initialization when a transient DNS or gRPC connection error escapes from `RemoteInput::new`. Recovery then rebuilds the graph and immediately repeats the same connection burst, which can turn a short endpoint outage into a recovery loop.

This PR makes the recovery path resilient while keeping the retry boundary safe:

- Retry transient failures from `ComputeClientPool::get_by_addr` in the actor task with full-jitter exponential backoff from 100 ms to 10 seconds. This operation only establishes a cached client and has no server-side subscription state; aborting the actor on a term reset cancels the retry loop.
- Preserve transient-error classification through the RPC client cache's `Arc<RpcError>` wrapper, so cached client creation failures enter the retry path.
- Do not retry `get_stream`. A response can be lost after the server has already taken the output receiver, so retrying the subscription is not idempotent.
- Pace remote subscription starts with a compute-wide, cancellation-safe FIFO token producer. Dropped actors automatically leave the queue without reserving future slots, and missed ticks do not catch up in a burst. The default is 2048 subscriptions per second and can be changed with `[streaming.developer] remote_input_subscription_rate_limit`; `0` disables it. As a rule of thumb, keep the rate at or above the remote exchange inputs on the busiest compute node divided by the target recovery seconds. The pacer delay is on the recovery critical path for the whole graph: upstream dispatchers stay pending until downstream inputs subscribe.
- Limit start rate instead of in-flight concurrency. The server waits for the upstream output receiver before returning `get_stream`, so holding a bounded concurrency permit across that wait could deadlock actors with remote-input dependencies.
- Escalate persistent connection failures to a per-peer aggregated warning. Individual retries stay at debug level; once a peer keeps failing, one warning per peer is emitted at most every 5 seconds, carrying the aggregated failure count, so a long outage is visible without a warn-per-actor log storm.

This does not increase the gRPC connection pool or cap the number of established HTTP/2 streams. It only prevents transient client-connect failures from resetting recovery and spreads subscription startup over time.

The new knob is an internal developer config and is included in the generated example config and config reference. There is no supported external interface or compatibility change.

  - Improved recognition of connection errors wrapped by internal operations.
  - Added clearer, rate-limited reporting for repeated upstream connection failures.

The new layer separates the lifetime of a raw event producer from temporary polling and PostgreSQL response boundaries, without changing the active cursor implementation.

- The adapters retain only unread formatted rows. They do not replay rows consumed by a cancelled FETCH. Transactional buffering/replay, per-FETCH raw-column reformatting, and typed seek-key correctness remain in PR5; underlying query formatting retains its existing lifetime.

## What's changed and what's your intention?

This is the third dependency-ordered extraction from #26675 for #26611, based on #26906.

- Add raw cursor chunks with schema/provenance metadata and ordered events for query completion, subscription query startup, log-store epoch transitions, idle boundaries, and schema changes.
- Add a persistent query producer that owns the existing `CursorQueryStream` wrapper, preserving its EOF and unfinished-execution cleanup semantics. Add the subscription stream container, metadata-only state, and weak session planning context without a replacement startup path.
- Add query and subscription PostgreSQL response adapters that reuse existing row formatting and subscription projection helpers. FETCH boundaries retain the producer and unread rows; terminal completion or failure releases the source and metadata.

title: mysql-cdc: finished CDC table enters a recovery loop when upstream MySQL is reachable but binlog is disabled
body:
### Describe the bug

An upstream MySQL that is **reachable but has binary logging disabled** hurts RisingWave more
than one that is **completely unreachable**.

- MySQL stopped (unreachable): the shared `mysql-cdc` source's reader rebuilds its Debezium
  engine once per second (`build stream source reader error, retry in 1s`), no actor exits,
  barriers keep flowing, and streaming resumes by itself when MySQL is back. A `RECOVER` in
  this state was not tried.
- MySQL up with binlog disabled: identical tolerance as long as no recovery happens. But the
  first recovery (manual `RECOVER`, or any other trigger) makes every `mysql-cdc` table with a
  finished backfill fail on startup, which triggers another recovery, and the database loops
  with a ~3 s period until binlog is re-enabled upstream.

The cause is the CDC backfill executor unconditionally querying the upstream binlog position on
startup, even though it has a persisted offset and no longer needs one:

```rust
// src/stream/src/executor/backfill/cdc/cdc_backfill.rs
state.last_cdc_offset.map_or(upstream_table_reader.current_cdc_offset().await?, Some)
```

`map_or` evaluates its default argument eagerly, so `current_cdc_offset()` (`SHOW MASTER STATUS`)
runs on every start and its error kills the actor before the stored offset is considered.

This is also why "unreachable" is the milder case. Before that query, the executor creates its
upstream table reader under an infinite retry backoff while still forwarding barriers, so an
unreachable MySQL keeps the actor alive in that retry (from the code; a recovery with MySQL
down was not tried). A reachable MySQL passes reader creation, and it is the offset query that
fails: with binlog disabled `SHOW MASTER STATUS` returns zero rows. Only a recovery restarts
the backfill executor, which is why the repro needs "binlog disabled" and "recovery" together.

### Error message/log

```text
# rw_event_logs, COLLECT_BARRIER_FAIL (repeats every ~3 s together with
# DATABASE_RECOVERY_START / DATABASE_RECOVERY_SUCCESS)
database 1 reset, in worker node 1: status: 'Internal error', self: "Actor 203 exited unexpectedly: Executor error: Connector error: expect exactly one row when reading binlog offset"

# compute node
ERROR risingwave_stream::task::actor_manager: actor exit with error actor_id=178 error=Executor error: Connector error: expect exactly one row when reading binlog offset
ERROR risingwave_stream::task::barrier_worker: suspend partial graph on error partial_graph_id=8589934591 failed_actor=Some(178) recv actor failure ...

# meta node
WARN risingwave_meta::barrier::worker: database entering recovery database_id=1
```

### To Reproduce

MySQL 8.0 with default settings (binlog on, ROW format), a database `cdc_db` with a table
`products(id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(255), description VARCHAR(512))` holding a few rows.

```sql
CREATE SOURCE mysql_src WITH (
    connector = 'mysql-cdc',
    hostname = 'mysql', port = '3306',
    username = 'root', password = '123456',
    database.name = 'cdc_db',
    server.id = '5001'
);

CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR, description VARCHAR)
FROM mysql_src TABLE 'cdc_db.products';
```

1. Wait for backfill to finish (`SELECT count(*) FROM products` returns the upstream row count).
2. Disable binlog upstream: add `[mysqld] skip-log-bin` to the MySQL config and restart mysqld,
   so that `SHOW MASTER STATUS` returns zero rows. RisingWave stays healthy at this point.
3. Trigger a recovery: `RECOVER;`
4. The loop starts. `SELECT * FROM rw_recovery_info` stays `RECOVERING`; the
   `recovery_latency_count{recovery_type="database 1"}` metric climbs by one every ~3 s.
5. Re-enable binlog and restart mysqld; the loop stops on the next round.

Any other failure of the offset query reproduces it as well, e.g. revoking `REPLICATION CLIENT`
from the CDC user (dynamic, no mysqld restart), which makes `SHOW MASTER STATUS` return
`ERROR 1227 Access denied`.

### Expected behavior

No recove

title: refreshable table: refresh state machine emits spurious Deletes (staging truncated by first finishing actor, recovery resumes merge with partial staging, Idle reset lets RefreshStart overlap CleanUp)
body:
## Describe the bug

The FULL_RELOAD refresh state machine (`MaterializeExecutor` + meta `GlobalRefreshManager`) relies on the invariant that, when an actor runs the merge phase (`main table minus staging table = rows to delete`), the staging table holds every primary key loaded in the current cycle. Three code paths in v3.0.3 break that invariant, so the merge emits `Delete` for rows that still exist upstream. Each spurious `Delete` reaches every downstream MV/index, and combined with the stale-cache problem in https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/27038 the downstream never recovers. On a production v3.0.3 cluster this left a `SELECT DISTINCT` MV missing about half of its groups while the base table was complete, with recurring `agg_group.rs:64 row count should be non-negative` panics.

### (a) Staging table is truncated as soon as the *first* actor finishes, while other actors are still merging

- Each Materialize actor reports refresh finished on its own CleanUp checkpoint barrier (`src/stream/src/task/barrier_worker/managed_state.rs`, `report_refresh_finished` inserts the staging table id into `truncate_tables` for that epoch).
- Meta commits `PruneTableIdsFromSsts(staging)` for that epoch (`src/meta/src/hummock/manager/transaction.rs`) and calls `mark_refresh_complete` (`src/meta/src/barrier/context/context_impl.rs`, `handle_refresh_finished_table_ids`) for every epoch that carries a report, not once after all actors reported.
- The staging table is one shared table partitioned by vnode. Pruning it removes every actor's staging data. Any actor whose merge is still running after that epoch is committed and propagated rebuilds its iterators at the next barrier (`make_mergesort_stream`), sees an empty staging table, and deletes every remaining row in its vnodes.
- The merge loop prefers input barriers (`select_with_strategy(..., PollNext::Left)`) and rebuilds the merge stream on every barrier, so under high barrier latency the spread between actors easily exceeds the commit-plus-propagation delay.

Evidence from the production cluster (2 compute nodes, 96 actors, barrier latency ~18 s):

- Meta logs 3 to 9 `Table refresh completed, state updated to Idle table_id=<t>` lines per refresh cycle, seconds apart (e.g. 8 lines at 14:21, 9 lines at 14:38).
- One cycle: `LoadFinish` received by all actors at 18:14:26; 59 actors logged `resuming CleanUp Stage` by 18:14:28; 36 actors on the other node logged it only at 18:16:30; one more actor entered `Starting table replacement operation` at 18:16:30 and finished at 18:16:34. In the same second five `HashAgg` actors logged `row count should be non-negative ... row_count=-1` and both compute nodes panicked.
- Stragglers of 8 to 120 s appear in most cycles in the log window.

### (b) Recovery resumes at the merge stage with a partially loaded staging table, and the fetch queue is lost

- On startup, if the progress table shows incomplete vnodes, the executor sets `is_refreshing = true` and enters `MergingData` directly (`materialize.rs`, "Recovery: Resuming refresh from merge stage due to incomplete VNodes"). The staging table only contains the rows that were loaded and committed before the crash; everything else in the main table is deleted.
- `BatchIcebergFetchExecutor` keeps `file_queue` / `in_flight_files` in memory only (`FetchState::new()` on every start), so the remaining files of the interrupted cycle are never loaded and `load finished` is never reported for that cycle.

### (c) Recovery resets the refresh job to Idle, so a new `RefreshStart` can overlap the resumed merge

- `src/meta/src/barrier/context/recovery.rs` calls `reset_all_refresh_jobs_to_idle()` during recovery; the scheduler may inject `RefreshStart` for the next cycle while actors are still in the resumed `MergingData`/`CleanUp` of the previous one.
- If that `RefreshStart` barrier is the checkpoint barrier an actor is waiting for in `CleanUp`, the handling order is: report finished, then process `Re

title: feat: support reading `_rw_timestamp` in streaming queries
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

The hidden `_rw_timestamp` system column is currently available in batch queries, but selecting it in a streaming query is explicitly rejected:

```text
Not supported: selecting `_rw_timestamp` in a streaming query is not allowed
```

It would be useful to expose this column to streaming SQL for debugging and observing when rows in an upstream RisingWave table or materialized view were last updated, and to retain that timestamp in downstream materialized views or sinks.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Support explicitly selecting `_rw_timestamp` from a RisingWave table or materialized view in streaming queries. For example:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, payload VARCHAR);

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW events_with_write_time AS
SELECT id, payload, _rw_timestamp AS source_rw_timestamp
FROM events;
```

Preserve the existing batch semantics: a `timestamptz` derived from the upstream row version's storage epoch. Reading or backfilling a row should not replace its timestamp with the current processing time.

Correct retractions are essential for mutable inputs. If a row is inserted at T1 and updated at T2, the stream should retract the old row with T1 and insert the new row with T2:

```text
+ (id=1, payload=A, source_rw_timestamp=T1)
- (id=1, payload=A, source_rw_timestamp=T1)
+ (id=1, payload=B, source_rw_timestamp=T2)
```

Stamping both sides of an update with T2 would break downstream queries that filter, group, or join on this column. Deletes must likewise retract the previously emitted timestamp.

Expected coverage:

- Consistent timestamps across snapshot reads, changelog catch-up, and live upstream consumption.
- Correct insert/update/delete behavior, including multiple changes within an epoch and primary-key changes.
- Correct behavior after recovery and rescaling, including backfill-to-live transitions.
- Explicit rejection of unsupported scan/backfill modes if support is introduced incrementally.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Use batch queries to inspect `_rw_timestamp`; this works for ad hoc debugging but does not expose it to downstream streaming computations.
- Carry an application or connector timestamp as a regular column; this records a different event and does not generally represent the upstream RisingWave row's storage version.

### Additional context

Related original system-column request: #11629. The [documentation](https://docs.risingwave.com/sql/system-catalogs/information-schema) currently describes `_rw_timestamp` as batch-only.

Initial source inspection at `70b0ab709cfc2c6346d61334d0700b07ce72f489` suggests this needs more than removing the [frontend validator](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/blob/70b0ab709cfc2c6346d61334d0700b07ce72f489/src/frontend/src/optimizer/mod.rs#L720):

- **Snapshot backfill:** ordinary `BatchTable` snapshot reads already synthesize `_rw_timestamp` from the storage key. Changelog catch-up and live streaming need additional support. The [changelog row decoder](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/blob/70b0ab709cfc2c6346d61334d0700b07ce72f489/src/storage/src/table/batch_table/mod.rs#L1466) currently projects row values without synthesizing this system column. Catch-up may span several epochs, so assigning the range's end epoch to every row would be incorrect.
- **Arrangement backfill:** its replicated state-table read path needs separate handling to preserve and expose row-version timestamps.
- **Cross-database backfill:** use the upstream database's version timestamps across both snapshots and changelog reads.
- **Planning and live input:** the virtual system column is absent from normal upstream row output, so scan schemas/column mappings and old-row timestamp handling need a design. Possible approaches include retaining timestamps per primary key or exposing version information at storage/materialization boundaries; neither approach is prescribed b

body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).

## Expectations

- `heartbeat.table.auto.initialize` is a strict, connector-neutral boolean option that defaults to `false`; automatic initialization is currently implemented only for Oracle.
- When enabled, RisingWave may create the configured Oracle heartbeat table and insert its canonical seed row, but only within an existing schema and without replacing existing data.
- Concurrent source creation converges through Oracle object uniqueness and primary-key enforcement rather than an application-managed distributed lock.

## Limitations

- RisingWave does not create Oracle schemas or users, repair incompatible heartbeat tables, overwrite existing heartbeat values, or remove Oracle heartbeat objects when a source is dropped.
- If automatic initialization cannot safely produce a compatible table and seed row, validation returns complete state-specific SQL for a DBA to run. For incompatible existing objects, the DBA must resolve the conflict before running that setup SQL.
- The current Oracle e2e tests use direct CDC tables with `FORMAT DEBEZIUM ENCODE JSON`. Shared-source `FORMAT PLAIN ENCODE JSON` coverage remains deferred until Oracle shared-source support is complete.

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Stacked on #26903 and part of #26804. Stack order: #27017 → #26903 → #27128 → #26937 → #26959. This PR is inserted before the Oracle external-reader and event-decoding steps.

- Adds strict frontend and Java validation for `heartbeat.table.auto.initialize`, including CREATE and ALTER handling and rejection for unsupported connectors. Oracle uses its inherited default heartbeat interval when no explicit override is supplied.
- Adds bounded, race-safe Oracle heartbeat initialization for missing tables and seed rows while validating existing table compatibility before writing anything.
- Preserves existing heartbeat values and uses Oracle DDL/object uniqueness and primary-key constraints to recover from concurrent `ORA-00955` and `ORA-00001` races.
- Produces state-specific DBA setup SQL for missing schemas, tables, seed rows, access grants, and incompatible existing objects. Cross-schema setup grants only `UPDATE (HEARTBEAT)` to the exact connector user.
- Adds reusable Oracle service configuration and readiness support to RiseDev and integrates the Oracle fixture into the existing CDC source Buildkite lane.
- Gives the managed Oracle image up to ten minutes to emit its readiness marker while retaining the existing one-minute default for other log-based readiness checks.

## Unit tests

- No new helper-only Java or frontend unit tests are added in this PR; the Oracle initialization contract is covered through the real-Oracle SQLLogicTests below.
- Existing RiseDev tests provide baseline coverage for profile/config expansion while the log-readiness timeout remains configurable per service.

## E2E tests

- Adds serial real-Oracle coverage for missing, empty, and pre-seeded heartbeat tables, including concurrent table/seed initialization, runtime heartbeat activity, and retention of upstream heartbeat objects after RisingWave tables are dropped. These cases omit an explicit interval and exercise Oracle's default.
- Adds exact state-specific DBA SQL assertions for missing schemas, missing tables, missing seed rows, missing UPDATE access, and incompatible tables; the incompatible-table case also verifies that its original schema and data remain unchanged.
- Runs these scenarios through the focused local Oracle profile and the existing CDC source CI lane.

title: feat(common): introduce async stack trace
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [Singularity Data, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/skyzh/0663682a70b0edde7ae991492f2314cb#file-s9y_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

This PR introduces a brand new tracing of _async stack trace_, which allows one to check where all tasks are pending and why it's pending. Note that multiple futures can be polled in a single task with `select` and `join`, so the pending status snapshot is actually a tree instead of a stack.

### Samples

To make it intuitive, here're some samples.

- The chain actor has been running for 1s. The rearranged chain steals a barrier 427ms ago, while the batch query executor on the other arm has waited for the epoch for 829ms and is still unfinished yet. Since there're multiple iterators for different vnodes and we `try_join_all` on them, they're in the same level in the tree.
```
Actor 5170 [1.005471416s]
  Epoch 2771234005188608 [427.634708ms]
    RearrangedChain (actor 5170, executor 181) [427.632666ms]
      BatchQuery (actor 5170, executor 180) [829.7615ms]
        store_wait_epoch [829.638ms]
        store_wait_epoch [829.655416ms]
        store_wait_epoch [829.576041ms]
        ...
      ReceiverExecutor (actor 5170, executor 0) [427.644333ms]
        LocalInput (actor 4111) [427.642458ms]
```

- The source executor received a barrier of `2777905903042560` 156ms ago, while there are no new chunks received for 8s.
```
Actor 8 [8.000397291s]
  Epoch 2777905903042560 [156.222541ms]
    SourceExecutor 800000001 (actor 8, executor 1) [156.219166ms]
      source_recv_barrier [156.218875ms]
      source_recv_chunk [!!! 7.996535125s]
```

- This actor tried to dispatch the barrier to the downstream, but has been back-pressured for 7.5s! Will there be some problems in actor 68?
```
Actor 122 [13.001253875s]
  Epoch 2776266980392960 [!!! 7.793291666s]
    dispatch_barrier [!!! 7.550658708s]
      LocalOutput (actor 68) [!!! 7.5506555s]
```

- For actor 68, there's only one arm in the trace of hash join's barrier aligning, which means the other side has been ready for a while. However, we've waited for 11s on the remote inputs and no messages have been received. There must be some issues.
The epoch number in this actor `2667` is also smaller than the actor 122 `2669`, showing that the concurrent checkpoint is stuck. (A real case from [here](https://github.com/singularity-data/risingwave/issues/4270#issuecomment-1202273243) 😄)
```
Actor 68 [14.501581875s]
  Epoch 2776266751148032 [!!! 11.714676875s]
    ProjectExecutor 4400000082 (actor 68, executor 130) [!!! 11.714678s]
      FilterExecutor 4400000080 (actor 68, executor 128) [!!! 11.714679208s]
        HashJoinExecutor 440000007E (actor 68, executor 126) [!!! 11.714680208s]
          hash_join_barrier_align [!!! 11.714681125s]
            MergeExecutor (actor 68, executor 124) [!!! 11.714596916s]
              RemoteInput (actor 141) [!!! 11.714595583s]
              RemoteInput (actor 142) [!!! 11.714596458s]
              RemoteInput (actor 143) [!!! 11.714597083s]
              ...
```

### Usages

To get the traces printed, one may **launch the cluster with env-var `RW_ASYNC_STACK_TRACE` set** and use `risedev ctl stream trace [--actor-id 233]` to find a recent captured report. You may also print it periodically in the logs by commenting out this line.

https://github.com/singularity-data/risingwave/blob/bc44aa526fced1ddfab523f6d133b05c4ff48a7c/src/compute/src/server.rs#L199-L205

The tags must be attached manually (unless we hack the future compiling in `rustc`). Luckily, it's easy enough by adding a chained call of `.stack_trace(..)`. `&'static str` and `String` are both acceptable here, while the former one may perform better.

https://github.com/singularity-data/risingwave/blob/bc44aa526fced1ddfab523f6d133b05c4ff48a7c/src/storage/src/monitor/monitored_store.rs#L232-L236
