title: feat: support DISTINCT ON in batch query
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [Singularity Data, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/skyzh/0663682a70b0edde7ae991492f2314cb#file-s9y_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

This PR adds `DISTINCT ON` support to batch query.

- In parser, the `select.distinct` field is changed from boolean to an enum `Distinct`.
- In binder, `Distinct` will be transformed to a new enum `BoundDistinct`.
- In planner, the `DISTINCT ON` will be planned to a `LogicalAgg` node **before** projection.
  - the group list is the expressions being distincted on.
  - the aggregations is all other expressions in the select list, with a new `first_value` agg.
  - the `first_value` agg will keep the first non-null value it has seen.
- In expr module, it adds a new `first` aggregator. So far the batch query works.

Note that even we keep the first value in aggregation, the output value of `SELECT` is still unpredictable if no `ORDEY BY` is specified on that column:

```sql
v1 v2
-----
1  2
4  3
4  2
1  3

select distinct on(v1) v2 from t order by v1;
---- 
2
3
----
3
2
----
2
2
----
3
3
# all of them are valid
```

If `ORDER BY` is specified on `v2`, the output **should be** predictable (`2 2`). But this feature is hard to implement on the streaming side (according to @TennyZhuang). So currently it is left unimplemented and the `ORDER BY v2` will be just **ignored**.

In the future PR I'll add a new `first_value` aggregation state to stream executor, in order to support `DISTINCT ON` in materialized view.

title: test(regress): enhance test runner to check expected erroneous query
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [Singularity Data, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/skyzh/0663682a70b0edde7ae991492f2314cb#file-s9y_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Our regress test runner can only test happy cases right now, because the error message is very different from PostgreSQL and the textural comparison of output would certainly fail. Allowing the erroneous queries to be tested has several benefits:
* Make sure RisingWave does not panic on these abnormal queries.
* Ease the progress of adding more regress test files. We no longer need to comment out all erroneous queries.

To achieve this, we simply allow any output messages starting with `ERROR:  ` to be considered matching. But this requires **accurate detection of output starting position of each query**, from a huge text file containing echoed input and execution results of multiple queries.

The old way was based on the empty line following a successful `select`. The new way in this PR is based on the difference between the input and output (either expected or actual). Any extra lines in the output file are assumed to be a result of the preceding matching lines between input & output. See the inline comments for example.

This PR also improves the error reporting of test runner. When a certain case failed, it outputs the diff of that specific query (after potential result sorting), rather than outputs the diff of the whole file, which contains a lot of false positives due to unordered result rows.

Note the diff view of this PR is rendered poorly because the old `compare_results`, `compare_query` and `read_lines` are mostly rewritten.

title: fix(storage): make sstable iter valid while fetching block
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [Singularity Data, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/skyzh/0663682a70b0edde7ae991492f2314cb#file-s9y_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Currently, in `next` of sstable iterator, we will first advance the block iterator, and if the block iterator it invalid, we will then fetch the next block in an `await`. However, when the future is dropped, the sstable iter will be at an invalid state, and in the upper level merge iterator, we wrap the sstable iter with a `Heap::PeekMut`, which when dropped, will get the key of sstable iter to do binary comparison, panic because the sstable iter is at an invalid state.

In this PR, we fix this issue by introducing `try_next` for block iterator, which will not advance when it is going to be invalid and return false, notifying the sstable iter to fetch next block. In this way, while the sstable iterator is fetching the next block, the block iterator is still valid, and there will not be any panic.

sync: new internal semaphore based on intrusive lists
body:
## Motivation

Many of Tokio's synchronization primitives (`RwLock`, `Mutex`,
`Semaphore`, and the bounded MPSC channel) are based on the internal
semaphore implementation, called `semaphore_ll`. This semaphore type
provides a lower-level internal API for the semaphore implementation
than the public `Semaphore` type, and supports "batch" operations, where
waiters may acquire more than one permit at a time, and batches of
permits may be released back to the semaphore.

Currently, `semaphore_ll` uses an atomic singly-linked list for the
waiter queue. The linked list implementation is specific to the
semaphore. This implementation therefore requires a heap allocation for
every waiter in the queue. These allocations are owned by the semaphore,
rather than by the task awaiting permits from the semaphore. Critically,
they are only _deallocated_ when permits are released back to the
semaphore, at which point it dequeues as many waiters from the front of
the queue as can be satisfied with the released permits. If a task
attempts to acquire permits from the semaphore and is cancelled (such as
by timing out), their waiter nodes remain in the list until they are
dequeued while releasing permits. In cases where large numbers of tasks
are cancelled while waiting for permits, this results in extremely high
memory use for the semaphore (see #2237).

## Solution

@Matthias247 has proposed that Tokio adopt the approach used in his
`futures-intrusive` crate: using an _intrusive_ linked list to store the
wakers of tasks waiting on a synchronization primitive. In an intrusive
list, each list node is stored as part of the entry that node
represents, rather than in a heap allocation that owns the entry.
Because futures must be pinned in order to be polled, the necessary
invariant of such a list --- that entries may not move while in the list
--- may be upheld by making the waiter node `!Unpin`. In this approach,
the waiter node can be stored inline in the future, rather than
requiring  separate heap allocation, and cancelled futures may remove
their nodes from the list.

This branch adds a new semaphore implementation that uses the intrusive
list added to Tokio in #2210. The implementation is essentially a hybrid
of the old `semaphore_ll` and the semaphore used in `futures-intrusive`:
while a `Mutex` around the wait list is necessary, since the intrusive
list is not thread-safe, the permit state is stored outside of the mutex
and updated atomically. 

The mutex is acquired only when accessing the wait list — if a task 
can acquire sufficient permits without waiting, it does not need to
acquire the lock. When releasing permits, we iterate over the wait
list from the end of the queue until we run out of permits to release,
and split off all the nodes that received enough permits to wake up
into a separate list. Then, we can drain the new list and notify those
wakers *after* releasing the lock. Because the split operation only
modifies the pointers on the head node of the split-off list and the
new tail node of the old list, it is O(1) and does not require an
allocation to return a variable length number of waiters to notify.


Because of the intrusive list invariants, the API provided by the new
`batch_semaphore` is somewhat different than that of `semaphore_ll`. In
particular, the `Permit` type has been removed. This type was primarily
intended allow the reuse of a wait list node allocated on the heap.
Since the intrusive list means we can avoid heap-allocating waiters,
this is no longer necessary. Instead, acquiring permits is done by
polling an `Acquire` future returned by the `Semaphore` type. The use of
a future here ensures that the waiter node is always pinned while
waiting to acquire permits, and that a reference to the semaphore is
available to remove the waiter if the future is cancelled.
Unfortunately, the current implementation of the bounded MPSC requires a
`poll_acquire

title: Budgeting with a conditional check against an always ready stream blocks the condition
body:
## Version

0.2.20

## Platform

playground

## Description

Taking the first correct example from the [`tokio::select!` docs](https://docs.rs/tokio/0.2.21/tokio/macro.select.html) and running it in the playground results in an infinite hang ([playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=36aebf033dfb30cdae6a21bd54dbe6a5) with println commented out).

The tested code includes an additional `time::delay_for(Duration::from_millis(10)).await;` bit of work in the `some_async_work` which avoids this issue.

This has the same underlying problem as https://github.com/rust-lang/futures-rs/issues/2157, the budgeting is only applied to the conditional and blocks it from ever becoming true, while the actual work continues running because it is not subject to the budgeting.

<!--
Thank you for your Pull Request. Please provide a description above and review
the requirements below.

Bug fixes and new features should include tests.

Contributors guide: https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md

The contributors guide includes instructions for running rustfmt and building the
documentation, which requires special commands beyond `cargo fmt` and `cargo doc`.
-->

## Motivation

For hard cancellation one typically uses `select!` + `oneshot`/`CancellationToken`. However `select` adds one more indent
level, and it creates some troubles for IDE (it is very hard to provide completion inside proc macro).

Alternatively, one can use `AbortHandle` from `futures-util`. However, since `AbortRegistration` is not `Clone`-able, user has
to manage e.g. `Vec<AbortHandle>` if they want to cancel multiple tasks.

That's why I propose implementing something similar to `Abortable` on top of `CancellationToken` (where token itself acts
as abort handle).

<!--
Explain the context and why you're making that change. What is the problem
you're trying to solve? In some cases there is not a problem and this can be
thought of as being the motivation for your change.
-->

## Solution
(Better naming appreciated, of course).
This PR adds new `Wrapped` future adapter that can be roughly defined as 
`Wrapped(fut) := select(token.cancelled(), fut)`.
This adapter is constructed using `wrap_future` method of CancellationToken.

Additionally, I provided `into_cancelled` method on CancellationToken, which returns `'static` future.
`WaitForCancellationFuture` now stores Cow<'_, CancellationToken>. Unfortunately, it made it size 8 bytes larger.
It is possible avoid this memory usage loss, because both CancellationToken and &CancellationToken are non-null
aligned pointers. Therefore, we can use it's lower bit as an enum discriminant. However, it requires some unsafe code
(or using some `crates.io` dependency), so I'd like to see maintainers opinion.

task: implement `JoinMap`
body:
Depends on #4530.

## Motivation

In many cases, it is desirable to spawn a set of tasks associated with
keys, with the ability to cancel them by key. As an example use case for
this sort of thing, see Tower's [`ReadyCache` type][1].

Now that PR #4530 adds a way of cancelling tasks in a
`tokio::task::JoinSet`, we can implement a map-like API based on the
same `IdleNotifiedSet` primitive.

## Solution

This PR adds an implementation of a `JoinMap` type to `tokio::task`,
using the `IdleNotifiedSet` that backs `JoinMap`, and a `HashMap` of the
`AbortHandle`s added in #4530. Keys are stored in both the `HashMap`
*and* alongside the task's `JoinHandle` in the `IdleNotifiedSet` in
order to identify tasks as they complete. This allows returning the key
in `join_one` regardless of whether a task was cancelled, panicked, or
completed successfully, and removing the corresponding `AbortHandle`
from the `HashMap`. Of course, this requires keys to be `Clone`.

 Overall, I think the way this works is pretty straightforward; much of
 this PR is just API boilerplate to implement the union of applicable
 APIs from `JoinSet` and `HashMap`.

Individual tasks can be aborted by key using the `JoinMap::abort`
method, and a set of tasks whose key match a given predicate can be
aborted using `JoinMap::abort_matching`.

When tasks complete, `JoinMap::join_one` returns their associated key
alongside the output from the spawned future, or the key and the
`JoinError` if the task did not complete successfully.

## Bikesheds & Future Work

* I used a mixture of `HashMap` and `JoinSet` naming. Tasks are
`spawn`ed rather than `insert`ed, and `abort`ed rather than `remove`d,
but other methods use map-inspired naming. Open to changing this, of
course!

* We also could change the `join_one` method to only return the future's
output, and not the task's key, but I thought it was nicer to do this

title: sync: fix `notify_waiters` notifying sequential awaits
body:
## Motivation

Closes: #5396

`tokio::sync::Notify` has an internal waiters queue locked behind a mutex. `Notify::notify_waiters` is a function to notify all waiters from this queue. It first acquires the lock, then removes waiters from the queue and wakes them up. However, the whole process is done in batches of 32 waiters to avoid deadlocks. The function has to release the lock before waking up a batch and re-acquire it before proceeding to the next one. In this short timespan another thread can acquire the lock and modify the queue and internal state. For example, it is possible to insert a new waiter to the queue, which will be included in one of the later batches. Current implementation of `notify_waiters` does not account for that, what leads to the unexpected behavior described in #5396.

## Solution

`Notify` tracks the number of calls to `notify_waiters` internally and each time a new `Notified` future is created, the current value of this counter is stored inside the future. The solution is to utilize this counter and compare its value with the number of the current call to `notify_waiters` inside this function. This way, futures created during the `notify_waiters` execution can be filtered out and kept in the queue.

> The select! macro is a powerful tool for managing multiple asynchronous branches, enabling tasks to run concurrently within the same thread. However, its use can introduce challenges, particularly around cancellation safety, which can lead to subtle and hard-to-debug errors. For many use cases, ecosystem alternatives may be preferable as they mitigate these concerns by offering clearer syntax, more predictable control flow, and reducing the need to manually handle issues like fuse semantics or cancellation safety.

task: add `JoinMap::try_join_next`
body:
## Motivation

`tokio_util::task::JoinMap` is a key-tracking wrapper around `JoinSet`. The
underlying `JoinSet` exposes both `join_next` and `try_join_next`, but
`JoinMap` only forwards the async `join_next`. That asymmetry forces callers
who need to drain completed tasks from a synchronous context — e.g. a
non-async `tick()` helper, or a non-async branch of a `select!`-driven event
loop — to pull in `futures-util` solely to call
`FutureExt::now_or_never(self.map.join_next())`.

There's no reason the wrapper should be more restrictive than the primitive
it wraps.

## Solution

Add `JoinMap::try_join_next`, mirroring the existing `join_next`
implementation but delegating to `JoinSet::try_join_next_with_id`. The
id↔key bookkeeping (looping past already-removed entries via
`remove_by_id`) is identical to the async path.

This intentionally does not add a `try_join_next_with_id` variant —
`JoinMap` does not currently expose `join_next_with_id` either, so adding
only the sync `_with_id` form would introduce an asymmetry on the JoinMap
surface. Both can be added together as a follow-up if a use case appears.

- Method documented with a rustdoc example.
- New unit tests in `tokio-util/tests/task_join_map.rs` cover:
  - `None` when the map is empty.
  - `None` when no spawned task has completed yet.
  - `Some((key, Ok(value)))` for a successfully-completed task.
  - `Some((key, Err(JoinError)))` for an aborted task.
  - Subsequent calls advance through additional completed tasks.

rt: add `LocalEventLoop` driven by a host event loop
body:
## Motivation

A Tokio runtime waits by parking a thread in its driver. Where the program is embedded in an event loop that already owns the thread (a GUI toolkit, or a JavaScript host under WebAssembly), the runtime must never block: it needs to return to the host and be called back when it next has work to do.

Today the only way to do that is to drive `block_on` from the host, which blocks. This adds a runtime flavour whose wait belongs to the host loop.

## Solution

Under `tokio_unstable`, `Builder::build_local_event_loop(options, waker)` builds a `LocalEventLoop`: a `LocalRuntime` with the same scheduler and drivers, where parking is replaced by waking the host.

```rs
let el = Builder::new_current_thread().enable_all().build_local_event_loop(Default::default(), host_waker)?;
el.spawn_local(async { ... });
// host: whenever `host_waker` is woken, call `el.drive()`
```

The embedder's whole contract is the `Waker` it passes in and `drive()`. Whatever would have unparked a native runtime's thread wakes the host instead:

* a spawn, or a task woken from another thread (the existing remote-schedule path);
* I/O readiness and timer deadlines: the event loop owns a thread that parks in the driver exactly as a native runtime's thread would, and the wakes it dispatches reach the scheduler through that same remote schedule;
* more ready work after a batch: the runtime wakes the host itself, so the host gets a turn between batches.

A nearer timer registered from a drive unparks the driver thread to re-arm, as on a multi-thread runtime. Nothing about the platform's reactor or timers is exposed, so the API is the same on every target with threads (checked with `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`).

* `drive()` runs one `event_interval` batch. A wake does not guarantee work: the host is woken from every path that would unpark a native runtime's thread, so an empty drive is normal, and calling it without a wake is harmless.
* `block_on(future)` runs the future along with any tasks that become ready, without ever waiting: where `Runtime::block_on` would park, nothing could wake the future from here (its wait belongs to the host loop), so the future is dropped and `block_on` panics. That includes I/O that is already readable, since readiness is delivered by the driver thread rather than by a turn inside `block_on`. Tasks it spawned continue from later drives, and the host is woken for any left ready.
* Like `LocalRuntime`, the event loop is `!Send` and is driven on the thread that built it; other threads spawn through the `Handle`, and `Handle::block_on` from another thread works as on a native runtime.
* `drive` and `block_on` panic if a task panicked under `UnhandledPanic::ShutdownRuntime`, as `Runtime::block_on` does.
* Dropping the event loop stops the driver thread and shuts the runtime down with `LocalRuntime::drop` semantics.
* Neither driver is required: without the I/O driver the thread parks on the usual condvar.

Internally: `CurrentThread::drive_batch` and `block_on_ready` (batches that never park), moving the driver out of the core for the driver thread and back for shutdown, a host `Waker` slot on `driver::Handle` woken from `unpark`, and `runtime/event_loop.rs`.

## Tests

`rt_event_loop` drives the loop the way a host would, with a waker that raises a flag and a host loop that drives when it is raised: idle does not wake; spawn wakes and queues until driven; a busy batch wakes again, including for tasks left in the inject queue when a batch ends at `event_interval`; a timer wakes at its deadline in a bounded number of wakes; a nearer timer re-arms; a cancelled timer does not wake; wakes from another thread, from another event loop, and a spawn from another thread through the `Handle`; a TCP round trip between two event loops; `block_on` of ready work, of a pending timer (panics at the caller without waiting, the timer disarmed and the runtime intact), and leaving spawned tasks behind in either queue (they run

title: configuration: ability to mark a component as `final`/`terminal` in the topology
body:
### Current Vector Version

```
vector 0.18.0 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu c77e085 2021-11-18)
```

### Use-cases

With the newly introduced ability to [route dropped events in Vector](https://vector.dev/highlights/2021-11-18-failed-event-routing/) 🎉 , a very common use-case for it (in our opinion) is to better instrumentalise our Vector pipelines.

For example, consider the following pipeline configuration where dropped messages are centrally logged by a logger transform, thus keeping the real-work transforms cleaner:

```yaml
sources:
  stdin:
    type: stdin
    decoding:
      codec: bytes

transforms:
  parse-syslog:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - stdin
    drop_on_error: true
    reroute_dropped: true
    source: |-
      . = parse_syslog!(.message)
  parse-key-value:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - parse-syslog
    drop_on_error: true
    reroute_dropped: true
    source: |-
      . = parse_key_value!(.message)

  dropped-logger:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - parse-syslog.dropped
      - parse-key-value.dropped
    drop_on_error: true
    source: |-
      host = string!(.host)
      message = string!(.message)
      component_id = string!(.metadata.dropped.component_id)
      log("component '" + component_id + "' dropped message from <" + host + ">: " + message, level: "warn")

sinks:
  console:
    type: console
    inputs:
      - parse-key-value
    encoding: json
```

However, the above topology has one little caveat: the `dropped-logger` transform does not go anywhere else because it is just there for calling the `log()` function and that is. This leads to Vector giving the following warning:
```
2021-11-19T13:52:23.397844Z  WARN vector::config::loading: Transform "dropped-logger" has no consumers
```

### Attempted Solutions

The only attempted solution for now is to simply ignore the warning from Vector. However, we believe that Vector can be smarter here and only emit that warning when a component truly _needs_ a consumer down the line. See the proposal section below.

### Proposal

To help Vector determine if a component should have consumers or not, we propose the addition of a new boolean configuration key named `is_final` or `is_terminal` (to give some examples). The purpose of this configuration is to mark a component either as final/terminal or not in the topology. For example:

```yaml
  dropped-logger:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - parse-syslog.dropped
      - parse-key-value.dropped
    drop_on_error: true
    is_final: true
    is_terminal: true  # alternative
    source: |-
      host = string!(.host)
      message = string!(.message)
      component_id = string!(.metadata.dropped.component_id)
      log("component '" + component_id + "' dropped message from <" + host + ">: " + message, level: "warn")
```

In this way, if a component is marked final/terminal, then Vector can safely ignore the fact that it doesn't have any consumers and avoid emitting the warning.

The above proposal would be quite general-purpose functionality for Vector, however another solution for the particular use-case described, is to introduce an `internal_logs` **sink** where dropped messages could be routed to. This sink could have all the typical configurations such as which fields you want to include in the log.

title: Implement a proper topology stop  strategy
chore(buffers): wait for space in disk_v2 write/flush when out of space I/O error occurs
body:
Currently, `SenderAdapter` will panic when it encounters errors from either `disk_v2::Writer::write_record` or `disk_v2::Writer::flush`. This happens even if the error is related to simply being out of space, vs an `fsync` failing or spurious errors because the volume is actually logically/physically degraded.

In the case of being out of space, we should be able to depend on the invariant that `std::io::Write` will [always return `Ok(n)` if it managed a partial write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/trait.Write.html#errors), so we should always be able to know our current state in terms of bytes written to the file, but not _flushed_ to disk.

All of that said, we could conceivably tweak the I/O flow path such that we could control all of the actual `write` calls, paying attention for "out of space" errors, and then retry again once there is more free space.

## Open questions

- How do we actually measure free space?
- How do we "wait" for it? (poll on interval? is there any sort of `inotify`-style approach available?)
- Do we need to tighten up anything in the "minimum buffer size" logic to ensure we don't overextend the maximum configured buffer size?
- If we had a way to check the amount of free space, could we also check total space of the volume where the buffer data lives?
- If we could do that, should we also make buffer creation error out if it's bigger than the maximum size of the volume, given the chance for hitting out of space issues?

title: fix(buffers): correctly handle partial writes in reader seek during initialization
body:
## Context

In some cases, a buffer can fail to reopen after Vector has been stopped in an impromptu fashion, due to a partially-written record that causes the reader to loop endlessly, waiting for data that can't possibly arrive.

Fixes #16525, #16463, and #16231.

## Solution

In this PR, we've simply piggybacked on some existing logic in the reader -- logic which decides whether or not it should keep waiting for data or should return that there wasn't enough data -- in order to avoid endlessly looping during the buffer initialization phase.

This ensures that when we indicate that the read should be "finalized" -- either the writer is done or we're still getting the buffer initialized -- and there's either not enough data to read the length delimiter, or there's not as many bytes as the length delimiter indicates there should be... we properly return an error indicating a partial write.

Additionally, we've tweaked the reader initialization logic to properly ignore these errors, and other non-I/O-based errors, as they should not be bubbled up to the user, as the errors may have come from previously-processed records _or_ will be correctly handled during the next read _after_ the buffer is initialized.

## Testing

A new unit test is included that exercises this behavior, and I approached it in the TDD style or writing it first, observing that it failed, and then fixing it.

title: fix(kafka source): fix acknowledgement handling during shutdown and rebalance events
body:
This adds some integration tests and a fix for the kafka source to fully drain acknowledgements during consumer group rebalancing and at shutdown, and should close #14761 

Prior related work: https://github.com/vectordotdev/vector/pull/16928

### Overview 

I discussed this a bit over in https://github.com/vectordotdev/vector/discussions/16827, the implementation here essentially follows that outline:

- Run a separate task to handle acknowledgements (additionally, handle acknowledgements for separate kafka partitions on separate streams, for cleaner handling when rebalancing partition assignments)
- Add coordination between the kafka client task and acknowledgement task, so that at rebalance and shutdown time, we have the best possible chance of processing all pending acknowledgements

Here is a visual representation of what I'm going for:

[![](https://mermaid.ink/img/pako:eNp1kluPmzAQhf_KyE9blaDEZJOAVnlaqa-V-tZSrSYwgAXYrG32FuW_d4Ds5qL0BaEZn8_njGcvMpOTSISj5550Ro8KS4ttqgE6tF5lqkPtocaixutiS85hSU8eXX3dw6z-qsMkn223388lCZTW9B1Y2mGDfDc8oHOq1C0xQOnCbCe1Np7AqrLyYIqJlcCPUascd1_5MCCkorPEHpQuT8xUgPPo6Rbp0szJRoZNs-MADnaNyWrwFdd6awdbp0znao72GXgAvZiaTdz96RYBdDKAMAz_BlzXOX28mN5BVqH-NmE-dbMLRm6RM3WsGNKMXgpjJzTl06S9MtrdynXCPJqhBQ2x8YpnRW8ZsXwINI4RHIdgDHjVkun9laXt9nJEoyvW3-XWdP_JczEWJhyfKzNtq_yTKQpH_uj6xhRnx-M_rRmdvipfnb2MCERLtkWV88ruB0oqOEzLz5zwb04F9o1PRaoPfBR7b36960wk3vYUiL7LeROOGy6SAhvHVV5XkezFm0gWq3C5iDfRchGt4pXcxIF4F4mU61Dey9U85m8s4_UhEB_GMGARRvfLjYwiOY9WG7mey5H2e2wOVx7-AUdIJk0?type=png)](https://mermaid.live/edit#pako:eNp1kluPmzAQhf_KyE9blaDEZJOAVnlaqa-V-tZSrSYwgAXYrG32FuW_d4Ds5qL0BaEZn8_njGcvMpOTSISj5550Ro8KS4ttqgE6tF5lqkPtocaixutiS85hSU8eXX3dw6z-qsMkn223388lCZTW9B1Y2mGDfDc8oHOq1C0xQOnCbCe1Np7AqrLyYIqJlcCPUascd1_5MCCkorPEHpQuT8xUgPPo6Rbp0szJRoZNs-MADnaNyWrwFdd6awdbp0znao72GXgAvZiaTdz96RYBdDKAMAz_BlzXOX28mN5BVqH-NmE-dbMLRm6RM3WsGNKMXgpjJzTl06S9MtrdynXCPJqhBQ2x8YpnRW8ZsXwINI4RHIdgDHjVkun9laXt9nJEoyvW3-XWdP_JczEWJhyfKzNtq_yTKQpH_uj6xhRnx-M_rRmdvipfnb2MCERLtkWV88ruB0oqOEzLz5zwb04F9o1PRaoPfBR7b36960wk3vYUiL7LeROOGy6SAhvHVV5XkezFm0gWq3C5iDfRchGt4pXcxIF4F4mU61Dey9U85m8s4_UhEB_GMGARRvfLjYwiOY9WG7mey5H2e2wOVx7-AUdIJk0)


A few oddities come up around how `rdkafka`, and particularly the rebalance handlers work in async code. The `pre_rebalance` hook is called internally by the kafka client while polling for new messages on the message stream, so that task (and the rebalance process itself) will be blocked until it returns. That callback handler isn't async, so it can't yield or receive on async channels, and must run on a `spawn_blocking` thread. The task handling acknowledgements can be async and can run as a normal `tokio::spawn` task. 

This just has implications for what can be used to coordinate between the two:

- the message task (on which rebalance hooks run) can _send_ messages on a tokio mpsc channel to the acknowledgement task, but must use an `Unbounded` channel since sending on a bounded tokio channel requires an async context. Overlapping rebalance events will not happen, so this unbounded channel should never have more than 1 message on it.
- the message task can receive on a `std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel`. This uses a bound size 0, to act as a rendezvous channel, so the acknowledgement task can signal when acks have drained (or when a timeout is reached).

I also found that to properly test this, the source needed to be able to "consume until the end of the partition(s)" rather than "consume a specified number of messages". This is enabled by the `enable.partition.eof` flag, which I've enabled as an option (gated by `cfg(test)` in a couple places where it's needed outside of the actual test module).

When running these tests locally, I've found it is easiest to use an existing kafka topic pre-populated with, say 100k messages (for some reason, the way the tests write messages in to kafka is very slow; I haven't looked into why that is, yet). For the automated runs in CI we may ne

body:
## Summary

Add optional `framing` and `decoding` configuration to the `splunk_hec` source. When set, the inner payload is decoded after the HEC envelope is parsed, with envelope metadata layered on top so decoder-produced fields win on conflict. Both endpoints supported; legacy behavior preserved when unset.

## Vector configuration

JSON second-stage decode on the `/event` endpoint:

```yaml
sources:
  hec:
    type: splunk_hec
    address: 0.0.0.0:8088
    valid_tokens: ["test-token"]
    event:
      decoding:
        codec: json
```

Per-token routing with a VRL decoder and `store_hec_token`:

```yaml
sources:
  hec_in:
    type: splunk_hec
    address: 0.0.0.0:8088
    valid_tokens:
      - "token-team-a"
      - "token-team-b"
    store_hec_token: true
    event:
      decoding:
        codec: vrl
        vrl:
          source: |
            token = get_secret!("splunk_hec_token")

            if token == "token-team-a" {
              .team = "team-a"
              .environment = "production"
            } else if token == "token-team-b" {
              .team = "team-b"
              .environment = "staging"
            } else {

sinks:

    encoding:

```

title: fix(gcp_pubsub source): recover from stalled streams and reduce error noise
body:
## Summary

The `gcp_pubsub` source could stop processing messages until Vector was restarted, and floods the logs with misleading `failed_fetching_events` errors on idle/low-volume/bursty subscriptions. This addresses both:

- Send HTTP/2 keepalive pings so a silently broken connection is detected instead of hanging (interval/timeout configurable via the new `keepalive` option, mirroring the `vector` sink).
- Use a non-blocking keepalive send so a backed-up request channel can't deadlock the task.
- Add `idle_timeout_secs` (default `900`) to restart a stream that stops delivering responses without erroring.
- Only escalate stream failures to a component error after `max_retry_errors` (default `5`) consecutive failures with no successful fetch in between; transient failures are logged at `debug`. A successful fetch resets the counter.

## How did you test this PR?

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, unit tests, and `vdev check events` all pass (run in a Rust 1.95 container).

Testing caveat, in the interest of transparency: the runtime behavior here is hard to cover with automated tests. The `code=8a75` "no messages" response is a real-GCP behavior that the Pub/Sub emulator does not reproduce, and exercising the stalled-connection recovery (HTTP/2 keepalive + idle timeout) would require fault-injection infrastructure that doesn't currently exist in the repo. The existing gcp_pubsub emulator tests are also disabled (#24133). Unit tests here therefore only cover the config validation; the retry-escalation and connection-resilience changes are validated by reasoning and would benefit from manual verification against a real GCP subscription.

title: feat(sources): add disconnect_mode option to TCP sources
body:
## Summary

Adds a `disconnect_mode` configuration option to TCP sources (socket, logstash, fluent, syslog, statsd) that controls how connections are closed on shutdown or when `max_connecti
on_duration_secs` elapses.

The two modes are:

- `drain` (the default and existing behaviour) - sends a `FIN` and waits for the client to close.
- `abort` - sets `SO_LINGER=0` to force close immediately with `RST`.

The original motivation is "write-only" clients such as [Serilog.Sinks.Network](https://github.com/serilog-contrib/Serilog.Sinks.Network) that never read from the socket and ther
efore cannot detect a graceful shutdown. Additionally, the "reference implementations" for the beats (logstash) and fluent protocols also use an abort style shutdown:

- [Logstash beats input](https://github.com/logstash-plugins/logstash-input-beats/blob/4898d37c63255c109bea73f3c7eccdd0421f532f/src/main/java/org/logstash/beats/Server.java#L72)
- [Fluentd server](https://github.com/fluent/fluentd/blob/ead4c3d06685de751d8c4c92e448411c617dded5/lib/fluent/plugin_helper/server.rb#L288-L289)

All sources default to `drain`, so this is opt-in with no behaviour change for existing configs.

## Vector configuration

```yaml
sources:
  tcp_in:
    type: socket
    mode: tcp
    address: "0.0.0.0:9000"
    shutdown_timeout_secs: 5
    disconnect_mode: abort  # omit for default drain behaviour
sinks:
  out:
    type: console
    inputs: [tcp_in]
    encoding:
      codec: text
```

## How did you test this PR?

- Manual testing with netcat and a write-only Python client against both modes, verifying FIN and RST behaviour using `tcpdump`.
- A new unit test added to `sources::socket`:
  - `tcp_disconnect_mode_abort_on_shutdown` - verifies RST is received immediately on shutdown.

title: feat(opentelemetry): Add two-stage request admission
body:
## Summary

Add shared two-stage admission control for OTLP/HTTP and OTLP/gRPC requests. The outer limit bounds queued plus active requests, while the inner limit bounds requests that can collect, decompress, decode, and send events. Overload and timeout responses remain retryable for both protocols.

### Detailed Explanation

#### Shared request controller

During source construction, the OpenTelemetry source creates one `RequestControl` and shares it between the HTTP and gRPC servers. Its two Tokio semaphores are therefore shared across every connection, protocol, and OTLP signal handled by that source: HTTP logs compete for the same capacity as gRPC metrics or traces.

The outer capacity is configured with `max_concurrent_requests` and defaults to ten times the Vector runtime worker count. The inner capacity is the runtime worker count. `request_timeout_secs`, which defaults to 30 seconds, applies to the complete admitted request lifetime.

#### Two-stage admission

Each protocol-specific layer constructs the following Tower stack, ordered from outermost to innermost:

```text
Timeout
  └─ LoadShed
      └─ outer global concurrency limit
          └─ bounded buffer
              └─ inner global concurrency limit
                  └─ existing OTLP service
```

The outer semaphore bounds all admitted work: both actively processing requests and requests waiting in the buffer. Once it is full, `LoadShed` immediately rejects new work instead of allowing another unbounded waiting population.

The bounded buffer lets admitted requests wait for processing capacity. The inner semaphore limits requests executing the OTLP handler to the runtime worker count, preventing an admitted burst from starting excessive concurrent decode, pipeline-send, and acknowledgement work.

The timeout wraps both stages. It includes time waiting for an inner permit, OTLP processing, delivery to the Vector pipeline, and acknowledgement handling. Timed-out or cancelled requests release their semaphore permits through the normal future-drop path.

#### Tower readiness handling

Tower communicates admission failures through `poll_ready`, before `call` receives the request. `RequestControlService` preserves that contract: it polls the wrapped service, stores any readiness error, reports itself ready, and converts the error into the appropriate HTTP or gRPC response on the corresponding `call`. This produces a valid retryable OTLP response instead of surfacing overload as a connection-level service failure.

Readiness reservations are local to a service clone and are intentionally not copied by `Clone`.

#### HTTP flow

```text
TCP/TLS listener
  └─ tracing and connection-age layers
      └─ request admission
          └─ Warp routing
              └─ capped_body()
                  └─ decompress and decode
                      └─ send events to the Vector pipeline
                          └─ optional acknowledgement
```

Admission wraps `warp::service(...)`, so it runs before the Warp filters reach `capped_body()`. A request rejected at the outer limit therefore has no body read, buffered, decompressed, or decoded.

HTTP overload returns `429 Too Many Requests`; timeout returns `503 Service Unavailable`. Both responses contain a protobuf OTLP `Status` with code `Unavailable`, allowing clients to treat them as retryable failures. Unexpected middleware failures return `503 Service Unavailable` with the same OTLP status code.

#### gRPC flow

```text
gRPC HTTP/2 stream
  └─ connection-age and tracing layers
      └─ request admission
          └─ DecompressionAndMetricsLayer
              └─ Tonic logs, metrics, or traces service
                  └─ decode OTLP payload
                      └─ send events to the Vector pipeline
                          └─ optional acknowledgement
```

The new routes-and-layer server helper inserts admission before `DecompressionAndMetricsLayer`. Requests rejected at the outer limit therefore do not consume decompression or ha

title: chore: Topology test refactoring
prevent select!-correctness problems for simple sources
body:
There is a subtlety when using `select!`: when one future finishes, the other is _dropped_. This CAN cause subtle logic bugs and data loss (see https://tomaka.medium.com/a-look-back-at-asynchronous-rust-d54d63934a1c for more details). In the case of this pr, if the `SimpleSource`'s `start`-ed future finishes, then the timestamper `tick` future could be stopped in the middle of sleeping, or worse, in the middle of sending a result onto the bounded channel (https://github.com/MaterializeInc/materialize/blob/56a39246007194914cd02cfdcef0c4874b2ac7f9/src/dataflow/src/source/mod.rs#L716-L732)

In practice, this doesn't happen, because simple-source futures are long-running, and when they finish we `break;` but if we add short-running ones, or add more futures managing state, we could see bugs, so I figured I should change it now.

I chose to use `Pin::set` to reset the `tick` future here because it was the simplest. I would have preferring moving the interval out into the `select!` statement, but this would require a larger refactor, where simple-sources's adopt some sort of poll model. @petrosagg let me know if thats better

title: persist: overhaul timeouts, errors, retries
body:
See individual commits for details.

Summary:
- persist methods no longer have timeouts and instead retry indefinitely. Instead, persist Futures offer "cancel on drop" semantic and users are free to wrap them in tokio::time::timeout.
- persist now returns ExternalError in only a few exceptional places, most notably WriteHandle::compare_and_append. This is because WriteHandle::compare_and_append is not always safe to retry depending on the usage pattern. We should be able to structure timestamp binding, source, and sink code so it's always safe to retry, but SQL txns will have to pass the error back to the user (or risk double committing the txn). Once we introduce a determinate/indeterminate split for ExternalError, WriteHandle::compare_and_append could also retry determinate errors and only send back indeterminate ones (the opposite of Location::open).
- InvalidUsage is now statically derivable from arguments. It should be safe for well-behaved users to `.expect("invalid persist usage")` on InvalidUsage.

title: Explain: show fast path.
body:
### Motivation

  * This PR adds a feature that has not yet been specified.

It is currently not obvious when we use fast path or slow path to answer a one-off select query. In this PR, fast path has been distinguished from slow path by adding a new operator `ReadExistingIndex` that can show up in `explain optimized plan` (which is the default `explain`).

Sample output for a query using fast path:
```
materialize=> explain select 1, * from foo where userid = 'blah' limit 1;
                    Optimized Plan                     
-------------------------------------------------------
 %0 = 
 | ReadExistingIndex materialize.public.foo_idx3
 | Map 1
 | Filter (#1 = "blah")
 | Project (#2, MaterializeInc/database-issues#1, #0)

 Finish order_by=() limit=1 offset=0 project=(#0..=#2)
```

Sample output for a query using fast path where evaluating a filter has been sped up by the presence of an appropriate index:
```
materialize=> explain select * from foo where action = 2 limit 1;
                    Optimized Plan                    
------------------------------------------------------
 %0 =
 | ReadExistingIndex materialize.public.foo_idx3
 | | Lookup value (2)
 | Filter (#0 = 2)
 | Project (#1, #0)

 Finish order_by=() limit=1 offset=0 project=(#0, MaterializeInc/database-issues#1)
```

I considered formatting the output as `ReadExistingIndex <index name> (<source/view name> (<columns>))` but decided against it for two reasons:
* The output gets long when you have both the index and source/view name. For the example above, it would look like: `ReadExistingIndex materialize.public.foo_idx3 (materialize.public.foo(<columns>))`
* The names of the columns are not in the catalog; they are in system tables. For the example above, the best I can do without issuing a system table query is `ReadExistingIndex materialize.public.foo_idx3 (materialize.public.foo(#1))`, which is not very useful.

In order to be able to identify whether we're being asked for an explanation of a view or one-off select query, I pass in the view id when asked for an explanation of a view. This means that I conveniently get to fulfill a TODO in the code, and the explain plan for a view has changed from something like:
```
> EXPLAIN PLAN FOR VIEW mv;
Source materialize.public.data (UID):
| Filter (#0 = 1), (#3 = 4)
| Project (#0, MaterializeInc/database-issues#3)

Query:
%0 =
| Get materialize.public.data (UID)
| Filter (#0 = 1), (#3 = 4)
| Project (#3)
```
to:
```
> EXPLAIN PLAN FOR VIEW mv;
Source materialize.public.data (UID):
| Filter (#0 = 1), (#3 = 4)
| Project (#0, MaterializeInc/database-issues#3)

View materialize.public.mv (UID):
%0 =
| Get materialize.public.data (UID)
| Filter (#0 = 1), (#3 = 4)
| Project (#3)
```

There has also been some minor refactoring:
* pretty-printing of indices has been moved from `src/expr/src/explain.rs` to `src/ore/src/str.rs`
* To me, it is kind of silly that we delegate the conversion of `RowSetFinishing` to `String` to different `*Explanation` objects when each `*Explanation` object prints out the `RowSetFinishing` exactly the same. So I implemented `Display` for `RowSetFinishing`.

### Discussion items/TODOs

Our optimization pipeline looks like this:
SQL -> Raw -> Decorrelated -> Optimized -> Physical -> PeekDataflowPlan

Thus, in order to have fast path show up in `explain optimized plan`, I have to run the optimization pipeline all the way to the end, and if the one-off query ends up going on the fast path, I overwrite its original optimized plan with the fast path plan.

Running the optimization pipeline all the way to the end has the downside that we wouldn't be able to use `explain optimized plan` to print the optimized plan if there is a crash in the `Optimized -> Physical` transformation. I would like to add an option `SAFE` to `explain` that if set to true would always only run the optimization pipeline up to just the optimized stage.

title: storage: resume ingestion on restart
body:
This is the first part of making source ingestion fault tolerant. With
this PR the storage controller durably records the persist shard ids of
all sources and the `storaged` process is changed in such a way that it
can resume appending data to the definite collection.

Tables are an exception to the above and maintain the previous behaviour
where new shards are minted every time the storage controller restarts
and are never durably persisted.

Postgres sources are also an exception to the above because unlike
sources like Kafka we lose the ability to generate a full snapshot at
the LSN of a replication slot once the initial transaction that created
it has ended. This means that a `storaged` instance that just restarted
has no way of reproducing the previous stream. This won't be an issue
when we wire up start offsets correctly in which case the postgres
source reader will completely skip the snapshot phase and just read from
the replication slot.

Lastly, while this PR makes source ingestion fault tolerant in the sense
that after restarts we can resume correctly it does not yet do the
optimization that we skip ahead in the upstream system. For example for
Kafka we will re-read everything from the beginning and just drop all
data that is not beyond the current upper frontier on the floor. This is
wasteful but has the sideeffect of fully re-hydrating the in-memory
state of the ingestion pipeline.

After this gets merged I'll work on a follow up PR that implements the
optimization described above for simple cases like NONE envelope
sources.

title: Internal sinks, part 3: coordinator plumbing
body:
This is the third PR in support of the internal storage sinks feature (#12860).

* Part 1 (#13251) massaged our existing persist sinks implementation to look like the internal sinks we want.
* Part 2 (#13324) added support for the `RECORDED VIEW` syntax in SQL.

Part 3 now introduces the necessary plumbing in the coordinator to connect everything together. This means recorded views work now (roughly) as intended:

```sql
-- demo that we can sink and source
materialize=> CREATE TABLE t (a int, b int);
CREATE TABLE
materialize=> INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6);
INSERT 0 3
materialize=> CREATE RECORDED VIEW v AS SELECT a + b FROM t;
CREATE RECORDED VIEW
materialize=> SELECT * FROM v;
 ?column?
----------
        3
        7
       11
(3 rows)

-- demo that other stuff can build on top of recorded views
materialize=> CREATE DEFAULT INDEX ON v;
CREATE INDEX
materialize=> CREATE RECORDED VIEW v2 AS SELECT * FROM v;
CREATE RECORDED VIEW
materialize=> DELETE FROM t WHERE a != 1;
DELETE 2
materialize=> SELECT * FROM v2;
 ?column?
----------
        3
(1 row)

-- demo that dropping takes dependents into account
materialize=> DROP RECORDED VIEW v;
ERROR:  cannot drop materialize.public.v: still depended upon by catalog item 'materialize.public.v2'
materialize=> DROP RECORDED VIEW v CASCADE;
DROP RECORDED VIEW
```

#### Future Work

After this PR, the following TODOs are left for the internal sinks feature to be complete:
* Remove support for `CREATE SINK ... INTO PERSIST` (https://github.com/MaterializeInc/materialize/pull/13380)
* Introduce a helpful error when a user does `DROP VIEW <recorded-view>`, `ALTER VIEW <recorded-view>`, or `SHOW CREATE VIEW <recorded-view>`
* Disallow creating recorded views on log sources.
* Add support for `EXPLAIN`.
* Add support for `SHOW OBJECTS`.
* Add support for `SHOW INDEXES`.
* Propagate dataflow errors.

Also, there is work left to switch away from the placeholder `RECORDED VIEW` name to something better (see [Internal storage sink syntax](https://www.notion.so/materialize/Internal-storage-sink-syntax-017251c532df465fb3a3ec7c344df54b)).

title: Record Storage Usage Snapshots in System Table
body:
Resolves MaterializeInc/database-issues#3700 

Capture periodic snapshots of Materialize storage usage at the storage object level, and keep them in a new system table: `mz_storage_usage`. Per [internal design doc Persist Storage Usage Data](https://www.notion.so/materialize/Persist-Storage-Usage-Data-19bd434424df4d8395d9355e05f46b1a)

```
materialize=> select * from mz_catalog.mz_storage_usage;
id | object_id | size_bytes |    collection_timestamp    
---+------------+---------------+-------------------------------
1  | <null>    |      12345 | 2022-07-19 05:43:16.853+00
2  | <null>    |      12345 | 2022-07-19 05:39:16.867+00
3  | <null>    |      12345 | 2022-07-19 05:41:16.88+00

```

The usage "snapshot" collection runs on an hourly interval, and queries the Persist API added in MaterializeInc/materialize#13754 and MaterializeInc/materialize#13969 to obtain storage utilization details. Each row represents a snapshot in time, and the table is append-only. A future PR for [cloud:#3716](https://github.com/MaterializeInc/cloud/issues/3716) will add cleanup/reaping of outdated rows past a certain time window.

In the first iteration of this table population, there will not be any `object_id`s, as there is additional work required to map the Persist API shard ids to our concept of mz storage objects.

#### Open questions:

- ~Should the collection interval be configurable?~ A small code change to alter the config is good enough
- What is the best format for the collection timestamp?
- ~Should the `object_id` be nullable, since we might expect some rows with no object information (such as orphaned blobs, MaterializeInc/database-issues#3876 ), even longterm?~ Yes

#### Future Work
- [cloud:#3716](https://github.com/MaterializeInc/cloud/issues/3716) - Reap entries older than x days (probably 60)
- Map storage object ids to shard ids returned by the Persist API

### Motivation

  * This PR adds a known-desirable feature. [Cloud:#1467](https://github.com/MaterializeInc/cloud/issues/1467), MaterializeInc/database-issues#3700 

We need to record storage utilization both for internal consumption as well as to provide users with storage metrics.

title: Remove some Threshold operators that have no effect
body:
This is preliminary work, up for handing off to the optimization team, to remove `Threshold` operators that can be seen to not have any effect. Essentially, in situations like
```
Threshold( A - Subset(A) )
```
where `A` contains no negative multiplicities, we can remove the `Threshold`, because we are certain that its argument will have no negative multiplicities.

This PR is a first cut at that, with some crude supporting methods and no tests yet. It has been tested by inspection to correctly remove the `Threshold` from cases such as
```sql
SELECT * FROM input EXCEPT ALL (SELECT * FROM input WHERE field = 7);
```
and 
```sql
SELECT * FROM input
EXCEPT ALL
SELECT * FROM
    (SELECT DISTINCT field1 FROM input) grp,
    LATERAL (
        SELECT field2 FROM bar
        WHERE field1 = grp.field1
        LIMIT 1
    )
```
In both cases, the outermost operator is a `Union` with the expected `Threshold` removed.

I had some surprising moments along the way, and there may well be some bugs and some opportunities for further optimization (e.g. `Distinct` could also be accepted, and there are broader strokes to use for determination if `A` contains no negative multiplicities).

Fixes MaterializeInc/database-issues#4018

title: sql: guard fallible cast expression
body:
SQL doesn't guarantee the order of execution of expressions in the
SELECT part of query and the WHERE part of a query.

It can happen that the optimizer chooses to run the SELECT expressions
*before* applying the WHERE clause, even if that particular row would be
filtered out in the opposite case. This has the bad sideeffect of an
error being produced from a row that would have participated in the
output.

This PR changes the SELECT project of postgres CREATE VIEWS such that it
only evaluates the CAST expressions if the WHERE condition is true by
wrapping each CAST expression in a CASE statement.

title: persist: bounded memory compaction
body:
<!--
Describe the contents of the PR briefly but completely.

If you write detailed commit messages, it is acceptable to copy/paste them
here, or write "see commit messages for details." If there is only one commit
in the PR, GitHub will have already added its commit message above.
-->

This PR updates compaction to work within a specific memory bound. It introduces the notion of a Run, which is a sequence of possibly-sorted batch parts. Compaction proceeds in a few phases:

1. Run selection, where we select an ordering for which runs should be merged into others. We select the first run of each input, then the second run ... until all runs are selected. We then chunk up runs to be physically compacted together, based on our memory bound and size of the largest part within each run.
2. Compaction over chunks of runs. We pull down 1 batch part from each run at a time, put the updates into a heap, and then read out of the heap until all updates are exhausted. When all updates for a part are consumed, we pull down the next part from its original run.

This gives a nice property that compacting N sorted runs together always yields 1 run. Inputs are not required to be sorted, and are expected to converge over time through compaction. For now, the memory bound is a fixed threshold, in the future it may be tied in to the specific container sizing allowing us to scale up and shrink down how many runs compaction can process together.

title: timely-util: no nonsense timely/async bridge
body:
## Motivation

This PR provides a new async/timely integration that as far as I can tell has no weird invariants that the user needs to now about and so it's hopefully much harder to misuse than the previous `build_async` method.

The piece that makes this possible is the `AsyncInputHandle` type that correctly wires up async `Wakers` and a manual `Future` implementation that allows users to naturally call `input.next().await` on a handle and/or safely use these future in a `select!` loop. 

The handle's `next()` method behaves like an async iterator, resolving to `None` when there are no more notifications to be received, and gives out an enum of `Event::Data(capability, data)` when there is data in the input or `Event::Progress(frontier)` when the frontier has advanced.

On top of the generic `builder_async::OperatorBuilder` this PR also implements `Operator::unary_async`, `Operator::binary_async`, `Operator::sink_async` and a freestanding function `operator::source_async`.

title: test: Fix flaky storage test
body:
The pg-snapshot-resumption test was flakey and sometimes failing. The reason was that in step 03, Materialize was sometimes unable to select a valid timestamp for the query and would hang forever.

The test purposely crashes STORAGED, which prevents the upper of t1 from advancing. However, the global timestamp does keep advancing. If the global timestamp advances past the upper of t1, then we are unable to select a valid timestamp under strict serializability, and the query hangs forever.

Switching the isolation level to serializable for this test increases the likelihood that we are able to select a valid timestamp for t1. Due to MaterializeInc/database-issues#4202, there is still some possibility that the test will flake. Once MaterializeInc/database-issues#4202 is fixed then this test should completely stop being flakey.

title: Coord: Implement timeout framework for clients
body:
This commits adds the functionality to register, remove, and execute client timeouts.

This is very roughly inspired by the PostgreSQL timeout framework: 
https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/fbfe6910eca0d6a61cbcdd27cdd5a8d9de6477fa/src/include/utils/timeout.h 
https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/d37776e451e3481d7364137a0b159102bb05992a/src/backend/utils/misc/timeout.c

Similarly to PostgreSQL, errors aren't returned to the client immediately after the timeout happens. They are only returned once the client tries to make another request.

Currently we only use this framework for the
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
(https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). However, it was designed to allow additional timeouts to be added in the future.

Works towards resolving MaterializeInc/database-issues#3895

title: Adapter: Fix handling of constant queries in txns
body:
Constant queries are queries that do not involve any data that
originates from a source. For example these involve queries like
`SELECT 1`, `SELECT mz_now()`, or `SELECT * FROM v` where v is a view
that doesn't contain any sources.

These queries can further be broken down into two categories.
  1) Timestamp/Timeline Dependent: The result of these queries depend
  on the timeline that they are executed in and the timestamp selected.

  2) Timestamp/Timeline Independent: The result of these queries do not
  depend on the timeline that they are executed in nor the timestamp
  selected.

Both types of constant queries should be able to be run in any
transaction, regardless of the transaction's timeline/timedomain.

Previously, we had two bugs with these types of queries.
  1) Timestamp/Timeline Dependent queries would cause panics in
  transactions that had already selected a timeline/timedomain.

  2) Views and Materialized Views that were Timestamp/Timeline
  Independent were mistakenly classified as Timestamp/Timeline
  dependent.

This commit fixes both these issues. Additionally, it refactors much
of the timestamp and timeline related code to make the different types
of queries more explicit.

Fixes #16488

This PR fixes a recognized bug.

title: storage: implement simple version of souce-specific statistics
body:
As described here: https://www.notion.so/materialize/User-facing-metrics-for-Sources-9603b61224a04a749969702e04662ed3#ca9365f66fb947128c0608906e556620

The implementation was relatively straightforward, but revealed a few subtleties around how we want to present some data. These are mostly documented in the docs I added to this pr, but I feel we should discuss them here:
- In general I counted retractions and insertions the same.
- `messages_received` and `messages_committed` can diverge because envelopes like `UPSERT` consolidate in within timestamps AND can produce 2 messages to commit (an insert and a retraction).
  - Its possible to move `messages_received` to just track the rows (both retractions and inserts) we are putting in persist batches, but that might is technically a different concept. Do we want two metrics?
- `bytes_received` has numbers that depend on the type of source.
- Its unclear how we want multi-output sources to work. In this pr, I just consolidated them into the same data, but its possible we want different rows for each sub-source.
  - I didn't add a test for multi-output sources because I want to discuss this first
  - Moving to this will likely fix a data-race bug in this pr, where `snapshot_finished` can be updated by the underlying sources too early. 
- Note also that these stats are also reset to 0 on restart...this seems reasonable to me, as this is the same way prometheus works!
- When sources are dropped, I don't yet clear out the data in the shard
  

Overall, the above issues show that we may want to add columns in the future...which means we need to expect users to not materialize `select * from mz_storage_source_statistics`, and that the ui will select specific columns...are these reasonable expectations?

title: Pre-tidy planner output
body:
The SQL planner produces HIR and MIR with various nits that we expect subsequent optimization to clean up. However, we present HIR and unoptimized MIR at users, and as someone who's had to read this recently it has seemed that there are various low hanging fruit to clean up such that we don't emit grotty moments in the first place.

The examples here are:
1. For a `Union`, only produce casting `Map` and `Project` nodes if non-trivial casts occur.
2. For existential subqueries, `Map(true)` rather than cross join a singleton collection containing the literal `true`.
3. For row comparison desugaring, remove the `AND true` as we are certain to have elements to compare.

There is unknown SLT fallout that I'll let CI discover rather than wait the half a day for my laptop to do it.

title: MIR type checking
body:
This PR introduces an MIR type checker that goes beyond `col_with_input_cols` to do thorough internal consistency checking.

The type checker is run at the beginning and end of each phase of the optimizer; as the checker runs, it collects type information for the plans corresponding to every global ID. When the type checker re-encounters a global ID's optimized plan, it checks the optimized plan for consistency and confirms that the new plan's type agrees with the old one.

Note that this type comparison is about the external, visible type of the expression---internally types can change radically, but the visible type of a global ID is treated as stable.

### Motivation

  * This PR adds a feature that has not yet been specified.

As we consider changes to the MIR optimizer, having thorough consistency checking will help us catch corner-case regressions before they manifest as runtime failures.

Initial runs of sqllogictest do not indicate any type errors in existing transforms (but caught several bugs in the type checker).

### Tips for reviewer

Some changes need particular attention, since I'm not confident about appropriate house style:

 - I've added `tracing` to the `expr` component to log information from the type checker.
 - Not all globals are accounted for---it may be worth pulling these from the catalog to be certain, but I don't know where to get that information.
 - The existing optimizer interface runs `Transform::transform` on plain `MirRelationExpression`s, but consistency checking of global IDs needs to run on the `BuildDesc`. I've extended this trait appropriately with `transform_query` (which has a sensible default), but it means some invocations of the typechecker won't be doing these stronger consistency checks unless we refactor every use of `transform` to instead call `transform_query`. Inspection makes it seem like this won't be too bad, but I'm not 100% certain.

title: compute: better-fueled linear join
body:
This PR changes the way linear joins are fueled. Rather than checking the remaining fuel only between keys, the new approach checks every time all matches for a batch value have been produced.

Doing so enables the join operator to regularly yield even when computing joins that have only a single or few keys. This should lead to much better responsiveness of replicas that have dataflows with cross-joins or skewed joins installed.

As this fueling change requires more control over the internals of the join operator than the DD API affords us, part (really: the bulk) of this PR is concerned with copying the join operator code from DD into the MZ codebase. In doing so, it also significantly simplifies the original join operator code, by removing logic and genericity not required by MZ. In general, no attempt is made at keeping the compute join implementation close to the one in DD. This will make it harder to upstream changes, should we ever want to do so, but at the same time gives us the opportunity to make the code more readable. I anticipate that we will want to perform more tuning on the join code in the future (e.g. by adding a shutdown token), so making it easy to modify seems more important than attempting compatibility with DD.

See performance test results here: https://github.com/MaterializeInc/materialize/pull/19186#issuecomment-1540078479

### Proof of Efficacy

To test that this actually has the desired effect of making the join operator more responsive, we can run a test with a cross join:
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (a int);
INSERT INTO t SELECT generate_series(1, 10000);
SELECT sum(t1.a + t2.a * 10000) FROM t t1, t t2;

-- in a second session:
\timing
\o /dev/null
SELECT * FROM mz_internal.mz_dataflow_operators;
SELECT * FROM mz_internal.mz_dataflow_operators;
SELECT * FROM mz_internal.mz_dataflow_operators;
```

On main, this yields the timings on my laptop:
```
Time: 39232.076 ms (00:39.232)
Time: 239.962 ms
Time: 6.080 ms
```

The first query only returns after the cross join has returned (or roughly at the same time). That's because the join operator never yields, so the replica can't process commands while it is running.

On this branch, these timings are printed:
```
Time: 538.751 ms
Time: 872.802 ms
Time: 865.107 ms
```

Queries return promptly even as the cross join is running. The experience is a bit sluggish, but I think this can be solved with a different (e.g. time-based) fueling strategy. I consider that out-of-scope for this PR though.

### Motivation

  * This PR fixes a recognized bug.

Fixes MaterializeInc/database-issues#5657.

### Tips for reviewer

There are two ways to read this PR:

1. Read the full diff. It's not huge, but perhaps overwhelming if you are not familiar with the DD join operator. Most of the positive changes are taken verbatim from the DD implementation and it's not easy to make out what the changes are. So I would generally recommend you go with option (2).
2. Look at the commits separately. I've tried to structure them in a way that makes it obvious what changes are made from the DD join implementation. The first commit simply copies over the relevant code from DD without changes, the subsequent ones modify it in various ways (applying rustfmt, fixing clippy warnings, simplifying). The second-to-last commit introduces the change in fueling. Look at the commit messages for more details.

~~Do you think this change warrants being rolled out with a feature flag? Personally I think that's not necessary, as we don't actually introduce new logic, just modify what's already existing. But I'd be fine with adding a feature flag if folk would like to move slower with this.~~ We agreed on adding a feature flag because there are (unlikely) workloads for this new join implementation is considerably slower than the old one and we want to option of switching back quickly. 

Also let me know if you think I should run other performance tests

title: Arranged per-worker pre-aggregation in `consolidate_named_if`
body:
This PR changes the `consolidate_named_if` function provided in `timely-util` to perform the consolidation in two stages. Firstly, a pipelined arrange step achieves per-worker pre-aggregation of differences. Secondly, a regular `consolidate_named` enforces data exchange and executes the final aggregation. The scheme is intended at improving the parallelism profile of forced consolidation in monotonic one-shot SELECTs, albeit at a higher overhead and memory cost. It is expected that the overheads of the newly introduced first step be manageable where the step is not helpful, but pay off in queries where parallelism can be recouped. The memory cost is non-trivial and equals about twice of the needs for a direct `consolidate_named`. However, these extra memory requirements only manifest in monotonic one-shot `SELECT`s, and are thus expected to be a temporary memory spike when forced consolidation is necessary.

### Motivation

title: Auto-indexing for `SELECT`s in `sqllogictest`
body:
This PR introduces automatic creation of indexed views and redundant execution for `SELECT` queries in `sqllogictest` by the new argument `--auto-index-selects`. The outcome for the vanilla execution of the query is contrasted with the outcome of creating an indexed view with the same `SELECT` query and selecting from this view. This feature will enable us to ensure via SLT-based testing that optimizations that change the planning and execution for one-shot `SELECT`s can be validated, in terms of produced results, against the standard optimization and execution pipeline for incremental view maintenance.
 
The feature is intended at allowing us to reuse existing corpora of SLTs while validating both view-based and one-shot query processing. It is an explicit non-goal to achieve 100% reuse, i.e., there will be SLTs where the feature will generate diverging results for view-based and one-shot query processing due to difficulties in extracting semantic information from the SQL syntax. For example, `SELECT`s allow for ambiguity in output column names, while views do not. Additionally, `ORDER BY` clauses in views are ignored, but are tricky to reliably reintroduce in the outer query in view-based execution. Only best-effort remediation of such potential issues is implemented by this PR. We aim at maximizing reuse of SLT corpora at manageable implementation effort for the feature. 

Advances MaterializeInc/database-issues#5543.

### Motivation

  * This PR adds a known-desirable feature. https://github.com/MaterializeInc/database-issues/issues/5543

### Tips for reviewer

I would suggest to consider the commits individually. Some small code organization was necessary prior to implementing the bulk of the feature. The code organization is performed in the first two commits, while the core of the feature is in the third commit. The fourth and sixth commits provide derivations of number of attributes and `ORDER BY` clauses. The fifth commit introduces unit tests and adds one SLT to the fast SQL logic tests being run with this feature. The seventh commit is code reorg / movement, so the diff ended up unfortunately a bit hard to parse (sorry!). The eighth commit refines the rewrite strategy by attempting to not use analysis information about the number of attributes at first (thus we can reuse `ORDER BY` with expressions on attributes projected, for example), but falling back in using the information and attempting a more involved `ORDER BY` / `SELECT` projection rewrite in case of error. Note that we needed to exclude `mz_sqllogictest` from Miri, as the new unit test raises the unavailability of `rust_psm_stack_pointer()` due to heavier use of the parser.

title: Enable monotonic oneshot SELECTs in selected SLTs
body:
This  PR turns on the feature flag `enable_monotonic_oneshot_selects` in a selected set of SLTs. The set comprises:
1. _The fast SLTs that are _currently_ run with `--auto-index-selects`_: Since these SLTs may be expanded in the future, we can also think of a complementary strategy for a follow-up PR wherein the feature is activated whenever `--auto-index-selects` is provided. This PR, however, has value in that a manually validated set of tests will now be subsequently be run with the feature turned on in CI.
2. _All SLTs that include EXPLAIN PHYSICAL PLAN commands_: We only need to touch SLTs with `EXPLAIN PHYSICAL PLAN` commands, as only physical plans can be changed by one-shot refinements. Even in this subset, some of the tests do not have their output affected, since they do not use LIR operators that can be replaced by monotonic variants. In the tests where output is changed, we now include two physical plan outputs. The first corresponds to creating a view with the `SELECT` command and then issuing `EXPLAIN PHYSICAL PLAN FOR VIEW <view>` (non-monotonic operators, equivalent to what would be planned if the view were indexed), and the second to issuing `EXPLAIN PHYSICAL PLAN FOR SELECT * FROM <view>` (monotonic operators, equivalent to a one-shot `SELECT` on the unindexed view).

title: adapter: correct initial timestamp determination in transactions
body:
In MaterializeInc/materialize#19026 various timestamp functions were refactored to allow `EXPLAIN TIMESTAMP` to reflect (and effect) the current transaction. This is tricky code and the refactor incorrectly changed the behavior of transactions. In a transaction our intention is to find a timestamp during the first statement that will be valid for any other object a user might query later in the transaction, then aquire read holds on all those referenced objects. In that change, the first statement only used the referenced IDs when determining a timestamp, not all nearby (objects in the same schema) IDs. Read holds were still correctly aquired on all nearby objects.

This could cause the transaction's timestamp to not be in advance of the since of other nearby objects. For example, take two objects in the table. At the first query, object A has a since of 10, object B has a since of 20. A first query in the transaction `SELECT * FROM A` would choose 10 as its timestamp, then aquire read holds on A and B at 10. A later query in the transaction `SELECT * FROM B` would choose 10 as its timestamp (which it fetched from the in-progress transaction state), and panic because B's since is in advance of 10.

One of the reasons this happened is the transaction metadata only held on to the TimestampContext. `EXPLAIN TIMESTAMP` needs a larger struct, a TimestampDetermination. Teach the session metadata to track this outer struct so EXPLAIN can use it. This allows us to now only call determine_timestamp once during transaction start, instead of during each query in a transaction. Refactor some of the other read handling code to look more like it did pre-19026.

After this code, the test repro from 19743 no longer causes crashes.

Fixes MaterializeInc/database-issues#5936

title: Introduce warnings in `sqllogictest` with `--auto-index-selects`
body:
This PR introduces a warning outcome in `sqllogictest`, and utilizes that outcome to avoid failing tests with `--auto-index-selects` in selected situations. A warning is printed like an error, depending on the verbosity, but does not cause the run to fail. 

Warnings are produced for inconsistent view outcomes whenever unfixable errors for creation of indexed views are observed, including uses of unmaterializable functions, `SHOW` commands, and unstable dependencies, among others. At the moment, some errors that are treated as unfixable originate from our inability to rewrite the `SELECT` into a form usable in an indexed view. This is due to `--auto-index-selects` relying only on syntactic cues and simple analysis.

Fixes MaterializeInc/database-issues#6029.
Advances MaterializeInc/database-issues#5543.

### Motivation

  * This PR adds a known-desirable feature. https://github.com/MaterializeInc/database-issues/issues/6029

### Tips for reviewer

The commits can be looked at individually. It seems to me that we can resolve most of the problems by the strategy outlined above. Just let me know if you find this sufficient to close MaterializeInc/database-issues#6029.

One item that is left unaddressed by this PR is to ignore errors that are raised inside transaction blocks (or to proactively avoid creating indexed views if we can detect that we are inside a transaction block). From looking at specific usages in our tests, we see that SLTs that contain `SELECT`s in transaction blocks fail to execute with indexed views almost in their entirety, so there is not much gain from ignoring these failures. The same would happen to runs with `--auto-transactions`, so it just seems that tests with transactions are at odds with issuing DDL to create indexed views at the moment. This is why I am arguing that we should not implement this extension for now (nothing against revisiting later if we have evidence that it'd be important to have).

Important note: There are errors in `test/sqllogictest/list.slt` when executed with `--auto-index-selects` that I think are flagging a previously unreported bug. I am filing a report in MaterializeInc/database-issues#6181.
