title: fix(query): Ensure visibility of all columns in subqueries
body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary This PR addresses an issue where internal fields of tuples and virtual columns were not visible in the outer query when accessed through a subquery and a `SELECT *` statement in the outer query. **Background:** In Databend, internal fields within tuples and virtual columns are, by default, marked as `InVisible`. This means they are typically hidden from `SELECT *` queries unless explicitly referenced. **The Issue:** When a subquery accessed these `InVisible` tuple fields or virtual columns, and the outer query used `SELECT *`, these columns were not included in the final result set. This resulted in data loss and unexpected behavior for users relying on `SELECT *` to retrieve all available columns. - fixes: #[Link the issue here] ## Tests - [ ] Unit Test - [x] Logic Test - [ ] Benchmark Test - [ ] No Test - _Explain why_ ## Type of change - [x] Bug Fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) - [ ] New Feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) - [ ] Breaking Change (fix or feature that could cause existing functionality not to work as expected) - [ ] Documentation Update - [ ] Refactoring - [ ] Performance Improvement - [ ] Other (please describe): - - - This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/databendlabs/databend/17934)

title: refactor(meta-semaphore): release meta semapore immediately after permit is dropped
body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary The QueriesQueueManager relies on Meta Semaphore, which needs to schedule multiple queries per second. I noticed that the time between when a query releases the semaphore and when the next query acquires it is too long and inconsistent. To address this, I refactored the semaphore release process so that it no longer checks for permit drops during extension, but instead performs the release immediately after the permits are dropped. --- use https://github.com/databendlabs/wizard/tree/main/threads to benchmark. title: feat: initial support for table branching and tagging
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

This PR introduces Git-like branching and tagging for Databend's Fuse tables, inspired by **Apache Iceberg**. Users can create independent branches for development/testing and read-only tags for marking important snapshots.

### 1. Core Concepts
**Branch**
- **Writable**: Supports INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and other write operations(not implemented in this PR)
- **Independent Evolution**: Each branch maintains its own snapshot chain

**Tag**
- **Read-only**: Does not support write operations, only used to mark important snapshots

### 2. SQL Syntax

#### 2.1 Creating Branches or Tags
```sql
ALTER TABLE <database>.<table> CREATE BRANCH | TAG <name> 
[AT (
    SNAPSHOT => '<snapshot_id>' |
    TIMESTAMP => <timestamp> |
    STREAM => <stream_name> |
    OFFSET => <time_interval> |
    BRANCH => <branch_name> |
    TAG => <tag_name>
)]
[RETAIN <n> DAYS | SECONDS];
```

**Parameters**:

- `BRANCH | TAG`: Specify whether to create a branch or tag
- `AT`: Specify the point in time to base the creation on (optional, defaults to current snapshot)
  - `SNAPSHOT`: Based on a specific snapshot ID
  - `TIMESTAMP`: Based on a specific timestamp
  - `STREAM`: Based on the current position of a Stream
  - `OFFSET`: Based on a relative time offset
  - `BRANCH`: Based on the current state of another branch
  - `TAG`: Based on a tag
- `RETAIN`: Set the retention period for the branch|tag (optional, defaults to none)

**Examples**:

```sql
-- Create a development branch based on current state
ALTER TABLE sales.orders CREATE BRANCH dev;

-- Create a test branch based on yesterday's data, retain for 7 days
ALTER TABLE sales.orders CREATE BRANCH test 
AT (TIMESTAMP => '2024-11-27 00:00:00') 
RETAIN 7 DAYS;

-- Create a tag for current state
ALTER TABLE sales.orders CREATE TAG v1;

-- Create a tag based on a specific snapshot
ALTER TABLE sales.orders CREATE TAG backup_before_migration
AT (SNAPSHOT => '9828b23f74664ff3806f44bbc1925ea5');
```

#### 2.2 Dropping Branches or Tags

```sql
ALTER TABLE <database>.<table> DROP BRANCH | TAG <name>;
```

**Note**: Drop operations are irreversible. Use with caution.

**Examples**:

```sql
-- Drop development branch
ALTER TABLE sales.orders DROP BRANCH dev;

-- Drop tag
ALTER TABLE sales.orders DROP TAG v1;
```

#### 2.3 Querying Branch Data

```sql
-- Query data from a specific branch (similar to Git's remote/branch syntax)
SELECT * FROM <database>.<table>/<branch_name>;

-- Query development branch
SELECT * FROM sales.orders/dev;
```

### 3. Data Structure Design

```rust
pub struct TableMeta {
    // ... other fields ...
    
    /// Stores all branch and tag references
    pub refs: BTreeMap<String, SnapshotRef>,
}

pub struct SnapshotRef {
    /// The unique id of the reference.
    pub id: u64,
    /// After this timestamp, the reference becomes inactive.
    pub expire_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,
    /// The type of the reference.
    pub typ: SnapshotRefType,
    /// The location of the snapshot that this reference points to.
    pub loc: String,
}

pub enum SnapshotRefType {
    Branch = 0,
    Tag = 1,
}
```

### 4. Storage Layout
```
<table_prefix>/
├── _ss/                          # Main branch snapshot directory
│   ├── <snapshot_file>
│   └── ...
├── _refs/                        # Branch and tag directory
│   ├── <id1>/                      # dev branch
│   │   ├── <snapshot_file>
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── <id2>/                     # test branch
│   │   └── ...
│   └── <id3>/                     # v1 tag
│       └── <snapshot_file>
├── _sg/                          # Segment files (shared)
└── _b/                           # Block files (shared)
```
- Main branch snapshots stored in `_ss/` directory
- Branch and tag snapshots stored in `_refs/<ref_id>/` direct

title: feat(query): support experimental table branch
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

This PR implements table branches for FUSE tables, including branch creation, branch-qualified reads and writes, branch lifecycle metadata, and branch-aware garbage collection. It also extends vacuum2 and virtual-column vacuum so historical files referenced by active branches or tags remain protected until they are no longer reachable. 

A **branch** is a lightweight, writable fork of a table's snapshot history — it shares the base table's storage (segments/blocks) via **copy-on-write** semantics and maintains its own independent snapshot chain.

```
<database_root>/
├── <table_A_prefix>/                # base table A
│   ├── _ss/                         # snapshots
│   │   ├── <snapshot_A1>
│   │   ├── <snapshot_A2>
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── _sg/                         # segments (shared)
│   │   ├── <segment_1>
│   │   └── ...
│   └── _b/                          # blocks (shared)
│       ├── <block_1>
│       └── ...
│
├── <table_A_dev_prefix>/            # branch "dev" (independent table)
│   ├── _ss/                         # snapshots (cloned from A at some point)
│   │   ├── <snapshot_dev_1>
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── _sg/                         # segments (initially shared, COW)
│   │   └── ...
│   └── _b/                          # blocks (initially shared, COW)
│       └── ...
│
├── <table_A_test_prefix>/           # branch "test" (independent table)
│   ├── _ss/
│   ├── _sg/
│   └── _b/
│
└── <table_B_prefix>/                # another unrelated table
    ├── _ss/
    ├── _sg/
    └── _b/
```

### **Syntax**
```sql
-- Create a branch
ALTER TABLE <table>[/<source_branch>]
  CREATE BRANCH <name>
  [AT ( SNAPSHOT => '<snapshot_id>'                                                                                           
      | TIMESTAMP => <timestamp>
      | STREAM => <stream_name>
      | OFFSET => <time_interval>
      | TAG => <tag_name> )]
  [RETAIN <n> {DAYS | SECONDS}];

-- Drop a branch
ALTER TABLE <table> DROP BRANCH <name>;

-- Query a branch (read)
SELECT * FROM <table>/<branch_name>;

-- Write to a branch
INSERT INTO <table>/<branch_name> VALUES (...);
```

###  **Implementation Details**

 ####  KV Metadata Model
Branches are persisted as explicit KV entries in meta-service:

| Key | Value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `__fd_table_branch/<table_id>/<branch_name>` | `TableBranch { expire_at, branch_id }` | Active branch entry |
| `__fd_dropped_branch/<table_id>/<branch_name>/<branch_id>` | `DroppedBranchMeta { drop_on, expire_at }` | Dropped branch entry |
  | `__fd_table_by_id/<branch_id>` | `TableMeta` | Branch table metadata |
  | `__fd_branch_id_to_name/<branch_id>` | `TableIdBranchName { table_id, branch_name }` | Branch reverse mapping for metadata lookup and display |
  
Each branch gets its own table_id (allocated via fetch_id) and its own storage prefix (<db_id>/<branch_table_id>/). The branch's TableMeta.options records **OPT_KEY_BASE_TABLE_ID** and **OPT_KEY_REFERENCED_BRANCH_IDS** for cross-table GC protection.

#### Ref API

  New meta-service APIs in ref_api.rs:
  - create_table_branch — Create branch (normal or staged/hidden)
  - drop_table_branch — Soft-drop (move to dropped-branch namespace)
  - undrop_table_branch — Restore dropped branch (with expire_at preservation)
  - get_table_branch — Resolve branch name to TableInfo
  - list_history_table_branches — List all branches (active + dropped) for vacuum
  - gc_drop_table_branch — Hard-delete branch metadata after retention expires

#### Vacuum2 Semantics

  fuse_vacuum2() is now branch-aware. It:
  - walks active and dropped branch history
  - computes which snapshots, segments, and blocks are still protected by active branches or tags
  - preserves cross-branch references
  - final-GCs dropped branches only when their protected d

title: bug: Incorrect implementation of Hex Literal `X'...'` (Inconsistent with SQL Standard)
body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/issues) and found no similar issues.


### Version

1.2.890

### What's Wrong?

### 1. Description
Currently, Databend treats the hex literal `X'...'` as a **PostgreSQL Hex Integer Literal** (`PGLiteralHex`) in the lexer/parser, which is then interpreted as an `Integer`.

```rust
// Current problematic regex in Databend lexer
#[regex(r"[xX]'[a-fA-F0-9]*'")]
PGLiteralHex,
```

However, this implementation deviates from the **SQL Standard**, confuses the behavior of **PostgreSQL**, and creates functional limitations for binary data.

### 2. Evidence of Non-Compliance

#### A. SQL Standard (ISO/IEC 9075)
According to the **SQL:1999** (and subsequent versions like SQL:2016) specification, **Section 5.3 `<literal>`**, the syntax `X'<hexit>...'` is explicitly defined as a **`<binary string literal>`**.
- It is intended to represent `BINARY` or `BLOB` data types.
- It is **not** defined as an integer literal.

#### B. Misconception of PostgreSQL Behavior
The naming `PGLiteralHex` suggests alignment with PostgreSQL, but PG's behavior is different:
- In PostgreSQL, `X'0A'` results in a **Bit String** (`BIT VARYING`), not an `Integer`.
- `SELECT X'0A' + 1;` fails in PG because a Bit String cannot be implicitly used as an Integer.
- PostgreSQL 16+ introduced `0x...` for hex integers, but `X'...'` remains a Bit String.

### 3. Comparison of Database Implementations

The following table shows that Databend's current approach is an outlier compared to major SQL engines:

| Implementation Group | Databases | Result Type of `X'0A'` | SQL Standard Compliant? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Standard-Compliant** | **DuckDB, Trino, Snowflake, MySQL, SQLite** | **Binary / BLOB** (Byte Stream) | **Yes** |
| **Dialect (Bit-string)** | **PostgreSQL** | **BIT VARYING** (Bit Array) | **No** |
| **Non-Standard** | **SQL Server** | **Syntax Error** (Only supports `0x`) | **No** |
| **Databend (Current)** | **Databend** | **Integer** | **No** |



### 4. Impact & Risks
1. **Integer Overflow**: Binary literals (like SHA-256 hashes `X'df4... '`) frequently exceed 64 bits. Forcing them into an `Integer` type causes overflow errors where they should have been valid `BINARY` data.
2. **Migration Barrier**: Users migrating from Snowflake, MySQL, or ClickHouse expect `X'...'` to work for binary ingestion.
3. **Inconsistent Logic**: Databend lacks a standard-compliant way to input `BINARY` literals if `X'...'` is occupied by the `Integer` type.

### 5. Suggested Fix
1. **Refactor Lexer**: Map `X'...'` literals to a `Binary` type instead of `PGLiteralHex` (Integer).

### Reference
- ISO/IEC 9075-2 Section 5.3 `<binary string literal>`
- [PostgreSQL Docs: Bit String Constants](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-bit.html)

### How to Reproduce?

```
root@localhost:8000/default/default> select X'ABCD';

SELECT 43981

╭────────╮
│  43981 │
│ UInt16 │
├────────┤
│  43981 │
╰────────╯
```

title: Optimize: CASE WHEN / if with constant condition is not simplified to selected non-constant branch
body:
**Summary**

CASE WHEN is rewritten internally to if(...). When the condition is constant, the expression should be simplified to the selected branch even if that branch contains column references.

### Example:


  EXPLAIN SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN true THEN id > 0
      ELSE region = 'APAC'
    END
  FROM rap_case_fold_test;

  or equivalently after binding:

  if(true, id > 0, region = 'APAC')

  Currently this remains as:

  if(true, id > 0, region = 'APAC')

  instead of being simplified to:

  id > 0

###  Why It Matters

  Execution can still be correct because if evaluation can short-circuit, but the optimizer keeps unreachable branches. This blocks downstream simplifications and predicate reasoning that would otherwise see the selected branch directly.

###  Expected

  These rewrites should happen during constant folding or scalar normalization:

  if(true, then_expr, else_expr)  -> then_expr
  if(false, then_expr, else_expr) -> else_expr
  if(NULL, then_expr, else_expr)  -> else_expr

  For multi-branch CASE/if, constant false/null conditions should be removed, and the first constant true condition should select its branch and discard following branches.

  Actual

  The constant condition is folded, but the if expression is retained when the selected branch is non-constant:

  if(true, id > 0, region = 'APAC')

title: fix(query): mark async sink finish after completion
body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary - fixes: #20020 This PR fixes async sink lifecycle bookkeeping for `AsyncSinker` and `AsyncMpscSinker`. Previously, both wrappers set `called_on_finish = true` before awaiting the sink's `on_finish()` future. If the processor `async_process()` future was cancelled while `on_finish()` was still pending, the wrapper could record finish as complete even though the awaited finish work had not completed. This PR moves the `called_on_finish = true` assignment after `on_finish().await` returns successfully, so a pending or cancelled finish future is not recorded as completed. Regression tests cover both async sink wrappers by making `on_finish()` remain pending, dropping the `async_process()` future, and asserting that finish is not marked complete. ## Tests - [x] Unit Test - [ ] Logic Test - [ ] Benchmark Test - [ ] No Test - _Explain why_ Validation run: ```bash cargo test -p databend-common-pipeline test_cancel_pending_on_finish_does_not_mark_finish_called cargo clippy -p databend-common-pipeline -- -D warnings ``` ## Type of change - [x] Bug Fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) - [ ] New Feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) - [ ] Breaking Change (fix or feature that could cause existing functionality not to work as expected) - [ ] Documentation Update - [ ] Refactoring - [ ] Performance Improvement - [ ] Other (please describe): - - - This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/databendlabs/databend/20021)

title: feat(query): Implement Materialized Views
body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary ## Summary Implement Materialized Views (MV) as first-class DDL objects backed by Fuse tables with reserved metadata options. This PR focuses on MV DDL and metadata behavior: create, initial materialization, show, describe, drop, and protection against invalid table operations. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` is intentionally deferred until the incremental refresh design is finalized. ## Supported Syntax ```sql CREATE [OR REPLACE] MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF NOT EXISTS] [db.]view [CLUSTER BY [LINEAR | HILBERT] (...)] AS SELECT ... DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF EXISTS] [db.]view SHOW CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW [db.]view SHOW MATERIALIZED VIEWS [FROM [catalog.]database] [LIKE ...] ``` REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW is parsed but currently returns Unimplemented. ### Unsupported MV Definition Forms The following forms are rejected in MV definitions: - user-specified materialized CTEs: WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (...) - executor-dependent PIVOT forms: - PIVOT ... IN (ANY) - PIVOT ... IN () Regular CTEs and PIVOT with explicit literal values remain supported. These forms are intentionally unsupported because MV definitions are stored as SQL text and replanned later during REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. Materialized CTEs and PIVOT ANY / subquery values require a planning-time query executor: materialized CTEs materialize intermediate results during binding, while PIVOT ANY / subquery must execute a query during rewrite to determine the generated pivot columns. The MV refresh replan path currently uses a planner without that executor, so accepting these forms at CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW time would create MVs that can be initially built but cannot be refreshed reliably. ### Design - MVs are stored as Fuse tables with reserved metadata options: - materialized_view - materialized_view_query - materialized_view_query_catalog - materialized_view_query_database - CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS SELECT ... creates the backing Fuse table and materializes the initial query result. - The stored query is qualified at creation time so SHOW CREATE and future refresh logic can replay the definition from a stable context. - SHOW CREATE TABLE on an MV emits CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... DDL. - SHOW MATERIALIZED VIEWS is surfaced through system.tables with table_type = 'MATERIALIZED VIEW'. - MV metadata options are reserved and cannot be set or modified through regular table option syntax. - Table operations that would mutate or replace MV objects incorrectly are rejected. ### Unsupported MV Definition Forms The following forms are rejected in MV definitions for now: - user-specified materialized CTEs: WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (...) - executor-dependent PIVOT forms: - PIVOT ... IN (ANY) - PIVOT ... IN () These forms require a planning-time query executor. Since refresh semantics are not part of this PR, accepting them now would create MV definitions whose replay behavior is not well-defined. Regular CTEs and PIVOT with explicit literal values remain supported. ## Tests - [x] Unit Test - [x] Logic Test - [ ] Benchmark Test - [ ] No Test - _Explain why_ ## Type of change - [ ] Bug Fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) - [x] New Feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) - [ ] Breaking Change (fix or feature that could cause existing functionality not to work as expected) - [ ] Documentation Update - [ ] Refactoring - [ ] Performance Improvement - [ ] Other (please describe): - - - This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/databendlabs/databend/20117)

title: feat(query): adaptively distribute lazy row fetch
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

### Problem

Lazy materialization first scans the columns needed by filtering and sorting, keeps `_row_id`, and reads the deferred columns only after `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` has selected the final rows.

In a distributed top-N plan, scan workers send their partial results through a Merge exchange. The coordinator produces the final top-N row IDs and currently performs the entire RowFetch itself. This is efficient when the selected rows are concentrated in a few storage blocks, but the coordinator becomes a remote-I/O bottleneck when those rows are spread across many storage blocks. Always distributing RowFetch would remove that bottleneck but add unnecessary shuffle overhead when the result has a low block count.

This PR keeps RowFetch local when the selected rows touch few blocks and distributes it when they touch many blocks.

### Scope

Adaptive routing is available only when the physical plan meets all three conditions:

1. **Distributed top-N.** Multiple executors produce partial top-N results, and the coordinator merges them before RowFetch. Without adaptive routing, the coordinator would fetch all deferred columns for the final result.
2. **Deferred columns from one table.** All RowFetch row IDs share one block-prefix domain, so routing by block prefix can send each block to one destination. Plans that fetch deferred columns from multiple tables keep the existing local RowFetch path.
3. **A large enough limit.** `LIMIT > max_threads * 4`. This planner heuristic avoids adding an exchange when the result is unlikely to contain enough blocks to benefit; it is not a correctness condition.

These are planner-time guards. For eligible plans, the runtime still counts the distinct blocks in the final top-N result and chooses between local and distributed RowFetch. If any guard fails, the physical plan remains unchanged.

For an eligible plan, the planner adds a RowFetch-specific exchange before RowFetch and a second Merge exchange after RowFetch:

```text
scan workers: scan narrow columns + partial sort
                         |
                         v
coordinator: first Merge + final top-N
                         |
                         v
              adaptive RowFetch exchange
                  /       |       \
                 v        v        v
        destination nodes: fetch assigned blocks
                  \       |       /
                         v
coordinator: second Merge + restore final order
```

### Runtime decision

The coordinator first coalesces all top-N input batches and counts distinct block prefixes in `_row_id`. Coalescing makes the decision against the complete result; deciding per batch could classify every small batch as local even when the combined result covers many blocks.

The routing rule is:

```text
local_block_threshold = max(max_threads * 8, 128)

distinct blocks <= local_block_threshold  -> local RowFetch
distinct blocks >  local_block_threshold  -> distributed RowFetch
```

Block count is used instead of row count because remote reads and metadata lookup are organized by block. The threshold allows a bounded number of local I/O waves before a cluster shuffle becomes worthwhile.

### Node behavior

**Coordinator before RowFetch**

- Consumes the first Merge exchange and produces the final top-N row IDs.
- Coalesces the result batches and makes one routing decision.
- In local mode, routes every row ID back to itself.
- In distributed mode, hashes row IDs by block prefix across all RowFetch destinations, including itself.

**RowFetch destination nodes**

- In local mode, workers receive no rows and perform no RowFetch work.
- In distributed mode, each worker and the coordinator receive only their assigned block prefixes.
- Rows from the same block always go to the same destination. The router does not split or rebalance a block away from its hash destination, preserving block

title: feat: support storing different columns in separate files
body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary Fuse currently rewrites an entire block for an `UPDATE`, even when only a subset of columns changes. This PR introduces an opt-in partial UPDATE path that stores updated columns in separate physical column-group files while preserving the semantics of a single logical block. Partial UPDATE requires both the `enable_partial_update` table option and session setting. Eligible direct UPDATEs write only the changed fields; operations that update all fields, affect cluster-key dependencies, or otherwise do not meet the eligibility requirements fall back to a full block rewrite. title: bug(query): staged CTAS temporary tables leak into the session table namespace
body:
Follow-up from #20234 (not a merge blocker for that PR).

### Description

`TempTblMgr` stages a two-phase CTAS replacement under a generated orphan name in the same `name_to_id` map that holds user temporary tables. Nothing reclaims that entry when the CTAS pipeline fails, so every abandoned attempt leaves a permanent staged entry for the lifetime of the session.

`CreateTableInterpreter::create_table_as_select` only commits on success:

```rust
pipeline.main_pipeline.lift_on_finished(move |info: &ExecutionInfo| {
    if info.res.is_ok() {
        // ... commit_table_meta ...
    }
    Ok(())
});
```

There is no failure branch, and unlike persistent tables there is no VACUUM to reclaim temporary ones. Only session teardown (`drop_all_temp_tables`) clears them.

### Why this got worse in #20234

Before that PR the orphan name was deterministic (`orphan@<table_name>`), so a later CTAS on the same name reused the key and evicted the stale entry — at most one leaked entry per table name:

```rust
let old_id = self.name_to_id.insert(desc.clone(), table_id);
if let Some(old_id) = old_id {
    self.id_to_table.remove(&old_id);   // stale orphan reclaimed
}
```

#20234 changed it to `__tmp_orphan@<table_id>`, unique per attempt. That was the right call — the deterministic name let one CTAS's commit publish another CTAS's staged table — but it removes the accidental reclaim, so the leak is now unbounded in the number of failed attempts.

The behavior is asserted by the PR's own test, `test_ctas_commit_publishes_its_own_temporary_table`: after `first` commits, `second`'s staged entry is still present in both maps.

### Impact

- One `name_to_id` + `id_to_table` entry retained per failed `CREATE [OR REPLACE] TEMP TABLE ... AS SELECT`, holding a `TableMeta` and a `copied_files` map.
- Staged entries are user-visible. `TempTblMgr::list_tables()` returns everything in `id_to_table`, which reaches users through `list_temporary_tables()` and the `temporary_tables()` table function, so `__tmp_orphan@<id>` rows show up as if they were real temporary tables.
- Session-scoped and non-corrupting: no wrong results, and teardown eventually cleans up.

### Reproduction

In one session, repeatedly run a temporary CTAS whose SELECT fails, then:

```sql
SELECT * FROM temporary_tables();
```

Each failed attempt adds a `__tmp_orphan@<id>` row.

### Suggested fix

The staged table never needs to occupy the user name namespace. The insert pipeline addresses it by ID (`TableInfo` is built with the staged `table_id`), and `commit_table_meta` already validates `orphan_id != req.table_id`, so it could look the staged table up by `req.table_id` directly.

Keeping staged replacements in a separate ID-keyed map would:

- remove the `temporary_tables()` pollution,
- make `TEMP_ORPHAN_TABLE_PREFIX`, `ensure_user_table_name()`, and the `rename_table` orphan guard unnecessary,
- leave a plain memory entry as the only residue, which a failure branch in `create_table_as_select` (or a per-query staged-entry sweep) can then drop.

Either fix alone helps; together they remove the class of problem.

title: bug(query): correlated subqueries cannot resolve internal columns from outer tables
body:
Follow-up from #20251 (not a merge blocker for that PR).

### Description

A correlated subquery cannot resolve an Internal Column belonging to an outer table.

Normal column resolution searches parent `BindContext`s, but Internal Column resolution creates an `InternalColumnBinding` in the current context before reaching the parent context. Later, `get_internal_column_table_index()` searches the current context for the qualified table and fails because that table belongs to the parent context.

This is a general Internal Column name-resolution issue and can already be reproduced with `_row_id`.

### Why it matters now

#20251 adds `_change_row_id` as a queryable Internal Column. It should behave like other table columns when referenced through a
correlated subquery:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    WHERE t._change_row_id IS NOT NULL
);
```

Regular subqueries that scan their own table work. The failure is specific to resolving an Internal Column from an outer scope.

### Reproduction

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(a INT, b STRING);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'a');

SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    WHERE t._row_id IS NOT NULL
);
```

Current result:

```text
error 1065:
Table `t` is not found in the bind context
```

A non-correlated derived-table query works:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM (
    SELECT _row_id FROM t
) q;
```

This confirms that the problem is outer-scope resolution rather than general Internal Column binding.

The same issue applies to `t._change_row_id`.

### Impact

Medium. Valid correlated queries using any Internal Column are rejected during binding. Users must rewrite the query to materialize the Internal Column in an intermediate derived table.

Regular qualified JOIN and self-JOIN queries are not affected.

### Suggested fix

Resolve the owner of an Internal Column together with the binding context:

1. Only create an Internal Column candidate when the current context contains the matching table.
2. Continue searching parent contexts when the table is not present in the current context.
3. Bind the Internal Column to the resolved outer `table_index`.
4. Register or reuse its metadata symbol by `(table_index, column_id)`.
5. Treat the resulting symbol as a correlated column so the owning outer Scan retains it.

Unqualified Internal Columns should continue to report ambiguity when multiple tables are visible.

body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary This fixes a `GROUP BY` name-resolution regression introduced by #19750. Before #19750, an unqualified `GROUP BY` name was resolved against input columns first, with SELECT aliases used only as a fallback. The binder alias refactor in #19750 changed simple scalar aliases to take precedence over same-name input columns. #19806 reported this conflict, but #19808 addressed it by adding `enable_group_by_column_first` with a default value of `0`. As a result, column-first resolution became opt-in while the affected alias-first behavior remained the default. #19814 later restored column-first resolution for names inside complex `GROUP BY` expressions, but simple names continued to use the setting-controlled alias-first path. title: fix(query): allow planner cache for more function calls
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

This PR removes a planner-cache regression for queries containing:

- expression forms handled by context-independent special-function or rewrite paths, such as `coalesce` and `ifnull`;
- execution-dependent expressions that can remain symbolic in the logical plan, such as statement-stable `now()` and volatile `rand()` calls.

Here, execution-dependent means that an expression's value may differ between executions.

It also prevents stale results: if binding or optimization evaluates an execution-dependent expression and stores the value in the logical plan, that plan is used for the current execution but is not cached.

Existing rewrites for immutable scalar subqueries and immutable large `IN` lists are kept as they are. The evaluation scope of volatile expressions is also preserved.

## Problem

Planner cache reuses the result of binding and logical optimization. The motivating query has wide tables, outer joins, subqueries, and eight `UNION ALL` branches, so repeating that work is expensive.

The motivating query does not enter planner cache in 1.2.911 for two independent reasons:

1. It contains `coalesce`, an example of an expression handled through a context-independent special-function path. The existing check does not distinguish this class from special functions that depend on session state. Context-independent rewrite expressions such as `ifnull` have the same problem through a different type-checking path.
2. It contains `now()`, an example of a statement-stable expression. The existing check rejects execution-dependent functions as a class. This is unnecessarily strict when the logical plan can keep the call symbolic and evaluate it for each execution.

For example, `coalesce` is rewritten during type checking to `if`, `is_not_null`, and `assume_not_null`. The rewrite itself does not depend on time or session state. This reasoning applies to every handler classified as context-independent, not only to `coalesce` and `ifnull`; nested argument expressions are still checked separately. Session-dependent expressions such as `current_user()` remain excluded.

Simply adding the example function names to an allow-list is not sufficient. The cache decision must be based on the expression category and on what binding and optimization have put into the completed logical plan.

## Correctness rule

A logical plan can be reused across executions only if it contains no planning-time value whose validity ends with the execution that produced the plan.

The cache decision depends on whether the plan keeps an expression or stores its value:

| State in the logical plan | Reusable? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Literal produced only from immutable inputs | Yes | The value is the same for every execution |
| Symbolic statement-stable expression, for example `now()` | Yes | The expression is evaluated again for each execution |
| Symbolic volatile expression, for example `rand()` | Yes, if its operator scope is unchanged | Each execution evaluates it with the SQL-defined scope |
| Literal produced by evaluating an execution-dependent expression during planning | No | A later execution would reuse the earlier execution's value |

### Scalar subqueries

For example:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(ts TIMESTAMP);

SELECT * FROM t WHERE ts < (SELECT now());
```

Before this PR, decorrelation can evaluate the scalar subquery and produce:

```text
Filter: ts < <timestamp from the current execution>
```

This is not a correctness bug on the base branch: `now()` prevents the plan from entering planner cache, so the next execution builds a new plan and obtains a new timestamp.

If the cache check were changed only to allow `now()`, the literal above would be cached. The next execution would then use the previous execution's timestamp.

This PR instead produces a reusable plan containing:

```text
Filter: ts < nullable(now())
```

title: fix(storage): disable automatic HTTP decompression
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/

## Summary

This PR fixes `COPY INTO` failures when reading externally gzip-encoded objects through OpenDAL after Lance support enabled reqwest's `gzip` feature in the shared dependency graph.

The affected objects are unusual: they were uploaded with `Content-Encoding: gzip` manually set in S3 object metadata. S3 does not normally infer this header from a `.gz` filename, so ordinary `.json.gz` objects without that metadata are unaffected.

Typical failure:

```text
StorageOther. Code: 4000, Text = Unexpected (persistent) => reader got too much data
Context:
  expect: 430
  actual: 8089
```

The fix makes the reqwest clients used by Databend's main OpenDAL storage path (`init_operator` / `StorageHttpClient`, including the shared global client and External-scope pinned clients) explicitly preserve encoded storage bytes by disabling automatic gzip, brotli, zstd, and deflate response decoding.

Two pre-existing operator construction paths still fall back to OpenDAL's default reqwest client and are not changed here: `IcebergFileIO::build_operator` (`Operator::via_iter` with no `HttpClientLayer`) and `bendsave`'s `Operator::from_iter`. Hitting those paths still requires object metadata with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, which is uncommon for parquet/orc. Follow-up if Iceberg table files or bendsave objects start carrying that header.

## Root cause

### What changed

The issue was introduced indirectly by `4f33092048` (`feat: support copy into lance dataset`). That change added Lance dependencies. Their generated REST namespace client, `lance-namespace-reqwest-client`, declares reqwest like this:

```toml
[dependencies.reqwest]
version = "^0.12"
features = [
    "json",
    "multipart",
    "charset",
    "gzip",
    "http2",
    "stream",
    "rustls-tls-native-roots",
]
default-features = false
```

Before that dependency was added, the resolved reqwest package did not include `async-compression`; afterward, `reqwest/gzip` was enabled for the process.

### Upstream behavior that exposes the bug

There are two upstream behaviors involved:

1. `lance-namespace-reqwest-client` unconditionally enables `reqwest/gzip` for its REST client instead of making response decompression independently configurable.
2. Cargo unifies features for the same package/version across normal dependencies. Therefore `reqwest/gzip` is not confined to Lance: the single resolved reqwest 0.12 package used by Databend is compiled with gzip support everywhere.

This is not a reqwest protocol bug. reqwest documents that when its `gzip` feature is compiled in, automatic gzip decoding is enabled by default for every newly constructed `ClientBuilder`. On a response with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, reqwest removes `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` and exposes decoded response bytes.

That behavior is appropriate for REST APIs such as Lance, but not for an object-storage transport. OpenDAL must receive the exact encoded object bytes returned by S3-compatible storage because object sizes, range boundaries, checksums, and retry offsets refer to the stored representation.

### How the failure happens

The failure requires all of the following:

1. The binary is compiled with `reqwest/gzip`; in the affected release this is enabled transitively by Lance.
2. The S3 object was uploaded with `Content-Encoding: gzip` explicitly set in its object metadata, so the storage service returns that HTTP response header. This is an uncommon, manually supplied metadata setting; it is not the normal consequence of storing a file whose name ends in `.gz`. A `.gz` suffix by itself does not trigger the issue.
3. Databend reads the object through the custom reqwest-backed OpenDAL HTTP transport.
4. OpenDAL performs a bounded/ranged read and expects the number of encoded bytes requested from storage.

For example, OpenDAL requests/expects 430 stored bytes. reqwest sees `Content-Encoding: gzip` a

title: Feature: add CURRENT_TENANT_ID() for self-service Data Share setup
body:
## Summary

Add a SQL context function, `CURRENT_TENANT_ID()`, that returns the tenant ID associated with the current authenticated session. This would let users retrieve the identifier required for Data Share setup through SQL in both Databend Cloud and self-hosted deployments.

Related: #20053 (Meta-backed cross-tenant data sharing).

## Background and problem

Data Share currently supports cross-tenant sharing within the same Databend Meta cluster. The current Cloud deployment prerequisite described for this workflow is the same region and Meta cluster; this request does not expand that boundary.

Providers and consumers must exchange tenant identifiers:

- The provider needs the consumer's tenant ID to authorize access:

```sql
ALTER SHARE <share_name>
ADD ACCOUNTS = <consumer_tenant_id>;
```

- The consumer needs the provider's tenant ID and share name to create a local read-only database:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE <local_database_name>
FROM SHARE <provider_tenant_id>.<share_name>;
```

The workflow needs a standard, self-service SQL entry point for retrieving the tenant ID used by these statements. Requiring users to inspect deployment configuration or contact a platform administrator creates unnecessary friction in setting up a share.

## Proposed solution

```sql
SELECT CURRENT_TENANT_ID();
```

Return type: `VARCHAR`, containing the tenant ID used by the current server-authenticated session.

Proposed semantics, consistent across Cloud and self-hosted deployments:

1. Return the tenant ID, not a mutable organization or tenant display name.
2. Resolve the value from the server-side authenticated session context. It must not be spoofable through an ordinary SQL session setting.
3. Switching roles, databases, or warehouses must not change the session's tenant identity or the returned value.
4. When a consumer queries a shared database, return the consumer's own tenant ID, not the provider's tenant ID.
5. The returned identifier must be usable in the existing Share SQL statements, with appropriate identifier quoting where required. Document those quoting rules.
6. Take no arguments and provide no capability to enumerate other tenants.
7. Treat the tenant ID as an identifier, not a credential. Knowing it must not grant access to a share or bypass existing authorization checks.
8. Evaluate the result in the current session/tenant context; do not reuse a value across tenants through constant folding or caching.

## Expected workflow

1. The consumer runs `SELECT CURRENT_TENANT_ID()` and sends the result to the provider.
2. The provider authorizes that ID using `ALTER SHARE ... ADD ACCOUNTS`.
3. The provider runs the same function and sends its tenant ID and share name to the consumer.
4. The consumer runs `CREATE DATABASE ... FROM SHARE` to complete setup.

Neither party should need an administrator or access to internal deployment configuration solely to discover its own tenant ID.

## Naming and alternatives

`CURRENT_TENANT_ID()` is recommended because the existing Share SQL uses tenant IDs.

`CURRENT_ORGANIZATION_NAME()` would return a display name and would not directly solve share authorization or lookup without an additional mapping mechanism. An organization should not be assumed to have a one-to-one relationship with a tenant.

If exposing the internal tenant ID as a long-term public identifier is undesirable, a stable public account/share identifier could be considered instead. However, that would also require defining identifier-to-tenant resolution, uniqueness, lifecycle guarantees, and support in Share SQL—not merely a function returning a new identifier. Confirming whether the current tenant ID is suitable for stable external use should be part of the design review.

## Follow-up suggestions and non-goals

The Cloud console could display the tenant ID with a copy action on the account information or Data Share page. It could also generate consumer setup SQL with correctly quoted identifiers. This UI work can be t

title: bug: NOT IN / <> ALL with a NULL in the subquery returns rows once the mark join spills
body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/issues) and found no similar issues.


### Version

`8.0.90-v1.2.943-nightly-419338dde9` (`SELECT version()`), image `datafuselabs/databend:nightly`
pulled 2026-09-15, single node, `QUERY_STORAGE_TYPE=fs`, Linux x86_64 (kernel 5.15.0-187).

Also reproduces on `v1.2.940-nightly-a280ed1f26`. The defect is visible in `main` @ `6b31170`.


### What's Wrong?

Under SQL's three-valued logic, if the subquery of `x NOT IN (SELECT ...)` produces **any**
NULL, the predicate is `NULL` for every probe row that has no match, so the query must return
**no rows at all**. Databend gets this right while the join stays in memory, but once the
hash join spills, `NOT IN` and `<> ALL` return a **nondeterministic subset of the rows that
should have been filtered out**. Nothing in the query fails or warns — it is a silent wrong
answer, and it appears only under memory pressure.

The same defect is visible in the exposed marker value: `k IN (SELECT ...)` returns `false`
(and `k NOT IN (...)` returns `true`) for rows whose correct value is `NULL`.

#### Minimal case (4-row and 2-row tables, `force_join_data_spill = 1`)

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE na_a (k INT NULL, v INT);
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE na_b (k INT NULL);
INSERT INTO na_a VALUES (1,10),(2,20),(3,30),(NULL,40);
INSERT INTO na_b VALUES (1),(NULL);
```

`na_b` is `{1, NULL}`, so `k NOT IN (SELECT k FROM na_b)` is `FALSE` for `k = 1` and `NULL`
for every other `k` (including `k IS NULL`). The correct result is empty.

| query (all with `force_join_data_spill = 1`) | correct | Databend |
|---|---|---|
| `SELECT k, v FROM na_a WHERE k NOT IN (SELECT k FROM na_b)` | *(no rows)* | **`(2, 20)`** |
| `SELECT k, v FROM na_a WHERE k <> ALL (SELECT k FROM na_b)` | *(no rows)* | **`(2, 20)`** |
| `SELECT k, v FROM na_a WHERE k NOT IN (SELECT k FROM na_b) OR v = 40` | `(NULL, 40)` | **`(2, 20)`, `(NULL, 40)`** |
| `SELECT k, v FROM na_a WHERE k NOT IN (1, NULL)` (with `inlist_to_join_threshold = 1`) | *(no rows)* | **`(2, 20)`** |

The marker expression shows the corruption directly — note that `k = 3` is still correct,
i.e. only *some* rows lose their NULL marker:

```sql
SET force_join_data_spill = 1;
SELECT k, v, k IN (SELECT k FROM na_b) AS in_expr,
              k NOT IN (SELECT k FROM na_b) AS notin_expr
FROM na_a ORDER BY k;
```

| k | v | `in_expr` (correct) | `in_expr` (spilled) | `notin_expr` (correct) | `notin_expr` (spilled) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | `true` | `true` | `false` | `false` |
| **2** | **20** | **`NULL`** | **`false`** | **`NULL`** | **`true`** |
| 3 | 30 | `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` |

and consequently `CASE WHEN k IN (...) THEN 'in' WHEN k NOT IN (...) THEN 'out' ELSE 'unknown' END`
reports `'out'` for `k = 2` where it must report `'unknown'`.

MySQL 9.7.2 on the same data returns no rows for the filter and `NULL`/`NULL` for the marker
columns of `k = 2` and `k = 3`, matching the non-spilled Databend result.

#### It is specifically the null-aware (mark) path, and specifically the spill rounds

Same data, same query, one setting changed at a time:

| configuration | result | |
|---|---|---|
| no spilling (default) | *(no rows)* | correct |
| `force_join_data_spill = 1` | `(2, 20)` | **wrong** |
| `force_join_data_spill = 1`, `enable_experimental_new_join = 0` | `(2, 20)` | **wrong** |
| `force_join_data_spill = 1`, `join_spilling_partition_bits = 0` | *(no rows)* | correct |
| `force_join_data_spill = 1`, build side has no NULL (`na_b = {1}`) | correct rows | correct |

`join_spilling_partition_bits = 0` means a single spill partition, i.e. a single restore
round — and that is exactly the case that stays correct. `enable_experimental_new_join`
makes no difference because mark joins are not handled by the new join and always execute in
the legacy hash join.

`NOT EXISTS`, `<> ANY`, `> ALL`, scalar subqueries, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL joins and plain `IN` with
a NULL

title: refactor(query): capture query lineage from the bound plan
body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary Lineage describes what the user wrote, but it was extracted from the **optimized** plan in `InterpreterFactory::get`. The optimizer rewrites plans for execution without preserving data sources, so several shapes lost or misattributed edges: - `INSERT INTO dst SELECT a IN (SELECT b FROM r) FROM l` — decorrelation turns the projected IN subquery into a mark join whose marker column has no scalar definition; lineage came back **empty** (verified against current `main`). - `INSERT INTO dst SELECT max(a), count(*) FROM src` — `RuleStatsAggregateOptimizer` / count folding replace the scan with constants over a `DummyTableScan`. - `... WHERE false` — the scan is folded into an empty `ConstantTableScan`. - Materialized-view rewrite swaps `Scan(src)` for a read of the MV, so lineage would name the MV instead of the table the user referenced. The same applies to view definitions planned by `REFRESH LINEAGE` / `get_lineage`. This PR moves **extraction** to the bind stage. The **recording** path (attach to `QueryContext` in the factory, `update_query_lineage_target_id`, `log_query_lineage`) is unchanged. ## Implementation - `planner.rs`: after `binder.bind()` and before `optimize()`, call `plan.capture_bound_query_lineage()` when lineage is enabled. Add `Planner::bind_sql()` (parse + bind only, no optimize / plan cache) for lineage consumers. - `lineage.rs`: new `BoundQueryLineage` snapshot; `capture_bound_query_lineage()` stores it in the plan's `Metadata`; `Plan::query_lineage()` returns the snapshot when present and falls back to direct extraction otherwise (plans that never went through the planner, or COPY without a query part). `lineage_metadata()` locates the query metadata for CTAS / CreateView / Insert / Replace / CopyIntoTable / CopyIntoLocation / InsertMultiTable / DataMutation. - `metadata.rs`: `bound_query_lineage` field + accessors. `Metadata` already carries bind-time lineage side data (`view_lineage_source_columns`, `materialized_cte_lineage_sources`) and is the same `Arc` on the bound and optimized plan, so all 34 `InterpreterFactory::get` callers need no change. - `optimizer.rs`: drop the `CreateView.query_plan` optimize pass — it only fed lineage; access checks work on the bound plan. - `interpreter_refresh_lineage.rs`, `get_lineage/resolver.rs`: use `bind_sql` so view definitions are inspected before optimization. Plan cache is not affected: only `Statement::Query` is cached, and no lineage-producing statement is a bare query. ## Tests - [ ] Unit Test - [x] Logic Test - [ ] Benchmark Test - [ ] No Test - _Explain why_ Integration coverage in `tests/lineage/sqllogic/{setup,check}/04_statement_coverage.test`: - statistics-folded `max(a), count(*)` — guarded by an `EXPLAIN` asserting the optimized plan is a `DummyTableScan`; only reproducible on a real Fuse table with statistics, so it is not unit-testable - projected `a IN (SELECT b ...)` — decorrelated into a mark join; asserts both `a` and `b` feed the target column Both would produce no edges if lineage were still extracted from the optimized plan. The existing 24 planner lineage unit tests pass unchanged (`cargo test -p databend-common-sql`); `cargo clippy -p databend-common-sql --tests -- -D warnings` and `cargo check -p databend-query --tests` are clean. ## Type of change - [x] Refactoring - [x] Bug Fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) ## AI assistance - AI usage: A coding agent investigated the optimizer/lineage interaction, drafted the implementation and tests; the responsible human directed the design decisions and reviewed the full diff. - Responsible human: @youngsofun - [x] The responsible human has read every line of this diff and can explain each change - - - This change is [](https://reviewable.io/revi

title: ISSUE-3121: simple chunk strategy in insertion
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://databend.rs/policies/cla/

## Summary

- issue #3121 
- issue #3147

the simple strategy goes like this:

For each query node that processes the insertion, while consuming the `SendableDatablockStream`
 - for each `DEFAULT_CHUNK_BLOCK_NUM` of blocks, let's say B, the following reshape is applied: 
    for each n successive data block in B, if the sum of their `memory_size` exceeds  `BLOCK_SIZE_THRESHOLD`, they will be merged into one larger block.
    
NOTE:
- currently, `DEFAULT_CHUNK_BLOCK_NUM` and `BLOCK_SIZE_THRESHOLD` will be fetched first from table options
   if not there, default values will be applied
- the max size of merged-block will be 2 * block_size_threshold (in memory size)
- after compression, the on-storage size of the block varies
- for block that is larger than `block_size_threshold`, they will NOT be split
    it might be better to apply fine-grained strategy in table compact/optimization


after this simple strategy is applied, the read performance might be improved for somehow:

A very **non**-scientific, local debug test:

title: Query cache
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://databend.rs/policies/cla/

## Summary

Add Query cache layer when reading object in fuse table.
we have 4 config in query_config:
* table_cache_enabled
* table_memory_cache_mb_size
* table_disk_cache_root : where to put disk cache files
* table_disk_cache_mb_size: disk cache max campacity

We only cache `snapshots` and `segments` on the query node now. (so the metadata can hold all in memory).

We have two tier of cache, when reading data, we will try to get data from `memory cache` -> `disk cache` -> `S3`.

When `memory cache` is full, we will put the evict item from `memory cache` to `disk cache`. And when `disk cache` is full, we will use LRU policy to evict extra items.

Now we have a trait `QueryCache` to abstract  `query cache` layer, we can add more effective cache implementations in the future.

We do have some simple metrics about cache statistics and we can get them from the metrics HTTP API.


##  dataset and config 
test dataset, `ontime` table, load data by https://github.com/datafuselabs/databend/blob/main/tests/suites/0_stateful/12_0001_streaming_load.sh


* table_memory_cache_mb_size: 512mb
* table_disk_cache_mb_size: 1024mb

## ec2 with s3 test
test with 3 SQL each 50 times,
```bash
#!/bin/bash

timestamp() {
  date +"%s" # current time
}

timestamp
for i in {1..50}
do
 echo $i
 curl -s  --request POST '127.0.0.1:8001/v1/statement/' --header 'Content-Type: text/plain' --data-raw 'SELECT DayOfWeek, count(*) AS c FROM ontime WHERE Year >= 2000 AND Year <= 2008 GROUP BY DayOfWeek ORDER BY c DESC;' > /dev/null
 curl -s  --request POST '127.0.0.1:8001/v1/statement/' --header 'Content-Type: text/plain' --data-raw 'SELECT Year, avg(DepDelay) FROM ontime GROUP BY Year;' > /dev/null
 curl -s  --request POST '127.0.0.1:8001/v1/statement/' --header 'Content-Type: text/plain' --data-raw 'SELECT DayOfWeek, count(*) AS c FROM ontime WHERE DepDelay>10 AND Year >= 2000 AND Year <= 2008 GROUP BY DayOfWeek ORDER BY c DESC;' > /dev/null
done
timestamp
```

time total
| No.        | cache with 2 layer | no cache |
| ------- | ------------------ | -------- |
| 1       | 18s                | 28s      |
| 2       | 18s                | 27s      |
| 3       | 19s                | 28s      |
| 4       | 17s                | 27s      |
| 5       | 19s                | 27s      |
| Average | 18.2s              | 27.2s    |

cache metadata is only `76KB` size, we can sure cache all meta data in memory. So it seems that S3 is very slow.

## Changelog

- Improvement

## Related Issues

Fixes #1784

title: Insert into empty shouldn't return default value
body:
**Summary**
```sql
mysql> CREATE TABLE t(a INT);
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.03 sec)

mysql> insert into t values();
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.04 sec)

mysql> select * from t;
+------+
| a    |
+------+
|    0 |
+------+
1 row in set (0.03 sec)
Read 1 rows, 4.00 B in 0.007 sec., 147.57 rows/sec., 590.28 B/sec.
```

Table t doesn't have an explicit default value for a, but it got 0 when inserted empty.

The reason why it got 0 is because https://github.com/datafuselabs/databend/blob/main/src/common/io/src/buffer/buffer_read_number_ext.rs#L81

We should get error when executing ` insert into t values();`.

Directly changing the logic of https://github.com/datafuselabs/databend/blob/main/src/common/io/src/buffer/buffer_read_number_ext.rs#L81 seems unreasonable, because it'll affect other code places.

title: refactor: Rewrite Inspector implementation
body:
This commit refactors implementation of inspector.

The intention is to be able to move inspector implementation to "deno_core". 

Following things were done to make that possible:

* "runtime/inspector.rs" was split into "runtime/inspector/mod.rs"
and "runtime/inspector/server.rs", separating inspector implementation
from Websocket server implementation.

* "DenoInspector" was renamed to "JsRuntimeInspector" and reference to "server"
was removed from the structure, making it independent of Websocket server
used to connect to Chrome Devtools.

* "WebsocketSession" was renamed to "InspectorSession" and rewritten in such 
a way that it's not tied to Websockets anymore; instead it accepts a pair
of "proxy" channel ends that allow to integrate the session with different
"transports".

* "InspectorSession" was renamed to "LocalInspectorSession" to better indicate
that it's an "in-memory" session and doesn't require Websocket server. It was
also rewritten in such a way that it uses "InspectorSession" from previous point
instead of reimplementing "v8::inspector::ChannelImpl" trait; this is done by using
the "proxy" channels to communicate with the V8 session.

Consequently "LocalInspectorSession" is now a frontend to "InspectorSession". This 
introduces a small inconvenience that awaiting responses for "LocalInspectorSession" requires
to concurrently poll worker's event loop. This arises from the fact that "InspectorSession"
is now owned by "JsRuntimeInspector", which in turn is owned by "Worker" or "WebWorker".
To ease this situation "Worker::with_event_loop" helper method was added, that takes
a future and concurrently polls it along with the event loop (using "tokio::select!" macro 
inside a loop).

title: `--watch` can corrupt cache
body:
Recently, I've been using watch mode increasingly, i.e. `deno run --watch`. This corrupted something with the cache.

In particular, `deno cache` would always check the types, even if no files were changed in between. Terminating all other programs (no LSP running and so on), this happened:
```bash
$ for i in {1..5}; do deno cache src/main.ts; done
Check file:///home/steffen/git/dtapp/backend/src/main.ts
Check file:///home/steffen/git/dtapp/backend/src/main.ts
Check file:///home/steffen/git/dtapp/backend/src/main.ts
Check file:///home/steffen/git/dtapp/backend/src/main.ts
Check file:///home/steffen/git/dtapp/backend/src/main.ts
```

The same applied for `deno run`. I could run first `deno cache` and then `deno run` and both operations would type-check the project. I expect only the former one to do so.

The problem was local for the directory. When I `cp -r`ed the directory to `/tmp`, everything worked fine there. In other words, it was remembered that type-checking had been performed, so it was only done once. Subsequent `deno cache` commands completed instantly, exactly as expected.

The problem could be solved by `rm -rf ~/.cache`. (I'm reporting the bug anyway here so it can be fixed.)

I do not know how to reproduce this reliably. However, my suspicion is that the watch mode with its frequent recompilations broke something, perhaps due to partial file writes or other things caused by race conditions and starting and stopping a process repeatedly.

I'm using Deno 1.20.4.

title: `Deno.serve` issues
body:
Quick list of things I think we need to address with the new `--unstable` `Deno.serve` API.

- [ ] Rename the API. `Deno.serve` does not clearly communicate the relation to HTTP. Strawman: `Deno.listenAndServeHttp`. Anyone else have other ideas?
- [x] Change signature to `(handler: (Request, ConnInfo) => Response, opts?: ListenAndServeHttpOptions) => Promise<void>` (move handler out of options bag).
- [ ] Rename `cert` and `key` options to `certFile` and `keyFile`.
- [ ] Add `certData` and `keyData` options that don't require reading these files from disk.
- [ ] Errors returned from `server.serve()` should not be swallowed with a `.catch(console.error);`.
- [ ] <s>Errors occuring in `server.serve` should clean up server resources</s>
- [ ] <s>Each server should have it's own date interval, otherwise each invocation to the API creates a different number of resources, which is confusing to users when using the test resource sanitizer.</s>
- [x] #15574
- [x] #15572
- [ ] <s>Remove all of the unwraps when handing values from JS.</s>
- [ ] <s>Flash does not handle socket write failures at all. If a write fails, or only writes partial data, we completely ignore this and just go onto the next write... </s>
- [ ] <s>The safety comments very often don't explain why something is safe. They just say "it's safe".</s>
- [ ] <s>Flash can not handle arbitrary methods.</s>
- [x] #15573

title: refactor(ext/http): use scopeguard defer to handle async drop
body:
Use the [scopeguard](https://docs.rs/scopeguard/) defer macro to run cleanup code for `new_slab_future`.
This means it can be a single async function, avoiding the need to create a struct and implement `PinnedDrop`

Async cleanup in Rust is awkward because async functions may be cancelled at any await point when their Future is dropped.
The scopeguard approach comes from the following articles:
* [How to think about `async`/`await` in Rust](http://cliffle.com/blog/async-inversion/)

title: perf(lsp): cancel ts requests on future drop
body:
cc @bartlomieju @dsherret 

When an old request is obsoleted while the user is typing, the client will say so to the server and tower-lsp will drop the future associated with that request.

This wires that up to the ts server by having any request's token be cancelled when the surrounding state is dropped.

title: LSP: file extension changed from `.ts` to `.js` after renaming
perf(lsp): lock out requests until init is complete
body:
Previously we initialized with 'partial' config in the `initialize` handler and then fetched the proper per-workspace folder config in the `initialized` handler. The problem is `textDocument/didOpen` notifications arrive in between these, and it leads to diagnostics requests being started and then cancelled immediately. Also the init sequence is weirdly split between them, so for example the config tree walk doesn't take into account per-workspace folder enable settings on startup.

This unifies the init sequence into `initialized` and uses a token to prevent other request/notification handlers from running until it's complete. Also no longer send a diagnostics request on startup. Some tests which were subtly depending on this have been rewritten, but it all works in practice. Removes `LspNpmConfigHash`. It shouldn't be necessary since config changes are infrequent.

The token is a hack which is only required because the LSP spec doesn't allow `workspace/configuration` requests during `initialize`, which IMO it absolutely should. See https://github.com/Microsoft/language-server-protocol/issues/567#issuecomment-2085131917.

fix: prevent threadpool starvation with concurrent file locks
body:
## Summary

Fixes #22504.

`lock_async` used `spawn_blocking` to call the blocking `flock()` syscall, which parks a tokio blocking-threadpool thread for the entire duration of the lock wait. With the blocking pool capped at a couple dozen threads, acquiring 33+ concurrent locks exhausts all threads and deadlocks any other `spawn_blocking` work (like `readTextFile`/`writeTextFile`), which in turn may be what is needed to release the locks.

### The fix

Keep using the blocking `flock()` syscall (so the OS still schedules lock acquisition fairly and there are no spurious `try_lock` errors), but bound how much of the shared threadpool lock waits can consume:

- `lock_async` runs the blocking `flock()` via a new helper that caps how many concurrent lock waits may sit on the blocking threadpool at once (currently 8).
- Any waits beyond that cap run on dedicated threads, which don't compete with other blocking fs operations.

This preserves `flock()` fairness while guaranteeing the blocking pool can never be fully consumed by pending locks.

### Notes on earlier review feedback

An earlier revision used a non-blocking `try_lock` poll loop. That was reworked because:

- `try_lock` is not fair, so a waiter could starve for a long time under contention.
- On Windows, `try_lock` (`LOCKFILE_FAIL_IMMEDIATELY`) on a contended file returns `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`, which `std` maps to `TryLockError::Error` rather than `WouldBlock`, turning normal contention into a user-facing rejection (and failing the spec test on the Windows shards).

Going back to blocking `flock()` addresses both.

## Test plan

- New spec test: 50 concurrent lock acquisitions (well above the threadpool size) with interleaved file reads/writes, completes without deadlock and produces a correct serialized counter.

title: fix(ext/node): implement timeout, killSignal, and pid for child_process spawnSync
body:
## Summary
- Implements `timeout` and `killSignal` options for `spawnSync`/`execSync`/`execFileSync`
- Spawns a condvar-based timer thread that kills the child process (and its process group on Unix) after the deadline, then flags `killed_by_timeout` in the result
- Returns `pid` from `op_spawn_sync` so `spawnSync` results include the `pid` field as Node.js expects
- Uses a `KillSignal` enum to accept both numeric and string signal values directly from JS, avoiding string roundtrip
- On Unix, uses `process_group(0)` + `kill(-pgid)` to kill the entire process tree on timeout
- On Windows, uses `OpenProcess`/`TerminateProcess` with a brief pipe-reader timeout for orphaned grandchildren
- `pid` and `killed_by_timeout` are exposed as non-enumerable properties on the output object, keeping the `Deno.Command` public API unchanged

title: fix(ext/node): implement crypto.encapsulate / crypto.decapsulate (RSA)
body:
## Summary

Implements `crypto.encapsulate` / `crypto.decapsulate` (Node 24+ KEM API) for RSA keys, so the upstream Node test [`parallel/test-crypto-encap-decap.js`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/test/parallel/test-crypto-encap-decap.js) now passes — see the [2026-04-24 node compat run](https://node-test-viewer.deno.dev/results/2026-04-24) for the prior failure.

### Why RSA-only for now

The upstream test gates each key type by OpenSSL version (`hasOpenSSL(3, 2)` for DHKEM curves, `hasOpenSSL(3, 5)` for ML-KEM). Deno reports `process.versions.openssl = "3.0.7+quic"`, so all non-RSA paths take the `!supported` branch which expects an `ERR_OSSL_EVP_DECODE_ERROR` / `ERR_CRYPTO_OPERATION_FAILED` throw — exactly what RSA-only key parsing produces for non-RSA inputs. Bumping the reported OpenSSL version to `3.2.0` and adding DHKEM (P-256 / P-384 / P-521 / X25519 / X448, all implementable on top of crates already in the workspace — `p256`, `p384`, `p521`, `x25519-dalek`, `ed448-goldilocks`, `hkdf`) is queued as a follow-up PR.

### What changed

- **`ext/node_crypto/lib.rs`**: two new ops `op_node_rsa_encapsulate(key) -> (sharedKey, ciphertext)` and `op_node_rsa_decapsulate(key, ciphertext) -> sharedKey`. Implementation is straightforward [RSASVE](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5990#section-4) — pick a uniform random `Z ∈ [0, n)` via rejection sampling, ciphertext = `Z^e mod n`, decap recovers `Z = ct^d mod n`. Both outputs are big-endian byte strings of length `len(n)`, matching OpenSSL's `EVP_PKEY_encapsulate` output. Reuses existing `rsa_encrypt` / `rsa_decrypt_and_check` helpers.
- **`ext/node/polyfills/internal/crypto/encap.ts`** (new): JS polyfill. Accepts KeyObject, CryptoKey, PEM/DER bytes, JWK, and the `{ key, format, type }` object form (JWK and the object form route through existing `createPublicKey`/`createPrivateKey`). Sync and Node-style callback variants both supported; the async path uses `queueMicrotask` and on failure delivers the fixed `'Deriving bits failed'` error per Node semantics. Argument validation throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` for missing key / non-buffer ciphertext, matching the test's expected error shapes.
- **`ext/node/polyfills/crypto.ts`** + **`ext/node/lib.rs`**: re-export and register the new polyfill.

### Failure on `main`

```
error: Uncaught (in promise) AssertionError: Expected values to be strictly deep-equal:
  Comparison {
+   message: 'crypto.encapsulate is not a function',
```

### Test plan

- [x] `tests/node_compat/runner/suite/test/parallel/test-crypto-encap-decap.js` passes locally (full RSA path: sync / callback / promisified × KeyObject / PEM / DER+spki/pkcs8 / JWK + wrong-key error messages, and the throw-with-decode-error path for every non-RSA key type).
- [x] No regression in surrounding crypto compat tests (`test-crypto-from-binary`, `test-crypto-classes`, `test-crypto-keygen`, `test-crypto-padding` still pass; the others I sampled were already failing on `main` for unrelated reasons).
- [x] `./tools/format.js` and `./tools/lint.js` clean for changed code.
- [ ] CI green.

### Follow-up

Phase 2 PR (queued): bump `process.versions.openssl` to `3.2.0`, add DHKEM(P-256, P-384, P-521, X25519, X448) so the test exercises every non-ML-KEM curve. ML-KEM stays unimplemented (would require bumping the reported version to `3.5.0` plus a Kyber crate addition).

title: fix(ext/process): write IPC messages synchronously when possible
body:
`process.send(msg); process.exit(0)` in a forked child reliably lost the
message: the IPC write op only created a Tokio write future, and
`process.exit` terminated the process before that future was ever polled,
so no `write(2)` ever reached the kernel.

When nothing is queued ahead of the message (and no fd is being passed),
we now attempt a non-blocking `write(2)` directly on the pipe fd before
returning the async future. Tokio's own `try_write` can't be used here
because it returns `WouldBlock` until the socket has been polled writable
at least once. For typical IPC payloads the whole message lands in the
kernel buffer synchronously, so it survives an immediate `process.exit`;
if the kernel accepts only part of it, the existing async path drains the
remainder (`serialized[written..]`), so ordering is preserved and no bytes
are duplicated. On lock contention or on Windows (the named-pipe write
half exposes no `try_write`) we fall back to the unchanged async path.

Fixes #33085

title: fix(ext/node): normalize http2 respondWithFile/FD async errors to NGHTTP2_INTERNAL_ERROR (#33656)
body:
Closes #33656

### Summary

When `respondWithFile` or `respondWithFD` hit an asynchronous failure (for example after `fs.open` / `fs.fstat`) but the stream has already committed response headers, the stream should be reset with **`NGHTTP2_INTERNAL_ERROR`**, matching Node’s behavior, instead of surfacing the underlying filesystem error on the client stream in inconsistent ways.

### Changes

- **`ext/node/polyfills/http2.ts`**
  - Added `handleAsyncFileResponseError` to centralize the “headers already sent” path: **`closeStream(..., NGHTTP2_INTERNAL_ERROR, kForceRstStream)`** then **`destroy()`** without leaking the raw `fs` error to the peer in that state.
  - Wired **`doSendFD`**, **`doSendFileFD`**, and **`afterOpen`** to use this path when appropriate (including `onError` fallback behavior when headers are not yet committed).

- **`tests/unit_node/http2_test.ts`**
  - Regression: **`respondWithFile`** with a missing path + forced `respond` on next tick → client **`ERR_HTTP2_STREAM_ERROR`** with **`NGHTTP2_INTERNAL_ERROR`** in the message.
  - Regression: **`respondWithFD`** with invalid fd + `statCheck` + forced `respond` on next tick → same client error shape.

### Verification

- `cargo test -p unit_node_tests -- http2_test`
- `./tools/format.js`
- `./tools/lint.js --js`

### Related

- Closes https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/33656

title: feat(task): prefix output lines with task name when running in parallel
body:
Closes #27647

When running multiple tasks in parallel via `deno task`
(e.g. `"dev": { "dependencies": ["task_a", "task_b"] }`),
all stdout/stderr streams to the terminal without labels,
making interleaved output impossible to attribute.

This PR prefixes each output line with the task name so it
is always clear which task produced which output.

**Before:**
```
Task build tsc && node scripts/bundle.js
Task test jest --watch
src/index.ts
PASS src/index.test.ts
Compilation complete.
Test Suites: 1 passed
```

**After:**
```
Task build tsc && node scripts/bundle.js
Task test jest --watch
[build] src/index.ts
[test] PASS src/index.test.ts
[build] Compilation complete.
[test] Test Suites: 1 passed
```

### Changes

- `cli/task_runner.rs`: Add `PrefixedWriter<W>`, a
  `std::io::Write` wrapper that buffers each line and writes
  it atomically with a prefix, preventing byte-level
  interleaving between concurrent tasks. Add
  `make_prefixed_task_io(prefix)` which creates a piped
  `TaskIo` and spawns background reader threads to drain the
  pipes through `PrefixedWriter`.

- `cli/tools/task.rs`: Add `parallel_info: Option` to
  `RunSingleOptions`. When set, `run_single` uses
  `make_prefixed_task_io` with a colored `[task_name]` prefix
  instead of inheriting stdio. The prefix reader handles are
  awaited after task exit to flush all output before reporting
  completion. Only tasks that actually run concurrently with at
  least one other task get prefixed — single-task runs and
  purely sequential dependency chains are unaffected.

- Color assignment uses a stable sequential index based on
  topological order, cycling through cyan, magenta, yellow,
  green, blue, red. Short task names are right-padded so
  brackets align across rows.

- `cli/args/flags.rs`: Add `--no-prefix` flag to opt out of
  prefixing when it is not desired.

- Spec test `.out` files updated to reflect the new prefixed
  format, with `[UNORDERED_START]`/`[UNORDERED_END]` blocks
  where needed.

title: fix(ext/node): avoid retaining sync writev chunks
body:
Fixes #33848

This PR addresses a memory retention issue in `node:http` when writes are dispatched via `writev`.

Previously, `writevGeneric()` would keep a reference to `req._chunks` after every successful `writev` call, even when the native write completed synchronously. In scenarios with many small chunked HTTP responses, this caused unnecessary retention of per-request JS chunk arrays. Additionally, the native `writev` path eagerly allocated owned string storage before determining whether the write would actually need to be handled asynchronously.

### What's changed

* Synchronous native `writev` completions no longer retain JS chunks
* Asynchronous `writev` operations still retain chunks when required (e.g. buffer-backed iovecs)
* String iovecs use inline storage on the synchronous fast path
* String data is only copied into owned storage if the write falls back to the async path
* If a partial synchronous drain leaves only buffer-backed iovecs for the async tail, the string storage migration now returns without allocating

### Tests

* Added regression test to ensure `_chunks` are not retained for synchronous `writev`
* Verified that `_chunks` are still retained for asynchronous `writev`
* Added Rust unit tests for correct remapping of string iovecs into owned storage in async scenarios
* Added Rust unit test for the buffer-only async tail case, where string storage should not be retained

### Current status

* Rebased onto current `denoland/main` (`e69a05dbe`) after review `4255556700`
* PR head is now `fba50c50976ba64322be8a45c026b57be294b551`
* GitHub checks after the rebase: `license/cla` passing, `lint title` passing
* `fibibot` review `4255556700` had no actionable inline threads and described the change as approve-quality pending full CI authorization

I could not re-run the focused local Rust/Node tests in this checkout because this environment does not have `cargo` or `deno` on `PATH`. The relevant commands to run once the toolchain is available are:

