```sh
cargo test -p unit_node_tests --test unit_node -- "writev only retains chunks"
```

title: fix(permissions): allow non-recursive reads/writes on ancestors of deny
body:
`Deno.statSync("/")` (and other single-path ops like `Deno.open`,
`readFile`, `writeFile`, `readDir`, `lstat`) failed with `NotCapable`
whenever any deny scope lived under the queried path. With `--allow-read
--deny-read=/mnt`, `stat("/")` was rejected because `/mnt` is a
descendant of `/`, even though `stat` does not recurse into the denied
scope. The same surprise applied to writes: `writeFileSync("/foo", ...)`
failed under `--allow-write --deny-write=/foo/bar`.

The strict `UnaryPermission::check` is meant for recursive operations
(e.g. `fs::remove_all`) where every path below the query must be
allowed. `check_open` was using it for every fs op, including ones that
only touch a single path. This routes `check_open` through
`check_partial` for both read and write, and adds the missing
`check_partial` for `UnaryPermission<ReadDescriptor>` to mirror the
existing one for writes. Strict `check` is unchanged and continues to
gate recursive callers.

Closes #27622

title: refactor(fetch): remove tower-http decompression
body:
## Summary

This removes the `tower-http` dependency from `deno_fetch` by replacing `tower_http::decompression::Decompression` with a focused local `DecompressionService` around the existing retrying Hyper client.

The local service preserves transparent decoding for ordinary single-encoding `gzip` and `br` fetch responses, keeps the service future boxed as `Send + Sync`, and avoids the previous `ext/kv` workaround. `ext/kv` is no longer part of this PR's diff, so remote KV request cancellation behavior is unchanged.

## Behavior Notes

- Adds `Accept-Encoding: gzip,br` when the request does not already provide `Accept-Encoding`.
- Preserves explicit caller-provided `Accept-Encoding` values.
- For Range requests without an explicit `Accept-Encoding`, sends `Accept-Encoding: identity` and returns the response body raw. This is intentional: partial compressed byte ranges cannot be transparently decoded as complete gzip/br representations.
- For Range requests with an explicit caller-provided `Accept-Encoding`, preserves that value and still returns the response body raw with `Content-Encoding` intact.
- Leaves `Accept-Encoding: identity` responses raw.
- Keeps `send_no_decompress` responses raw.
- Decodes only single `gzip` or `br` `Content-Encoding` values, with case-insensitive matching and token whitespace trimming.
- Leaves multi-value or stacked `Content-Encoding` responses such as `gzip, br` undecoded with the original `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` headers intact. This matches the single-encoding behavior relied on from the removed `tower-http` layer.
- Passes empty `Content-Length: 0` gzip/br responses through without decoding, stripping `Content-Encoding` so empty compressed responses do not fail with decoder EOF errors.
- Strips `Content-Encoding`, `Content-Length`, and `Transfer-Encoding` from decoded responses.

## Changed Files

This PR changes 5 files:

- `Cargo.toml`: removes the workspace `tower-http` dependency.
- `Cargo.lock`: removes `tower-http` and records the focused `deno_fetch` dependency changes.
- `ext/fetch/Cargo.toml`: replaces `tower-http` with `async-compression` and `tokio-util`.
- `ext/fetch/lib.rs`: adds the local decompression service and raw-body bypass handling.
- `ext/fetch/tests.rs`: adds coverage for gzip, br, accept-encoding injection and preservation, Range/identity behavior, Range with explicit `Accept-Encoding`, empty compressed bodies, multi-encoding passthrough, transfer-encoding stripping, and `send_no_decompress` raw responses. The fetch tests also install the Rustls aws-lc crypto provider before constructing clients so the lib tests are deterministic in workspace CI.

## Validation

- `cargo check -p deno_fetch`

title: perf(ext/http): use captured file ranges for serve responses
body:
## Summary

This adds a raw H1 response path for file-backed `ReadableStream` bodies returned from `Deno.serve`.

When a response body is backed by an auto-closing `FileResource`, the raw H1 path now captures the file's current `{ offset, length }` and streams exactly that range. This lets Deno emit a fixed `Content-Length` for common file responses instead of falling back to chunked framing.

The generic resource-stream path is unchanged for non-file resources and non-auto-closing file streams.

## Details

- Detect `FileResource` bodies in `op_http_set_response_body_resource` on the raw H1 path.
- Wrap auto-closing file resources in a raw file-body resource that uses positional reads from the captured range.
- Carry the known file length into the raw stream response writer for fixed-length framing.
- Add unit coverage that verifies `new Response(file.readable)` emits `Content-Length` and not `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`.

This is not kernel `sendfile`; TLS still needs plaintext bytes in userspace. The captured file range gives us the right representation for a future plain-TCP `sendfile` optimization and a tighter TLS read/write loop.

## Perf

Benchmark script:

```ts
Deno.serve({}, async (_req) => {
  const file = await Deno.open(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);

  return new Response(file.readable, {
    headers: {
      "content-type": "text/plain",
    },
  });
});
```

Command:

```sh
oha -n 1m -c 100 --disable-compression http://127.0.0.1:<port>/
```

Results, 3 runs each:

| binary | requests/sec runs | median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| canary `2.8.2+aff8385` | 28688.5431, 28698.0906, 28124.9463 | 28688.5431 |
| this PR `target/release-lite/deno` | 39957.2979, 39821.9811, 40573.3755 | 39957.2979 |

Median throughput improvement: **+39.3%**.

## Validation

- `cargo build --bin deno`
- `cargo build --profile release-lite --bin deno`
- `cargo test --test unit autoResponseWithFileReadableKnownLength -- --nocapture`
- Manual curl of the benchmark script:
  - before: `transfer-encoding: chunked`
  - after: `content-length: 142`

feat(task): git-changed filtering for deno task --filter (pnpm [ref] grammar)
body:
### Context

`deno task --filter` currently matches **package names** only: `package_filter_to_regex()` (`cli/tools/task.rs:1377`) escapes the input and turns `*` into `.*`. There's no way to select packages by what changed in git — the single biggest CI speedup for large monorepos ("only build/test packages affected since `origin/main`"). pnpm expresses this with a `[<since-ref>]` suffix grammar.

### Behavior to implement

Extend `--filter` parsing to recognize a git-ref selector in brackets, pnpm-compatible:

- `--filter "[origin/main]"` — select workspace packages whose files changed since the git ref `origin/main`.
- `--filter "...[origin/main]"` — changed packages **plus their dependents** (leading `...`).
- `--filter "[origin/main]..."` — changed packages **plus their dependencies** (trailing `...`).
- Combinable with a name pattern: `--filter "@scope/*[origin/main]"`.

Implementation outline:
1. Parse an optional trailing `[<ref>]` out of the filter string before the existing name-regex step.
2. Run `git diff --name-only <ref>...HEAD` (and include uncommitted/untracked changes) to get changed files; map each to the owning workspace member by path prefix.
3. Apply dependency-graph expansion (`...` prefix/suffix) using the same workspace dependency graph the topological scheduler already builds.
4. Intersect with any name pattern also present in the filter.
5. If not in a git repo, or the ref is unknown, error clearly.

### Out of scope

- A standalone `deno task --affected` shorthand (can follow later).
- Non-git change detection.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--filter "[<ref>]"` selects only packages with changes since `<ref>`.
- [ ] `...[<ref>]` additionally includes transitive dependents; `[<ref>]...` includes transitive dependencies.
- [ ] Works combined with a name pattern (intersection).
- [ ] Uncommitted + untracked changes are counted, not just committed diffs.
- [ ] Clear error outside a git repo or on an unknown ref.
- [ ] Docs + `deno task --help` updated with the bracket grammar.
- [ ] Tests: changed-only, +dependents, +dependencies, name-pattern intersection, no-git error.

title: feat(cli): unstable relaxed default permission profile
body:
Closes https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/29784

This is groundwork for the Deno 3 default-permissions change. Today `deno
run` denies every capability by default and prompts one by one, which trains
users into reaching for `-A`. For example `deno run npm:cowsay hello` needs
two prompt rounds today, one of them just so the package can read its own
data file.

This adds a relaxed default permission profile that, when active, grants a
pragmatic baseline so most CLI tools run without prompts while still blocking
the two things that matter: exfiltration (net stays gated, so anything read
cannot leave the machine) and persistence outside the project (write is
confined to the working directory and the OS temp directory). Concretely the
profile grants:

- read: allowed everywhere on disk
- write: allowed only under the cwd (recorded at process start) and the OS
  temp directory
- env: allowed
- net, run, ffi, sys: unchanged, still prompt in a TTY and deny
  non-interactively
- import: unchanged, keeps its existing implicit trusted-host allowance

The profile is gated by the `DENO_UNSTABLE_RELAXED_PERMISSIONS` env var. It is
on by default and setting the var to `0` opts back out to today's
deny-by-default behavior. Gating it behind the unstable var lets us gather
feedback before committing to flipping the default.

The profile only applies when the user provided no explicit allow-side
permission configuration: no `--allow-*`, no `-A`, no `-P`/`--permission-set`,
and no permission set from the config file. Any of those means behavior is
byte-for-byte identical to today. `--deny-*` flags do not disable the profile;
they compose on top since deny always wins. The check reuses a new
`PermissionFlags::has_allow_permission()` helper that, unlike the existing
`has_permission()`, ignores deny/ignore flags.

The profile is applied centrally in `flags_to_permissions_options`'s caller so
it covers `deno run`, `serve`, `test`, `bench`, `task` and the repl uniformly.
It deliberately does not touch `deno eval` (already implicit allow-all), `deno
x` (has its own allow-all default), or `deno compile` (permissions are baked
at compile time; explicitly out of scope).

## Sharp edges handled

- Temp dir canonicalization: the write allow-list includes both the raw and
  canonicalized forms of the cwd and the OS temp dir, so a write to `/tmp/x`
  still matches when it is canonicalized to `/private/tmp/x` at check time
  (macOS symlinks `/tmp` and `/var/folders` under `/private`). `TMPDIR` is
  honored via `std::env::temp_dir`.
- cwd semantics: the grant is the path recorded at process start, so
  `Deno.chdir()` does not widen it. A spec test proves this.
- Worker inheritance: child workers derive from the parent's
  PermissionsContainer, so a default worker inherits the profile (reads
  anywhere but cannot fetch). A spec test covers it.

## Decisions

- env is included: node-compat code reads env pervasively (yargs reads `env._`
  before doing anything), and the exfil risk of readable env is mitigated by
  net remaining gated. Deno's env permission does not separate get from set;
  that is acceptable here.
- sys is not included in v1 (`os.cpus()`, `hostname`, etc. keep prompting). If
  testing shows this is the next biggest prompt-fatigue source for npm CLIs it
  is a follow-up candidate rather than scope creep here.
- Non-interactive behavior is unchanged: non-granted capabilities still
  auto-deny when there is no TTY.
- A reserved `-P standard` built-in set name that selects this profile even
  with the gate off was considered but deferred (left as a TODO) to keep the
  central default minimal.

## Tests

New spec tests under `tests/specs/permission/relaxed_default/` cover: read
anywhere, write under cwd and temp, env read, denied writes outside both,
gated net, explicit-flag opt-out (an `--allow-net` flag disables the profile
so a cwd write then fails), `--deny-write` comp

title: fix(ext/net): abort pending Deno.connect during DNS resolution
body:
The signal option added in #27113 fetched the cancel handle from the
resource table only after address resolution completed. Since aborting
closes that resource, an abort that fired while the DNS lookup was still
in flight removed the resource before the op could fetch it, the
cancellation was silently lost, and the connection attempt kept running
until the OS timeout (~75s on macOS).

This fetches the cancel handle before the first await point (async ops
are polled eagerly, so this runs before any abort can be delivered),
makes the DNS lookup itself cancellable, and removes the cancel handle
resource on every exit path so it no longer leaks in the resource table
when resolution fails. Includes a regression test that cancels the op
while it is parked in the DNS lookup.

Fixes #26819

title: fix(ext/node): retry DNS query when its per-attempt timeout fires
body:
## What

`node:dns`'s `Resolver` retry loop (`ext/node/polyfills/internal_binding/cares_wrap.ts`) enforces the per-attempt `timeout` with a manual `setTimeout` that closes the op's cancel handle when it elapses. The op is not given any timeout itself, so this timer is what bounds each attempt.

When the timer fires the in-flight `op_dns_resolve` throws `Deno.errors.Interrupted`. The catch block treated **all** `Interrupted` as an explicit `cancel()` ("don't retry"), so a query to an unresponsive server gave up after a **single** attempt instead of honoring `tries`. Retries only happened when hickory's own (much longer, ~5s default) internal timeout happened to win the race and surface `TimedOut` first.

## Why it was flaky

`node_compat::parallel::test-dns-resolver-max-timeout.js` measures resolve time for two configs against a server that never answers the `nxdomain` query:

- `timeout1`: `{ timeout: 500, tries: 3 }` — uncapped, so attempts should take 500 + 1000 + 2000 ≈ 3500ms
- `timeout2`: `{ timeout: 500, tries: 3, maxTimeout: 500 }` — capped, so 500 + 500 + 500 ≈ 1500ms

and asserts `timeout1 > timeout2`. Because the manual timer (500ms) almost always beat hickory's ~5s timeout, the `Interrupted` path fired and **no retry** happened, so both configs did one ~500ms attempt and reported equal times — the reported failure was `timeout1: 502, timeout2: 502` → `502 > 502` is false. It only passed on the rare runs where hickory's timeout won the race, hence the flake.

## Fix

Track whether the abort came from the attempt's own timeout timer. If so, treat it as a timeout and retry with the next (longer) timeout — identical to the existing `TimedOut` path — while an explicit `cancel()` still stops immediately. This makes the increasing-vs-capped timeout behavior deterministic (timeout1 ≈ 3500ms, timeout2 ≈ 1500ms, a robust ~2s margin), so the `flaky` marker is dropped and the test is enforced normally.

Closes #35066

title: Complete native Windows ARM64 support across Deno's distribution surface
body:
## Summary

Deno's core Windows ARM64 port is complete enough to ship native releases, but the surrounding distribution surface is still inconsistent.

The standard PowerShell installer downloads x64, an x64 installation continues upgrading to x64, and several CLI, Desktop, npm, and package-manager paths either lack ARM64 propagation or native validation.

This issue tracks the remaining distribution and compatibility work. It does not reopen #13331 or propose another V8/runtime port.

## What already works

- [x] [Deno v2.9.2](https://github.com/denoland/deno/releases/tag/v2.9.2) publishes native Windows ARM64 `deno`, `denort`, `libdenort`, checksums, and binary upgrade deltas.
- [x] Deno has native `windows-11-arm` build and test jobs.
- [x] The original runtime issue, #13331, was closed by #31917.
- [x] `deno compile --target aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` target parsing landed on `main` in #36004. This was merged after v2.9.2 and has not shipped in that release.
- [x] The npm wrapper publishes an [`@deno/win32-arm64`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deno/win32-arm64) binary package.
- [x] [Laufey v0.6.0](https://github.com/littledivy/laufey/releases/tag/v0.6.0) publishes native Windows ARM64 WebView2 and raw/winit backends.
- [x] Deno's native Windows ARM64 CI already exercises its internal N-API and FFI integration suites.

## Immediate user-visible problem

The documented Windows installation command is:

```powershell
irm https://deno.land/install.ps1 | iex
```

However, [`deno_install/install.ps1`](https://github.com/denoland/deno_install/blob/1f1d6faeaf3a58b6709d34bbaf8af51ec56ff566/install.ps1#L21-L41) still hardcodes:

```powershell
$Target = "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"
```

A Windows ARM64 machine therefore receives the x64 executable and runs it through Windows emulation. This is already tracked narrowly in [denoland/deno_install#347](https://github.com/denoland/deno_install/issues/347).

After installation, this command should report a native build:

```powershell
deno eval 'console.log(JSON.stringify(Deno.build, null, 2))'
```

Expected:

```json
{
  "target": "aarch64-pc-windows-msvc",
  "arch": "aarch64",
  "os": "windows",
  "vendor": "pc",
  "env": "msvc"
}
```

The installer must detect the native operating-system architecture rather than the architecture of the PowerShell process. This matters when x64 PowerShell is running under emulation.

`RuntimeInformation.OSArchitecture` reports the native architecture on modern .NET, but Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on .NET Framework and may still report x64. The robust source of truth is [`IsWow64Process2`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wow64apiset/nf-wow64apiset-iswow64process2) and its native-machine result, with `RuntimeInformation.OSArchitecture` retained only as a guarded fallback. See also the [.NET 7 emulation behavior change](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/compatibility/interop/7.0/osarchitecture-emulation).

## Proposed work

### 1. Correct Windows release checksums

Current Windows release jobs [write `.sha256sum` files using `Get-FileHash | Format-List`](https://github.com/denoland/deno/blob/dff3cbe35bf9139a3d774f9cbf93a90ff93dbbde/.github/workflows/ci.ts#L819-L829). [Deno's upgrade checksum parser](https://github.com/denoland/deno/blob/dff3cbe35bf9139a3d774f9cbf93a90ff93dbbde/cli/tools/upgrade.rs#L1629-L1642) expects GNU-style output beginning with a 64-character hash, so Windows delta verification cannot consume the published files and falls back to a full archive.

- [ ] Emit canonical `<hash>  <filename>` checksum files for Windows release assets.
- [ ] Keep the client parser compatible with both canonical files and historical PowerShell `Hash : ...` files.
- [ ] Test the parser with fixtures copied from real Windows release assets.
- [ ] Apply the same parser compatibility to `deno_install` archive verification.

### 2. Fix `deno_install`

- [ ] Resolve the native Windows architecture with `IsWow64Process2`.
- [ ] Map nativ

title: AbortSignal.timeout() throws uncaught TimeoutError after fetch already completed
body:
## Summary

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` still delivers an **uncaught** `TimeoutError` after the abortable consumer (`fetch`) has already completed successfully. The timer is not tied to the lifetime of the request: when it later fires, Deno treats `controller.abort(TimeoutError)` as an unhandled rejection.

This is distinct from [#20663](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/20663) (sanitizeOps leak of the sleep op, fixed in [#23842](https://github.com/denoland/deno/pull/23842)). Ops sanitizer is not involved here — the process dies on an uncaught `TimeoutError` even with `sanitizeOps: false`.

## Environment

- Deno 2.9.5+a883d13 (canary, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
- OS: Windows 10/11 (NT 10.0.26200)
- Also expected on any platform; the abort-signal timer is in `ext:deno_web/03_abort_signal.js`

## Reproduction

```js
const r = await fetch("https://example.com", { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(50) });
await r.arrayBuffer();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 200));
console.log("still alive");
```

```
deno eval --allow-all "<the snippet>"
```

## Observed

Process exits 1 before "still alive"`:

```
error: Uncaught (in promise) TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout
    at Object.<anonymous> (ext:deno_web/03_abort_signal.js:1:2081)
    at listOnTimeout (ext:core/02_timers.js:307:17)
    at Object.processTimers (ext:core/02_timers.js:250:7)
    at __processTimers (ext:core/01_core.js:448:21)
```

Inside `deno test`, the same rejection is wrapped as:

```
Uncaught error from ./some.test.mjs FAILED
error: (in promise) TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout
This error was not caught from a test and caused the test runner to fail on the referenced module.
It most likely originated from a dangling promise, event/timeout handler or top-level code.
```

A `try/catch` around `fetch` does **not** help: the rejection is from the timeout timer, after `fetch` has already settled.

## Expected

After `fetch` completes, aborting the unused timeout signal is a no-op (WHATWG: abort with no listeners). The snippet should print `still alive` and exit 0.

Alternatively, `AbortSignal.timeout` should cancel its timer when the last consumer is done, same as the intent of #23842.

## Downstream (fount)

Repo: https://github.com/steve02081504/fount

We pass `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` into `fetch` in the test hub (module-check ready, GitHub-issue probe, kernel health) and in long-lived product paths (log viewer ping, WeChat API). A 15s module-check ready fetch that returns in milliseconds still explodes ~15s later. In a multi-file `deno test` process that is attributed to whichever file is current (`testkit:kernel` → `display.test.mjs` in our last wave).

**When fixed:** no fount workaround will be applied (rewriting every call site to `AbortController` + `clearTimeout` is the wrong layer). Re-run `fount test testkit:kernel` and confirm the uncaught `TimeoutError` is gone.

title: fix(ext/node): keep writev buffer boundaries in TLS record framing
body:
## Problem

`npm:tedious` (and therefore `npm:mssql` and `@prisma/adapter-mssql`) connections to SQL Server / Azure SQL fail with `socket hang up` / `Connection lost - socket hang up` whenever a query's TDS message spans 3 or more TDS packets (roughly > 8 KB with the default 4096-byte packet size). Small queries work; the same code works on Node. This is distinct from the implicit session-resumption issue fixed by #36592 and from the JSStreamSocket deadlock fixed for #33907 — with both of those fixes in place (Deno 2.9.6), large writes still kill the connection.

Mechanism, verified against a real SQL Server 2022 with a record-level wire capture:

- tedious writes one TDS packet (4096 bytes) per stream write. Packet 1 flushes alone; while it is in flight, packets 2..n queue in the `Writable` and are submitted together through `_writev`.
- Deno's `TLSWrap.writev` flattened all chunks into one slice before feeding rustls, and rustls fragments records per `writer().write()` call — so the resulting application-data record spanned two TDS packets. For a 3-packet message the capture shows Deno sending records of 4096 + 4150 plaintext bytes where Node sends 4096 + 4096 + 54.
- Node encrypts each writev buffer with its own `SSL_write` (`TLSWrap::DoWrite` loops over the buffers), so records always align with TDS packet boundaries. SQL Server appears to require this alignment: in our captures it closes the connection (TCP FIN, no TLS alert) as soon as a record crosses a packet boundary. Capping the record size alone (rustls `max_fragment_size = 4096`) did **not** help — alignment is what matters, not size. tedious's `setMaxSendFragment(packetSize)` call points at the same server behavior.

The total plaintext Deno sent was byte-identical to Node's — only the record framing differed.

## Fix

Track the end offset of each write chunk in `pending_cleartext_boundaries`, have `writev` record those offsets alongside the concatenated buffer instead of discarding them, and make `clear_in` never pass bytes from two chunks to a single rustls `write()` call. Since rustls fragments per `write()` call, each chunk now gets its own TLS record(s), matching Node's per-buffer `SSL_write`. Single-buffer writes and the `MAX_CLEAR_IN` rate-limiting behave exactly as before; a chunk that straddles a `MAX_CLEAR_IN` cut is still only split *within* itself, never merged with the next one.

Tradeoff: a `writev` batch of many small chunks now produces a record per chunk (~22 bytes overhead each) rather than one coalesced record. That is Node's behavior, and it is the property protocols like TDS depend on.

## Testing

- New regression test in `tests/unit_node/tls_test.ts`, run for both TLS 1.2 and 1.3, builds the same topology tedious uses (TLS client over a back-to-back Duplex pair), corks three writes (4096/4096/54) so they flow through one `_writev` batch, and asserts one application-data record per chunk by parsing the record headers off the encrypted side. Both versions fail without the fix (the three chunks arrive as one merged record) and pass with it.
- New Rust unit test for the boundary walk, including resuming mid-chunk after a `MAX_CLEAR_IN` cut.
- End-to-end repro against SQL Server 2022 in Docker (tedious 19.2.1, `encrypt: true`): before the change every INSERT whose TDS message needs > 2 packets fails with `socket hang up` (threshold bisected exactly to the 2-to-3 packet boundary); with the change, inserts up to 1 MB pass and the client's TLS record sizes match Node's byte-for-byte.
- `cargo test unit_node::tls_test` and the existing `tls_wrap` Rust unit tests pass.

Likely also relevant to older reports of `mssql`/Prisma failures that persisted after #33914, e.g. the "more than N rows" symptom in #32271.

I used Claude Code to help investigate and write this change.

We have a UDS server that looks for DHCP leases for a client. When the client disconnects we would like to be able to recognize this and stop DORA on the server side - otherwise the server just keeps searching for a lease. It would be useful in this case to recognize that the client disconnected and that we can do clean up on the server side.

### Proposal

Im unsure of how this would be implemented. I do think having some sort of channel which sends messages about disconnected clients which would give specific information on which client disconnected would be helpful.

title: The connection is not reconnected after disconnection
option to not abort server task if client request cancels or times out
body:
## Feature Request

### Motivation

When a client RPC times out, tonic aborts the server task that is servicing that request. This takes the form of an .await never returning control to my code.

This behavior is a surprise for the unwary. Consider:

```
  <acquire resource>
  some_async_call().await;
  <release resource>
```

If the .await doesn't return control because the task is aborted by tonic (due to e.g. client timeout), then my logic leaks the acquired resource.

At [https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/index.html#cancellation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/index.html#cancellation) Tokio documents this behavior as "When tasks are shut down, it will stop running at whichever .await it has yielded at. All local variables are destroyed by running their destructor."

Because locals are destroyed, using RAII solves the resource management aspect of a blackholed .await.

In addition to using RAII in my logic, I am also spawning long-running operations to a separate task, so that if the client RPC times out, the dropped task will not take my task down.

### Proposal

Four requests:

1. Please prominently document the task dropping behavior.
2. Maybe provide an option to log task drop occurrences.
3. Consider providing an option to NOT drop server tasks when a client cancels or times out, and
4. Allow server logic to discover that the task has a pending cancellation due to client cancel or timeout (maybe via a RPC request context object) so the server logic can decide when and how to abandon its work.

title: dynamic-load-balance channel can not work
Cancellation via RST_STREAM
body:
Clients and servers must be able to cancel streams:

* Client-side:
  * Cancellation should result in a RST_STREAM frame, and is distinct from closing its send side of the stream (i.e. END_STREAM on a DATA frame).
  * Applications should be able to cause cancellation through some mechanism.
  * Cancellation must automatically propagate from an incoming call to an outgoing call.
  * Cancellation should also occur based on timeout - when the RPC's timeout elapses, RST_STREAM should automatically be sent, and the client should be able to discover this via an RPC status (libraries should drop unread messages; but not strictly required).

* Server-side:
  * Cancellation should result in a RST_STREAM frame, and is distinct from sending the status in a trailing HEADERS frame.
  * Applications should be able to cause cancellation, though it's very low priority if it's actually or ever implemented.
  * Cancellation should occur when the timeout (`grpc-timeout` header) is reached as with the client.  The server application should discover this presumably by having reads and writes on the stream fail.

* And on both sides:
  * If a RST_STREAM is received from the peer, it could be a race between the local timeout and the remote timeout.  The local timeout should be checked, and the status should be DEADLINE_EXCEEDED if the local timeout has also elapsed when this occurs, or CANCELLED otherwise.  This is important on both sides of the connection, and the server mostly cares because of metrics, so the metrics handlers need to see the result of this fixup.

title: Received 'Status::internal("Missing request message.")' in case of cancellation by client
body:
## Bug Report


### Version
Verified it in tonic 0.12 and 0.14.

### Platform
- 24.6.0 Darwin Kernel
- Verified on linux as well.

### Crates
tonic

### Description

If the cancellation is sent from the client before the full request message reached the server, it leads to `Status::internal("Missing request message.")`. 

I reproduced this issue locally by java gRPC client (with hedging) and tonic server with request size of around 1 MB.

Error is thrown [here](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/blob/d02ee2d1dba2f77570097cbbd87a611399ea98c1/tonic/src/server/grpc.rs#L386). 

Expected Behaviour:

- Case1: If the cancellation is sent from the client before the full request message reached the server, then request future must be dropped and no response/error should be returned to the tower layers.
- Case2: If the cancellation is sent from the client after the full request message reached the server, then request future must be dropped and no response/error should be returned to the tower layers. **This is working as expected.**

I'm not sure if this is the intended behaviour that needs to be handled by the server. In my opinion, case 1 should drop the future instead of return `Status::internal("Missing request message.")`.

title: Introduce generic RPC abstractions
body:
*See [PR comment below](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/pull/2493#issuecomment-3843005140) for a more detailed design of these changes.*

In this change:

- Add `Invoke` and `Handle` and related types.
- Add `client::RecvStreamValidator` which will be used by the codegen to enforce proper RPC response stream behavior for unary and non-unary streams.
- Update `Status` to `Result<(), StatusError>` so that a status in an Err() cannot be OK.

**Some very large, structural questions about these APIs remain to be answered:**

- Is it better to use generics for message types and streams instead of dynamic types?  (Generics may offer better flexibility for the future -- e.g. interceptors may one day be able to determine "does my message T implement trait Foo?", at the cost of larger binaries.)  It's unlikely generics would be significantly faster as there should be very few places where we make these calls.

- Do we need to support dyn compatibility on these traits?

- Should we use types that match Stream / Sink?

- Are we sure this is the optimal API?  There are three different models we have been investigating:

1. call(request_stream, response_sink)
2. call(request_stream) -> response_stream
3. call() -> (request_sink, response_stream)

This change proposes (3) for clients and (1) for servers, but we need more time working with this before deciding for sure.

**In spite of the unanswered questions**

I believe this proposal is ready for review so we can start tying the pieces together and to enable people to work on different things that are dependent on these APIs at the same time (e.g. proto codegen, channel implementation, server implementation, contents of headers/trailers, etc).  Moderate changes to these APIs are likely and large changes are possible, but we can refactor the implementation as the types evolve.

title: Do not warn if setsockopt fails due to ECONNRESET
body:
## Motivation

In case a client disconnects early, setting socket options (nodelay/keepalive) fails and causes warnings. These warnings have little value, given that modifying options on an already broken connection is basically a noop.

This can happen in case of bad connectivity/congestion, but also by design like in haproxy, which "uses RST to close the health check as it free’s[sic!] resources on haproxy and the backend server immediately".

Due to the above we encounter quite some log spam:

    WARN tonic::transport::server::incoming:error trying to set TCP_NODELAY: Connection reset by peer (os error 54)
    WARN tonic::transport::server::incoming:error trying to set TCP_KEEPALIVE: Connection reset by peer (os error 54)
    ...

(This is on FreeBSD, hence "os error 54" (ECONNRESET)).

## Solution

Do not warn in case setting socket options fails due to the connection being reset by the client.

title: Modify the ServerMessage abstractions and Generic Streams API
body:
- Add a new type `SendMessage`. Mostly the same as client `RecvStream` without the `StreamClosed` because that isn't needed.
- Change the API for RecvStream `next` to return Option<Result<(),()>> .
   - `Some(OK())` - Successful next
   - `Some(Err())` - End of stream with error
   - `None` - Eos 
   - Subsequent calls after end stream result in error.
- Change the API for SendStream to return `Result<(),()>` 
- All CallOptions to the `Handle` and friends.

title: Difference between dropping server manually and serve_with_shutdown
Mock example fails when shutdown signal is set
body:
## Bug Report

When adding a shutdown signal to the [mock example](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/blob/e78a2d832fdab61e82586cc1cf954f31b16da02a/examples/src/mock/mock.rs) the client channel stream is accessed twice, leading to a panic.

### Version

0.6.2 and recent master e78a2d832fdab61e82586cc1cf954f31b16da02a

### Platform

```
Darwin MPB 20.6.0 Darwin Kernel Version 20.6.0: Mon Aug 30 06:12:20 PDT 2021; root:xnu-7195.141.6~3/RELEASE_ARM64_T8101 arm64
```

### Description

This branch contains the slightly altered code to start the server with a shutdown signal: https://github.com/SuperFluffy/tonic/tree/mock_shutdown_fails

Running the server with the shutdown signal leads to this error:

```shell
❯ cargo run -p examples --bin mock
    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.07s
     Running `target/debug/mock`
thread 'tokio-runtime-worker' panicked at 'tried accessing client twice', examples/src/mock/mock.rs:47:40
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
Error: Status { code: Unknown, message: "transport error", source: Some(tonic::transport::Error(Transport, Closed)) }
```

The only change is in how the server is spawned:

```rust
    let mut shutdown_signal = signal(SignalKind::terminate()).unwrap();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        Server::builder()
            .add_service(GreeterServer::new(greeter))
            .serve_with_incoming(futures::stream::iter(vec![Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(
                mock::MockStream(server),
            )]))
            .serve_with_incoming_shutdown(
                futures::stream::iter(vec![Ok::<_, std::io::Error>( mock::MockStream(server),)]),
                async move {

```

title: RFC: flow control
body:
HTTP/2 flow control applies on individual streams as well as on connections. Flow control
applies bidirectionally: receiving from the remote to the local peer, and sending from
local to remote peer.

## Receiver Flow Control

- Track the local window size.
  - Configured with local `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (including updates)
  - Count received DATA frames against flow control.
  - Reset stream / fail connection on violation.
- Send `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames to the remote.
  - When received DATA is _dropped_ to allow effective memory constraints.
  - With buffering (for small frames) -- nagle's algorithm?

## Sender Flow Control

- Track the remote flow control window.
  - Configured with local `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (including updates)
  - Count sent DATA frames against flow control.
  - Ensure the outbound window is not violated.
  - _Apply backpressure_ when writing would violate window.
- Allow reset/data eos/trailers to be transmitted even when window is closed.
- Receive `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames from the remote.
  - Unblock writer

## Example: assymetric windows

Intermediary proxies may forward between endpoints with assymetric window sizes and must
buffer.

- A proxy is forwarding a stream from the _src_ remote to the _dst_ remote.
- The _src_ local window size is 1000B. The _dst_ remote window size is 100B.
- A 300B frame is received from _sbrc_ and 100B is sent to _dst_.
- The _src_ local window size is now 700B. The _dst_ remote window is empty. And 200B are
  buffered in memory.
- A 700B frame is received from _src_ and buffered since the _dst_ window is empty.
- The _src_ window is now empty. 900B are buffered. The _src_ receiver MAY send a 100B
  window update.
- The _dst_ sends a window update of 100B.
- 100B are sent to _dst_ and now 800B are buffered.
- ...

## Challenges

1. Sender flow control should cause _backpressure_.  A sender must not be able to violate
   the flow control window. However, it's inappropriate to apply this backpressure on a
   connection's _frames_, since resets/trailers/etc must proceed even when windows are empty.
2. Receivers must not send window updates until the memory is _released_. This _should_
   allow for the partial contents of a data frame to be released, and _should not_
   necessarily cause an immediate window update (esp in the case of small frames).
3. Flow controllers must receive settings updates.

## Thoughts

This seems to suggest that, at the highest level, we want to model a stream's data as
something like `AsyncRead` and `AsyncWrite`. Specifically, we want to allow for partial
writes on a sender -- trying to send 1000B on a stream with a 300B window should write
300B and return the remaining 700B to be buffered.

Flow control cannot enforce backpressure on streams of frames, only on bytes themselves.
It seems natural, then, for flow control to be integrated directly with buffering so that
creation of a buffer can deduct from a local window and dropping part of a buffer can
deposit into a remote window.

Something like:

```rust
trait ReceiverStream {
    fn read(&mut self) -> Poll<Data, StreamError>;
}

trait SenderStream {
    /// Writes to the local side of a stream, to be read by the Remote.
    fn write<D: Buf>(&mut self, data: D) -> LocalWrite<D>;
}

type LocalWrite<D> = Result<AsyncWrite<D>, StreamError>;
enum AsyncWrite<D> {
    Complete,
    Incomplete(D),
}

struct Data {
    flow_controller: FlowControllerReleaser,
    ..
}
impl Buf for Data {
    fn advance(&mut self, sz: usize) {
        self.flow_controller.release(sz);
        ..
    }
}
```

It _seems_ like this API would have to sit on top of a muxer/demuxer -- if we're enforcing buffering/backpressure, we'd want that buffer to be associated with an Http message (and above the Frame based API).

title: perf: allow multiple DATA frames per write
body:
#### Summary
This PR addresses the sender-side perf issue described in #902
by allowing multiple DATA frames to be coalesced into a single write_vectored() syscall,
rather than the current behavior of flushing each DATA frame individually.

#### Problem
The existing encoder holds at most one pending DATA frame at a time and blocks accepting new frames until it is fully flushed. With TCP_NODELAY enabled, each frame triggers its own write() syscall and TCP segment — inflating the syscall-to-payload ratio and cutting throughput roughly in half compared to raw TCP.
  
#### Solution
   - Replace the single next `Option<Next<B>>` slot with a `VecDeque<BufElement<B>>` that can queue multiple DATA frames (up to 512 on vectored-IO transports).
   - Implement `Buf` directly on the Encoder, providing `chunks_vectored()` so that all queued frame headers + payloads are written in one `poll_write_vectored()` call.
   - Replace the per-connection `in_flight_data_frame` field with a per-stream `in_flight_partial_send` field of type `Option<ControlFlow<()>>`, allowing each stream to send up to one partial data frame at a time without blocking other streams.
   - Introduce `take_used_data_frames()` iterator to reclaim all fully-written frames in a single pass, replacing the old `take_last_data_frame()` which could only return one.
   - Add a custom `poll_write_buf` that returns `ControlFlow` to cleanly distinguish "nothing left to write" from "wrote some bytes, keep going".
   
### Validation
- h2 cargo tests
- external scenario tests
- external perf tests

Perf results for a branch including the commit in this PR:
```
   OS: linux (kernel 6.6), Arch: arm64, TCP_NODELAY: True

   Data Frame Size │ master (throughput) │ batch-data-frames (throughput) │ Improvement
      4 kiB        │ 0.97 GB/s           │ 1.14 GB/s                      │ 1.18x
     16 kiB        │ 2.68 GB/s           │ 3.47 GB/s                      │ 1.29x
     64 kiB        │ 3.54 GB/s           │ 6.19 GB/s                      │ 1.75x
    256 kiB        │ 4.64 GB/s           │ 7.50 GB/s                      │ 1.62x
   1024 kiB        │ 4.28 GB/s           │ 7.81 GB/s                      │ 1.82x
```
Receiver-side PR: #904

body:
Continues the work started in https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/pull/2278 by adding bindings to allow using hyper's server stack from a C runtime.  The patterns are based on the model used on the client side, and the two can be used simultaneously (e.g. using the client bindings to make down-stream HTTP calls as part of serving an upstream request).

I understand that the project is currently focussed on the 1.0 stabilization (woo!) and I realise that this MR isn't part of that process, but there's various teams across my area of Microsoft who would really like to start using hyper in our C/C++ projects to take advantage of the benefits that hyper is already providing to our Rust codebases elsewhere.  Thus it would be really great to get a first-pass review of the approach soon to try and head off any churn down the line, if possible?

I've added an example C integration (`capi/examples/server.c`) that simply logs information about the request then responds with a 404 to everything.

Implementation details of note:

* The service callback (where the C code implements business logic for handling requests) is given the request and a channel handle and completes the request by passing a response back on the channel, this allows the service callback to be asynchronous/multi-threaded/deferred etc.
* I added a timer heap implementation so the server configuration can set timeouts (e.g. to protect against slow loris attacks) this currently exposes millisecond accuracy to the C code since that's the granularity of `epoll_wait`'s timeout argument though there is also `epoll_pwait2` which goes down to nanoseconds so maybe the FFI should expose them?
* I made the `ffi` feature depend on all the other related features for now, mostly as a QoL for people using the FFI bindings (since the FFI code isn't feature aware yet)
* I added an `AutoConnection` layer that restores the behaviour of "trying HTTP/1.x and, if it sees the HTTP/2 prelude rewinds and switches to HTTP/2 mode".  I've tried to make this generic so it is possibly in a fit state to be lifted to hyper-utils rather than being in the FFI code?

Other smaller notes:

* Simplified the header-generation code a lot by using `cargo expand`'s ability to show a single module from a crate (so we no longer need to build a fake crate to be able to run bindgen)
* Formatted the C example code with clang-format (with some rust-familar settings)
* Fixed some compiler warnings in the example C code
* Made `Sleep` auto-impl for things that look like `Sleep` again as a QoL thing

I've tested the server example code under `valgrind` and `-fsanitize=memory` to ensure there's no use-after-free/double-free/etc.

title: Dropping HTTP/2 response future doesn't cancel request body send and does not send RST_STREAM
Allow connection pools to stop reusing an HTTP/2 connection before its keep-alive timeout
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

An HTTP/2 connection can remain locally ready while its network path is unavailable. If no earlier transport or protocol error is observed, a connection pool can keep assigning new requests to that connection until the keep-alive PING timeout closes it.

A concrete scenario is a network failover or NAT/firewall state change after which new connections succeed but an existing connection remains unusable. The replacement path may have lost the old connection's state: a new TCP handshake can establish fresh state, while packets belonging to the old connection are silently dropped. If the client receives no FIN, RST, or other definitive error, the existing H2 connection can remain eligible for reuse locally even though it cannot make progress. Continuing to assign requests to it delays recovery despite a working path for new connections.

There are documented examples of the underlying network behavior:

- [Google Cloud NAT](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/troubleshooting#dropped_received_packets) documents that removing an external NAT IP without first draining it deletes the associated connection-tracking entries and drops all return traffic. With another usable NAT IP available, this provides a scenario where fresh connections can work while the old mapping no longer carries responses.

This does not assume that every network failover invalidates existing connections. A temporary interruption may also recover, which is why stopping reuse should not itself terminate existing streams.

There are two different policies involved: how long to keep existing streams alive during a recoverable interruption, and how long to keep assigning new work to that connection. Reducing the keep-alive timeout improves replacement latency, but also terminates existing streams earlier.

For example, an application may want to retain a 60-second PING timeout for existing streams while stopping reuse after an outstanding keep-alive PING has waited 5 seconds for an ACK. These are example settings, not proposed defaults.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Would an optional reuse-timeout notification on the HTTP/2 client builder fit Hyper's API?

The proposal adds `keep_alive_reuse_timeout(Option<Duration>)` and a per-connection `KeepAliveObserver`. The observer would be exposed through `hyper::client::conn::http2`. A pool such as hyper-util's legacy Client could use the notification to retire its own connection entry.

- The option defaults to disabled.
- Its timer starts with the existing keep-alive PING timeout phase.
- An ACK ready before notification cancels the soft wait.
- On expiry, Hyper invokes a nonblocking observer once, outside the PING state lock.
- The original hard deadline continues to run. Notification does not close IO, send GOAWAY, cancel streams, or change direct `SendRequest` readiness.
- A late ACK does not generate a reversal notification; the consuming pool owns its retirement policy.

The implementation uses Hyper's Timer abstraction and does not require changes to h2 or its dependency constraints.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Shortening the hard timeout also reduces interruption tolerance for existing streams. Application-level health requests or rebuilding an entire Client can provide a separate signal, but add another probe and broader connection-management logic. Deriving the signal from the existing PING wait keeps it specific to one connection.

**Additional context**

This issue tracks both parts of the proposal, with one implementation PR per repository:

- **Hyper:** expose the optional PING reuse-timeout notification through the HTTP/2 client API.
- **hyper-util:** add `http2_keep_alive_reuse_timeout(Option<Duration>)` to the legacy Client builder and bind each H2 handshake to an observer holding only that connection's `PoisonPill`. Existing pool checks then retire the entry without canceling its active streams.

title: Regression in query regex handling (panic)
body:
__System info:__ InfluxDB 1.6.0, Debian stretch

__Steps to reproduce:__
With our existing data, the following query used to work without issue:
```
SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("tx"), 1s) * 8
FROM "interface_if_octets"
WHERE ("host" =~ /^gw101[ab]-\d\./ AND "plugin_instance" =~ /^eth2\.1\d{3}$/) AND time >= now() - 5m
GROUP BY time(1m), "host"
```

__Expected behavior:__ Results returned as per previously successful operation.

__Actual behavior:__ No data shown in Grafana, InfluxDB CLI reports a panic
Since upgrading to InfluxDB 1.6.0, it fails, and a panic can be see in the `influx` CLI tool:
```
> SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean("tx"), 1s) * 8 FROM "interface_if_octets" WHERE ("host" =~ /^gw101[ab]-\d\./ AND "plugin_instance" =~ /^eth2\.1\d{3}$/) AND time >= now() - 5m GROUP BY time(1m), "host"
ERR: SELECT non_negative_derivative(mean(tx), 1s) * 8 FROM perfdb."default".interface_if_octets WHERE (host =~ /^gw101[ab]-\d\./ AND plugin_instance =~ /^eth2\.1\d{3}$/) AND time >= now() - 5m GROUP BY time(1m), host [panic:runtime error: index out of range]
```

__Additional info:__
After some experimentation looking for workarounds, it seems to be failing on the `/^eth2\.1\d{3}$/` regex, specifically the `$` end-of-line match. Removing the `$` allows the query to work.

Also, changing the regex to `/^eth2\.1\d{1,3}$/` works, however `/^eth2\.1\d{3,3}$/` panics.

The tag in the database contains values such as `eth2.1xxx`, where `x` is a digit 0-9.

This has the hallmarks of an off-by-one error when comparing to the tag value, since the `/^eth2\.1\d{3}$/` regex would eat the entire string length of the values we have for that tag.

Somewhat mysteriously, the regex `/^e[a-z0-9]+\.1\d{3}$/` works successfully.

title: Allow selecting what data is used in a single stat
body: When a user visualizes a Flux query response as a single stat, we [attempt to display the latest single value in the response](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/blob/7403a181e1bed73c15ac578f92d312269e763a8d/ui/src/shared/utils/latestValues.test.ts). If there are multiple latest values, we pick one at random, which is a poor UX. Instead, we should add a dropdown to the single stat options that allows selecting which time series the latest value is picked from. In this context, selecting a time series means: - Select a query for the single stat view (since a view may have multiple queries) - Select a [result](https://github.com/influxdata/flux/blob/master/docs/SPEC.md#multiple-results) within that query response by name - Select a table within that result by the column names and values in its group key - We cannot use the `table` ID since it is not stable between multiple runs of the same query - We need to omit `_start` and `_stop` from this group key, since they often change between multiple runs of the same query but are irrelevant to the identity of the returned series - The table must have at least one time column (`_time`, `_start`, or `_stop`) - Select a column within that table that contains the values for the series. The time for each value will be looked up in the time column in the same table The dropdown will need a design to communicate this idea of a series. It will probably look something like the hover legend does now, which also has to display that group key columns and values of a table: We will need to store all of the above selection data in the single stat view. One possibility is to store a single field with a stringified representation of the selection.

title: Platform variable selected scoping
body:
__Proposal:__

The ability to scope variable's selected values at different levels.

To illustrate some limitations, an example:

* I create a variable in a dashboard and select value foo as the default
* i then create a task that utilizes said variable and is relying on the selected value as it were
* I then update the variable selected value (via API atm) to be bar
* Now tasks are looking at the wrong thing
* Also, the dashboard view is changed to use bar


The proposed change's impact on the scenario above:

* I create a variable in a dashboard and select value `foo`
   * the global variable is updated with `foo` as the selected value
   * the dashboard selected value (stored on dashboard/or query/perhaps both) is set to `foo`
* i then create a task that utilizes said variable and is relying on the selected value as it were
   * the task selected value (stored on dashboard/or query/perhaps both) is set to foo
* I then update the variable selected value (via API atm) to be bar in the dashboard
  * the dashboards local selected value is updated to `foo`
  * global var selected fields are unchanged
  * task is unchanged


To maintain backwards compatibility with existing functionality, global changes affect everything:
* add ability to update selected value on global variable and cascade changes to all associated 


__Current behavior:__
Changing variable selected valeu in one palce affects all places

__Desired behavior:__
Selecting values independent locals

__Alternatives considered:__
I'm not sure 🤔 

__Use case:__
A big place where this comes up is Templates. There are a lot of common variables like `bucket` variable, that has shared values of buckets, but we want to provide different selected values. This collision happens a fair bit b/c of bucket variable specifically.

```
  grok_patterns = ["^.*Error%{GREEDYDATA:msg:string}"]
  name_override = "logs"
  grok_custom_pattern_files = []
  grok_custom_patterns = ''''''
  data_format = "grok"
```
So any log message in test.log that has the word "Error" will generate a single field called "msg" with the contents after that.

In Chronograf, I can see the series is created, and if I select *only* the msg value (last column in Chronograf explorer), I can see the values in a table.
However, if I also select the "path" tag (which above has double back-slashes but in Chronograf is represented correctly with single back-slash) then no results are returned.

If I then amend the query directly and change the path name to have double back-slashes, it works.

So looks like when using the explorer view and drilling through metrics, Chronograf should convert a single backslash to double backslash before adding to the query.

title: refactor: Replace ctx.Done() with ctx.Err()
body:
```
Prior to this commit we checked for context cancellation with a select
block and context.Context.Done() without multiplexing over any other
channel like:

  select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
      // handle cancellation
    default:
      // fallthrough
  }

This commit replaces those type of blocks with a simple check of
ctx.Err().  This has the following benefits:

* Calling ctx.Err() is much faster than entering a select block.

* ctx.Done() allocates a channel when called for the first time.

* Testing the result of ctx.Err() is a reliable way of determininging if
  a context.Context value has been canceled.

There are a few places we optimized the select block by only entering it
every cancelCheckInterval times.  This commit checks ctx.Err() every
time -- this increases the cancellation granularity and is only
negligibly slower (sub-nanosecond).
```

title: Epic: Sync time series data to a remote InfluxDB Instance
body:
### Target Customer / Background data / Context / Market Size
 - As a user, I have multiple edge deployments of InfluxDB OSS that are collecting data locally. I would like an easy way to analyze this data in aggregate.
- As a user, I have multiple edge deployments of InfluxDB OSS that are collecting data locally with limited or no connectivity to the cloud. I would like an easy way to analyze this data in aggregate once network connection is restored.

### Goals
The goal of this epic is to provide a way for users to replicate data at the bucket level to one or more remote instances of InfluxDB

### Acceptance Crit

- as a user, i can configure an existing bucket to replicate all future points to one or more remote influxdb instances (add replication stream)
- as a user, i can remove a replication stream from a bucket (delete replication stream)
- as a user, i can list the replication streams for a bucket (list replication streams)
- as a user, i can see information about how full the queues are when listing replication streams.
- as a user, i can get a single replication stream by id for a bucket (get replication stream)
- as a user, i can update a single replication stream for a bucket (update replication stream)
- as a user, when i delete a bucket, i also delete any replication streams associated with that bucket
- as a user, i can validate the connection information is valid before saving the replication streams
- as a user, i can see status per replication stream indicating the connection is working
- as a user, i can see log messages indicating that points are being dropped if the queue size is too large
- as a user, i can see information about how full each queue is per replication stream per bucket (/metrics data)
- as an analytics user, i can see information about replication streams in the phone home data
- as an analytics user, the user agent should be set to something reasonable such as `influxdb-oss/<version>` 

### Release Plan
TBD

- Early work goes behind a feature-flag so we can merge to master without fear of releasing?

### Notes
- the minimum connection details needed for a bucket replication stream are host, token, org (or orgID), bucket name (or bucket id), queue size (bytes), and skip-verify/insecure TLS.
  - Dan opinion: would prefer to require IDs for both org and bucket; have heard rumors that Cloud APIs will move away from accepting names
  - Russ: I'm ok with using only IDs for this for the first pass but there are a few issues. Today, the CLI configs file only stores the org name, not the ID, so we should explore adding orgid to that (and auto-populating it from the token if we can). That way the CLI could work with the user only specifying the local and remote bucket ids + queue size (although the user could send a write only token to the command for added security). For the UI, i imagine we could allow the user to browse the remote influxdb instance to select the bucket, in which case, we could use id as well. The only issue is that if the user drops and recreates the remote bucket, you could end up with failures.
- Replication is configured at the bucket level via an API, which means a restart is not required
- Configuration options for the size of the replication queue should be configurable per replication stream
- Assumption: no support for injecting a query to filter/modify data before it's sent to the remote server
  - If users want that behavior, they can have a task execute the query and write results to a 2nd local bucket, and replicate that 2nd bucket
- Assumption: the auth tokens included in stream configuration are write-only (not included in list/GET metadata responses)
  - We should only require write to the specific bucket. In the experiences we build, they should fail gracefully if the user doesn't have permissions to do things like list buckets.
- Assumption(Sam): Only writes are streamed. Other data operations (e.g. deletes, backup restores)

title: feat: add `_series_id` to tables on write
body:
Closes #24821

### Summary 
* New `_series_id` column is added to tables; this stores a 32 byte SHA256 hash of the tag set of a line of Line Protocol. The tag set is checked for sort order, then sorted if not already, before producing the hash.
* Unit tests were added to check hashing and sorting functions work.
* Tests that performed queries needed to be modified to account for the new `_series_id` column; in general, `SELECT *` queries were altered to use a select clause with specific column names.
* The Column limit was increased to 501 internally, to account for the new `_series_id` column, but the user-facing limit is still 500

### Other Considerations
* The `_series_id` column was added as a `String` column, and is stored using the HEX-encoded form of the hash; where as, it may be nice to use a column that can store the raw bytes. There is no suitable `ColumnType` variant in the [data_types crate](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb3_core/blob/bb5eeb02614d32dbc244a17c7478030d5139d54b/data_types/src/columns.rs#L245-L253).
* When generating the `_series_id` hash, we [still need to check that it is sorted](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/pull/24842/files#diff-786737bb322e113951842b84574ed18ee04e82ec59e5acaa833f4e58acc716dbR754); which for very large tag sets could be inefficient.

title: [influxdb/v2] differing influxql results when comparing field to signed vs unsigned integer
body:
An external reporter sent an issue regarding InfluxQL queries in 2.x. Using 2.7.6, comparing a field to a signed integer works as expected. Eg:

```
$  export V1AUTH=$(echo -n "anything:$TOKEN" | base64 --wrap 0)

# generate some line protocol 
$ cat > file.lp <<EOM
t0,t0_tag0=initTag t0_f0=0i 1715694000
t0,t0_tag0=initTag t0_f0=1i 1715694001
t0,t0_tag1=initTag t0_f0=0i 1715694000
EOM

# write
$ curl -H "Authorization: Basic $V1AUTH" -X POST "$URL/write?db=test1&precision=s" --data-binary @./file.lp
$

# queries
# ok
$ curl -H "Authorization: Basic $V1AUTH" -H "Accept: application/csv" -X POST "$URL/query?db=test1&rp=autogen" --data-urlencode "q=select * from t0"
name,tags,time,t0_f0,t0_tag0,t0_tag1
t0,,1715694000000000000,0,initTag,
t0,,1715694000000000000,0,,initTag
t0,,1715694001000000000,1,initTag,

# ok with signed ints
$ curl -H "Authorization: Basic $V1AUTH" -H "Accept: application/csv" -X POST "$URL/query?db=test1&rp=autogen" --data-urlencode "q=select * from t0 where (1) < (17693) ORDER BY ASC LIMIT 2147483647"

t0,,1715694000000000000,0,initTag,
t0,,1715694000000000000,0,,initTag
t0,,1715694001000000000,1,initTag,

$ curl -H "Authorization: Basic $V1AUTH" -H "Accept: application/csv" -X POST "$URL/query?db=test1&rp=autogen" --data-urlencode "q=select * from t0 where (t0_f0) < (17693) ORDER BY  ASC LIMIT 2147483647"
```

title: feat: improve control of logs on test harness
body:
No issue for this. I was working on https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/issues/26216 and decided to make this change.

This alters the logging behaviour and UX for the [`TestServer`](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/blob/6fb4112dc3c51c9723eefd50077e439aa1b9771d/influxdb3/tests/server/mod.rs#L195-L200) harness that is used in our integration tests in the `influxdb3` crate.

### Changes

The primary change is the addition of a CLI argument for the `serve` command (`--tcp-listener-file-path`) that the server will use to write out the listener address that it is listening for TCP connections on.

The argument is hidden and defaults to `None`.

This can be used by our test harness, which uses a bind address of `0.0.0.0:0` in order to select a randomly available port.

The test harness creates a temporary file and waits for it to be written to acquire the selected address of the underlying process.

### Why this is an improvement

Previously, the `TestServer` was doing some weird business to capture the stdout of the running process and grab the log line that displays the listener address. This created a couple of issues:
* we couldn't customize the log filter on the running process via the normal means of setting the `RUST_LOG` environment variable
* the re-emitted logs were not formatted in the terminal and therefore were difficult to read

### Usage

The `TEST_LOG` environment variable is still respected, and is required in order to have logs emitted by the underlying `influxdb3` process.

One can run tests like so:
```
TEST_LOG= cargo nextest run -p influxdb3 --nocapture
```
This will have the underlying process emit logs at the `INFO` level (and above). This is how it operated before this PR.

Or, providing a filter:
```
TEST_LOG=influxdb3=debug,info cargo nextest run -p influxdb3 --nocapture
```
This will pass the provided filter down to the underlying `influxdb3` process (`influxdb3=debug,info`)

The `RUST_LOG` enfironment variable is also respected, so
```
TEST_LOG= RUST_LOG=influxdb3=debug,info cargo nextest run -p influxdb3 --nocapture
```
Will enable log output for the underlying `influxdb3` process while passing the filter provided to `RUST_LOG` to the underlying process.

title: Add Native Query Timeout and Safe Termination for Long-Running Queries in influxDB v2
body:
Problem Statement:-

InfluxDB v2 does not provide a native, configurable way to terminate long-running queries on the server side. Inefficient or unbounded Flux queries can continue executing for extended periods, leading to sustained CPU and memory usage and affecting other workloads. Current mitigations typically rely on reverse proxies or service meshes, which cancel client connections but do not reliably stop backend query execution within InfluxDB.

Comparison with InfluxDB v1:-

InfluxDB v1 supported native query timeout and termination mechanisms that helped protect system resources by internally cancelling long-running queries. InfluxDB v2 lacks an equivalent server-side capability increasing operational risk and reliance on external infrastructure for query control.

Proposed Enhancements:-

1.A Configurable server-side query execution timeout

2.Guaranteed backend termination of queries exceeding the timeout

3.Safe, resource-aware cancellation (no memory leaks or CPU spikes)

4.Metrics/logs for visibility into queries terminated due to timeout

Question to the InfluxDB Team:-

1.Does InfluxDB v2 already support any hidden or undocumented configuration for server-side query timeouts or execution limits?

2.If not, is there any plan or near-term roadmap to introduce native query timeout or safe termination functionality?

title: [v3] Core 3.10.1: query results for an overwritten point depend on query plan shape — non-tag-filtered plans serve the old field values indefinitely (survives restart; can tear a single atomic write)
body:
## Summary

After an in-place overwrite (same measurement/tags/timestamp, new field values), two
SQL queries against the same table return **different generations of the same row**,
and which one you get depends on the *shape* of the query:

- A query with an **equality predicate on a tag** (`component_id = 'X'`) always
  returns the new values (fresh within ~1 s; never observed stale in 85/85 checks
  across six probe campaigns).
- Queries **without** that predicate — a bare table/time-range scan, an `IN` list,
  or a `count(*)` filtered only on a *field* — can permanently return the **old**
  values for some or all of the overwritten series. "Permanently" is literal: no
  affected plan was ever observed to recover (watched ≥ 20 min), and the stale
  state **survives a full server restart**.

The mis-arbitration happens per *(query plan × per-series chunk of the write)*, so a
single atomic write (one `write_lp` call, 12 rows across 2 series) can be **torn**:
the wide scan serves series A's new rows and series B's old rows indefinitely, while
per-series queries serve both correctly. Incidence is roughly 40–50 % per overwritten
series in our environment; 27 of 28 two-series overwrite trials left at least one
query plan permanently stale.

## Environment

- InfluxDB 3 Core **3.10.1** (revision `ff6872a3d8`), official Docker image `influxdb:3-core`
- Default server config: `influxdb3 serve --node-id=node0 --object-store=file --data-dir=/var/lib/influxdb3`
- Linux x86_64 host; single node; one database
- Reproduced identically: via the `influxdb3-python` (Flight) client **and** via the
  raw HTTP API (`/api/v3/write_lp` + `/api/v3/query_sql`) with a stdlib-only Python
  script (attached) — so no client library is involved
- Reproduced identically with writes using `no_sync=true` and default sync writes
- Also reproduced under `--disable-parquet-mem-cache` and under `--wal-flush-interval=5s` (see "Additional evidence", below)

## Reproduction

[`repro_standalone.py`](https://gist.github.com/PascalRaux-EP/9d2490c1aaed286e57081b19717880bc) (Python 3, stdlib only, ~200 lines; also inlined at the bottom of this issue). Steps it performs:

1. **Seed**: one table (`repro_pac`), tags `plant_id` (1 value) and `component_id`
   (20 values), fields `value` (float) and `run_id` (string); 144 points per series
   at 10-min cadence over one day = 2 880 rows. Then 3 value-identical full rewrites
   (so keys carry a few duplicate generations, as any idempotent ingest produces).
2. **Overwrite**: for two series, rewrite one hour (6 points each, `value` + 1000,
   fresh `run_id`) — 12 rows in **one** `write_lp` call.
3. **Poll** three query shapes until each reflects the new values (90 s cap):
   - A. `... WHERE plant_id='P' AND component_id='X' AND time >= .. AND time < ..`
   - B. `... WHERE plant_id='P' AND time >= .. AND time < ..` (no series predicate)
   - C. `SELECT count(*) WHERE plant_id='P' AND run_id='<new>'` (field predicate)

Typical output (this exact run captured 2026-07-17; 3 of 4 trials stuck, all torn):

```
server: InfluxDB 3 Core 3.10.1 (ff6872a3d8)
trial 2: overwriting RINV02+RINV12 @ 03:00 (12 rows, ONE write_lp call, run a187dcc1)
  t=0.0s single-component(RINV02) reflects
  t=0.0s single-component(RINV12) reflects
  t=0.0s plant-wide reflects for RINV02
  RESULT: {"single_component_s": {"RINV02": 0.0, "RINV12": 0.0},
           "plant_wide_s": {"RINV02": 0.0, "RINV12": null},
           "count_run_id_s": null, "count_final": 6,
           "stuck_plant_wide": ["RINV12"], "torn": true}
```

The stale rows are then directly demonstrable — same server, same instant, the only
difference is the tag predicate:

```sql
-- fresh (new generation, the correction's run_id):
SELECT time, component_id, value, run_id FROM repro_pac
WHERE plant_id='REPRO01' AND component_id='RINV14'
  AND time >= '2023-03-01T07:00:00Z' AND time < '2023-03-01T08:00:00Z';
--> value=2001.914..2001.919, run_id=9d4da7ec-...   (6 rows, correct)

-- stale (old gen

When I use the *-selector to select all columns then the returned data will be ordered so that the ordering in the "columns"-data matches the ordering in the "values"-data. This is a good property since it allows for generic interpretation.

However, when I issue a query with specific selectors the ordering of the returned "columns"-data and "values"-data wont always match.                         [
```

                            23.073
                        ],(...)
```

In this example the "time" and "value" attributes are interchanged in the "values"-data but not in the "columns"-data.

EXAMPLE 2 (two tags):
Query:
`SELECT tag1, tag2, value, time FROM test WHERE tag1='-1' AND tag2='0'`
Result:

```
{
    "results": [
        {
            "series": [
                {
                    "name": "test",

                    "values": [

```
Again the "columns"-data match the ordering in the query. The data in "values", however, is ordered by time - tag - value - tag which does not seem logical.

title: Query Engine Design
body:
# Query Engine
## Overview

The current state of the query engine makes it difficult to maintain and to add features. This is a proposal to refactor the engine from its current map/reduce design to a streaming design.

This proposal has the following design goals:
1. Ease development of additional statistic functions
2. Minimize allocations
3. Well-defined, performant remote serialization
4. Support joining multiple series
5. Support subqueries
6. Unify the separate raw & aggregate execution paths
## Current Model

The existing query engine works as a 2-level map/reduce. On the aggregate side, one Mapper is created for each shard and the Executor explicitly handles draining each one for a given time window and handing off the values to the Reducer. The results from the reducers are then processed for fills, derivatives, and other aggregate preprocessing before being sent back as rows to the client.

For raw queries, a 2-level map/reduce is performed, however, the raw mapper sorts the points as they're being streamed out using `container/heap`.

There are several issues with the current approach:
1. The fixed 2-level map/reduce does not allow us to support joins or subqueries
2. Points returned from the mapper can be either a primitive value or a map of keys to primative values. This breaks the type system and causes a LOT of handler code as well as a lot of memory allocations.
3. Aggregate & raw execution paths are separated because the processing in them is not broken out into encapsulated pieces.
## Proposed Model

The model that I propose reduces everything to a pull-based stream of points. These points are composed of a timestamp, a typed value (`int`, `float`, `string`, etc), and a set of tags. Since this is a pull model, these are called "iterators":

```
type Float64Iterator interface {
    Next() (timestamp int64, value float64, tags map[string]string)
}

type Int64Iterator interface {
    Next() (timestamp int64, value int64, tags map[string]string)
}

type StringIterator interface {
    Next() (timestamp int64, value string, tags map[string]string)
}

...
```
### Iterator types

The following types of iterators would exist:
- Raw data from the storage engine. Each field in a series is a separate iterator.
- InfluxQL functions. These would include the parameters for the function (interval, top/botton N, etc). Many functions output simple types (e.g. `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max`), others operate on the raw stream (`stddev`, `median`, `percentile`) while a few would need specialized iterator types (`mean` would output a `TotalCountIterator` to be reduced into a `Float64Iterator`).
- Math operations. Binary operators would take two input iterators and add/subtract/multiply/etc and produce an output iterator.
- Select fields. By definition, since raw data, functions, and math operations produce an iterator, each field in a `SELECT` statement would be an iterator. This allows us to seamlessly allow nested queries by making the fields the input iterators to another query.

Single iterators could also be multiplexed as inputs across multiple iterators for efficiency. For example, if a query uses `min(x)` and `max(x)`, the `x` iterator should be multiplexed into 2 iterators as input to the `min` and `max` iterators but the data should be read from the storage engine only once. This is outside the scope of this proposal but is a consideration in the design.
### Joins & filters

Consolidating everything down to an iterator poses two problems:
1. Values from one iterator may need to be filtered with values from other iterators.
2. Iterators are not synced in terms of timestamps so output points need to be joined on timestamp.

So another construct needs to be added: the join. A join takes `N` input iterators and returns `N` output iterators. The purpose of the join is to:
- Send a value to each of the output iterators for the next timestamp available across the input iterators. Input iterators without a point matching this times
```
