title: Add a `Bytes` array based send interface to quinn-proto
body:
Add a `Bytes` array based send interface to `quinn-proto`

This change modifies quinn-proto to allow callers to submit a list
of one or more owned `Bytes` chunks for transmission instead of
pure byte slices. This will provide a more efficient zero-copy
interface for applications which already make use of owned
`Bytes` buffers.

The internals of quinn-proto have been refactored in order to keep
the ability to pass `&[u8]` buffers and defer the conversion into
`Bytes` as long as possible, in order to avoid unnecessary allocations
if no data can be stored due to flow control.

title: Generic Send Offload (GSO) Support
body:
Generic Send Offload (GSO) Support
    
This change implements an initial version of GSO support [1][2][3]
for Linux, which improves the effiency of sending data.

The approach taken in this change is to create a buffer which contains
multiple datagrams in `Connection::poll_transmit`. This was picked
over trying to merge packets in the endpoint task, since packets
seem to need to be padded to a common segment size in order to
make them sendable via GSO.

In order to to this in an efficient fashion, the `poll_transmit`
method was restructred. Instead of selecting spaces upfront, it
will now loop through all possible packet spaces, check if there is
pending data to send and create packets and datagrams out of this.

The last packet which was written to a datagram buffer is not
finalized until it is clear whether follow-up packets need to be
written, since we need to know whether this packet should get padded
to MTU length or not.

This change doesn't enable GSO yet, since it will only produce a
single datagram. I will create a separate change for this.

Performance measurements:

**No GSO:**

```
Sent 1073741824 bytes on 1 streams in 4.31s (237.66 MiB/s)
```

**With GSO (up to 8 packets):**

```
Sent 1073741824 bytes on 1 streams in 3.02s (339.18 MiB/s)
```

[1] http://vger.kernel.org/lpc_net2018_talks/willemdebruijn-lpc2018-udpgso-paper-DRAFT-1.pdf
[2] http://vger.kernel.org/lpc_net2018_talks/willemdebruijn-lpc2018-udpgso-presentation-20181104.pdf
[3] https://lwn.net/Articles/752956/

title: Named futures + replace NewConnection with Connection methods
body:
Experimenting with a return to named 'static futures, motivated by downstream use cases. See e.g. https://github.com/hyperium/h3/pull/80.

Open questions:
- Which interfaces specifically need to be named?
- Is 'static needed, or just names?
- Are GATs + TAIT close enough that none of this matters?

Also included is an idea to drop `NewConnection` in favor of unobtrusive async methods on `Connection`, bundled because they would have to be rewritten to match this PR's approach if it move forwards. I'd like feedback on this change before I invest the effort to actually remove `NewConnection` and update all the examples/docs.

title: connection: wake 'stopped' streams on stream finish events
body:
In the event that the SendStream Stopped future is polled once and then dropped before the remote side has stopped the stream, and instead the stream has been finished, the waker registered in the connection stopped map is never removed and is effectively "leaked" until the connection is closed. This can lead to a large amount of memory being retained when a connection is very long lived and many streams are used over the life of that connection.

This particular issue can be seen with this type of usage of SendStream::stopped: https://github.com/bmwill/anemo/blob/main/crates/anemo/src/network/request_handler.rs#L170-L177.

This is one such way to fix this memory retention, although it may not be the project's preferred way. Another option would potentially be to remove the waker from the hash map in a `Drop` impl for the `Stopped` type.

title: Assorted cleanup, panic fix
body: 0-RTT packets weren't being assigned a packet space, which meant no header crypto was selected for them, which lead to a panic in `PartialDecode::finish` which correctly assumed that all standard-form long-header packets have encrypted headers. This corrects the omission and drops 0-RTT packets prior to decryption since rustls isn't giving us 0-RTT keys yet anyway.

feat: Make the future returned by `SendStream::stopped` static
body:
Currently, the future returned by `SendStream::stopped` is bound to `&mut self`, and therefore cannot be stored and polled while also sending on the stream. This PR makes the future returned by `SendStream::stopped` be `'static`, so that it can be stored in futures combinators while also still sending on the stream.

This is useful when you want to clean up local state once the corresponding receiver to a send stream is closed or dropped, independently of actually using the stream. Especially if sends occur infrequently, tracking the stopped notification allows to clean up state at the earliest time and not only once you try to send again.

There's a complication though: Once `SendStream::stopped` returns a `'static` future, we'd have to account for the fact that there may be multiple futures waiting for a wakeup once the stream is stopped. Therefore, we'd need to store a *list* of wakers instead of a single waker per stream. I used a `Slab`, open to other ideas how to achieve this.

For the intended functionality I don't actually need the possibility to create multiple futures waiting for the stopped wakeup. However, I didn't yet come up with an API that encodes that only the last future returned from `SendStream::stopped` would be woken up reliably - if you have ideas here, please share.

I added two tests with various combinations of using stopped while stopping and/or dropping the send stream.

title: perf: display stats when drive tasks are cancelled by ctrl-c or timeout
body:
This is still a work in progress and is placed here for discussion.

This allow uploading or downloading an infinite amount of bytes for a given duration and still have throughput statistics at the end of the duration.

Under the hood, this is a big rework of async tasks to spawn them. It uses two tokio CancellationTokens to first stop the ```drive_uni``` and  ```drive_bi``` tasks, then stop the statistics tasks after having collected the statistics.

It work fine with upload only and download only but if you do upload and download at the same time (the default cas without any arguments), the download statistics are broken.

I did not tested the ```drive_uni``` part for now.

Example of call :
```
./perf_client localhost:4433 --duration 120 --upload-size 99999999999 --download-size 0
```

title: BBRv2
body:
Hi all,

  My current project relies heavily on Quinn. Thanks for a great library.

  Because of a specific WAN bulk-transfer need, I have been experimenting with BBRv2 support in a fork. The prototype currently includes:

  - selectable BBRv2 alongside the existing BBR path
  - round-bounded loss classification
  - inflight_hi / inflight_lo and bw_hi / bw_lo bounds
  - packet-derived delivery-rate sampling
  - first-class ECN/loss signal plumbing
  - a guarded experimental flag for the more aggressive inflight_hi shrink path
  - 29 focused BBR unit tests

  The branch is here if useful:

  https://github.com/JavaPerformance/quinn/tree/bbrv2-prototype

  I am not assuming this is PR-ready. Before spending time turning it into upstreamable patches, I wanted to ask about the preferred direction.

  One specific API question: current Quinn `main` exposes ECN through `is_ecn: bool` on `Controller::on_congestion_event`. In the prototype I used a typed congestion event enum internally/to the controller because it made BBRv2 loss-vs-ECN handling clearer.
  Would you prefer any BBRv2 work to build on the existing `is_ecn` API, or would a richer typed congestion event be worth discussing?

  If there is interest, I am happy to split this into smaller PRs, probably starting with either the congestion-event API question or the sent-packet/rate-sampling pieces.

  No pressure either way. If this is out of scope for Quinn right now, I am also happy to keep it fork-local.

  Paul

title: Add ClientHello server config selection
body:
## Summary

This is the 0.11-compatible callback bridge for selecting a rustls server config
from ClientHello data.

Related to quinn-rs/quinn#2024.

It targets the current rustls 0.23 integration.

The intended shape is:

```rust
let crypto = ClientHelloServerConfig::new(default_server_config, move |hello| {
    match hello.server_name() {
        Some("host-b.test") => Some(host_b_server_config.clone()),
        _ => None,
    }
})?;

let server_config = quinn::ServerConfig::with_crypto(Arc::new(crypto));
```

Returning `Some(config)` continues with that selected rustls server config.
Returning `None` falls back to the default config.

## What This Solves

This allows one Quinn server endpoint to serve multiple prebuilt rustls server
configs selected from ClientHello data.

That can be used for different certificate stores, or for different TLS policy
shapes that need separate `rustls::ServerConfig` values, while still using the
same Quinn endpoint/socket.

## Scope

- opt-in: only used when the caller wraps its crypto config in
  `ClientHelloServerConfig`
- keeps Quinn's existing `Incoming` API shape
- synchronous and snapshot/in-memory oriented
- parses only enough ClientHello data to select a config
- intended as a compatibility bridge

## Limitations

Because this bridge does not use a rustls `Acceptor`, the opt-in path parses the
small ClientHello subset needed for selection, and rustls later parses
ClientHello again during the normal handshake.

That duplication is intentional for this compatibility path. The longer-term
rustls-0.24 `Acceptor` direction avoids this by keeping ClientHello parsing
inside rustls.

## Test

Adds regression coverage:

```text
select_server_config_from_client_hello
```

The test verifies that the callback sees SNI and ALPN from ClientHello, selects
the matching server config, and the resulting connection reports the selected
ALPN/SNI in handshake data.

title: Porposal: New Clients sharding to connect to multiple Redis Nodes but sharding at client level
body:
Hi, I would like to have your opinion about introducing a new first class Redis Client type for connecting to multiple Redis nodes but implementing all sharding strategy at client level. This implementation would go side by side with the current client which connects to one single Reids node and the Cluster strategy which connects to multiple Redis nodes but delegates the sharding strategy to the cluster.


# Why implementing a version which does the sharding at client side?

Currently when using Cluster mode for Redis comes with some operation burden which reduces freedom at the client side, and specifically everything related to all actions for mutating the topology of the cluster. Specifically the operations for making the cluster larger or shrinking requires some choreography for reassigning slots manually by using the Redis Cluster commands. While this could be an option for clusters that do not change a lot becomes an operational burden for workloads that can and want to change the topology much often.

When using sharding at client level, the client can easily change the topology by adding or removing nodes with the tradeoff of having some degree of keys rebalancing across all nodes. Ideally a % value ~ of the % of nodes added ore removed when using algorithms like consistent hashing or rendezvous hashing.

This is a tradeoff that some workloads are willing to pay.

# Other benefits of implementing the sharding at client side.

Implementing the sharding at client side also unlocks other features like for example promoting the reads from closest replicas when possible, which could be achieved by allowing to the users to provide as an input a list of servers that could be enriched with the data-center location for later on implementing multiple writes (write to all data-centers) and reading from the closest node by default.

If there is some interest on adding this feature I would like to work on a PR for introducing this new client flavour.

title: Async timeout support
body: This adds some basic timeout support to MultiplexedConnection and ConnectionManager (https://github.com/mitsuhiko/redis-rs/issues/395) by wrapping the req_packed_command() and req_packed_commands() contents in a tokio timeout when a timeout is set. I've also added a simple example that can be used to induce a timeout with some special treatment of the redis server - SIGTSTP / Ctrl+Z it so that it accepts connections but never responds to commands. This should help with scenarios where an async redis connection stops responding but isn't broken.

title: Fix AsyncIter Stream trait implementation
body:
The `Stream` trait implementation was dropping the future on each `poll_next`, in some cases blocking forever if polling the Future returns `Poll::Pending`, ie. when more than 10 items are iterated

fixes: https://github.com/mitsuhiko/redis-rs/issues/583 and https://github.com/mitsuhiko/redis-rs/issues/537

It's my first time using Future's polling and streams, so reviews are more than welcome!

title: Timeout support for async connection?
body:

```rust

title: feat(expr): `array_{ndims,lower,upper,length,dims}`
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Support the following array functions:
* `array_ndims ( anyarray ) → integer`
* `array_lower ( anyarray, integer ) → integer`
* `array_upper ( anyarray, integer ) → integer` (currently returns bigint, to be fixed as breaking change)
* `array_length ( anyarray, integer ) → integer` (currently returns bigint, to be fixed as breaking change)
* `array_dims ( anyarray ) → text`

The key differences between PostgreSQL array (tensor) and RisingWave array (nested list) are exhibited in related e2e tests. See https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/3811#issuecomment-1556656529 for rationale.

As for implementation:
* `array_ndims` can be statically evaluated based on its type only, similar to `pg_typeof`.
* `array_lower` is always `1` for valid input, thus rewritten to a simple `case when` expression.
* `array_upper` is semantically same as `array_length`.
* `array_dims` can also be rewritten to `array_lower` + `array_upper` + `concat_ws`. But a direct implementation is simpler.

Limitations:
* `array_upper` / `array_length` second argument is limited to 1, even when the array is rectangular.
* `array_dims` only works for 1d array, even when the array is rectangular.

Resolves #8201
Resolves #10135

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Adds ArrangementBackfill, but feature gates it, until we pass more in-depth correctness and performance tests.

For now passing the existing test suite is enough.

After this PR is done, further testing and improvements needs to be done to make sure it can run in background, scale independently of upstream mv, and can work reliably.

## Note to Reviewers

⚠️ **Please read this section before reviewing. It will give a overview of the changes in this PR, to make it easier to review.** ⚠️ 

There are several major changes in this PR.
1. `LocalStateStore::init` and `StateTable::init_epoch` both are now async interfaces, as discussed with @wenym1. Additionally `LocalStateStore::init` also takes in an `EpochPair` instead of a `u64` (`HummockEpoch`).
    1. This means there's quite a bit of refactoring done to accommodate it.
    2. To make it more refactorable in the future, I have introduced a new `LocalStateStoreTestExt` with a singular `init_for_test` function.
3. Protobuf definition changes:
    1. The `Table` definition now includes an `output_indices` field. The replicated state table contains full upstream rows, without column pruning. To make sure that we yield the right rows downstream, we provide `output_indices`. TODO: Is this reeeeeaaaaaaaally needed?
4. Fixes for arrangement backfill:
    1. Ensure that we clear the builders after initial snapshot read. Otherwise it leads to error found in https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/10400/commits/87112202fa53d469315310497c5993ddb6def42f
    2. Ensure state_table waits for first epoch when initializing. Otherwise if the was data in previous epoch, and the barrier is checkpoint, there will be async checkpoint going on, and we may not see this data, wrongly assuming snapshot is empty.
    3. state_persistence TODO explain
    4. position TODO explain
    5. Ensure that for iter_chunks does not return `Option`. `iter_chunks` is used per vnode, and only AFTER all the vnode streams are exhausted, we want to yield none. So we move that logic to the `iter_chunks` caller.
5. Frontend changes to support arrangement backfill:
    1. We generate the necessary plans + feature gate arrangement backfill on `STREAMING_ENABLE_ARRANGEMENT_BACKFILL`.
    1. If using replicated state table, we will follow upstream's convention, if it supports versioning, we will use the appropriate `Serde`. See `from_proto/chain.rs`. Also it is expected that even if the upstream table is versioned, if there's an mview being created on it, it should not be `ALTERable`.

title: feat: support WITH ORDINALITY when using unnest()
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

# Syntax

``` sql
UNNEST(anyarray) WITH ORDINALITY → SETOF anyelement, bigint
```

# Description

The `unnest` function is used to expand an array to a set of rows. When
used with the `WITH ORDINALITY` modifier, it returns a second column
with a one-based index, which represents the position of each element in
the original array.

# Parameters

- `anyarray`: This is the array you want to expand to a set of rows.

# Returns

The function returns a set of rows, each containing two columns: - The
first column is of the type of the elements in the input array. - The
second column is a `bigint` that represents the position of the element
in the original array.

# Examples

``` sql
SELECT * FROM UNNEST(ARRAY['A', 'B', 'C']) WITH ORDINALITY;
-- Returns: A 1, B 2, C 3
```

In this example, the `unnest` function with `WITH ORDINALITY` expands
the input array to a set of rows and assigns a one-based index to each
element.

# Compatibility

The `unnest` function with `WITH ORDINALITY` modifier is a part of the
standard PostgreSQL distribution.

jsonb ?& text[] → boolean
Do all of the strings in the text array exist as top-level keys or array elements?
'["a", "b", "c"]'::jsonb ?& array['a', 'b'] → t
```

title: Optimize large case-when in simple form to constant lookup
body:
PostgreSQL supports a simple-form case-when expression:

```sql
create table test (a int);
insert into test values (1),(2),(3),(5);
SELECT a,
       CASE a WHEN 1 THEN 'one'
              WHEN 2 THEN 'two'
              ELSE 'other'
       END
    FROM test;
```

In such case, if there is a large number of arms (e.g. 500+), it's better to optimize it to a constant lookup.

```rust
struct LookupExpression<S: Scalar> {
    arms: HashMap<Option<S>, BoxedExpression>,
    fallback: BoxedExpression,
}
```

In addition, if users write a case-when expression that can be converted to the simple form, we can also normalize it in optimizer easily:

```sql
SELECT a,
       CASE WHEN a=1 THEN 'one'
            WHEN a=2 THEN 'two'
            ELSE 'other'
       END
    FROM test;
```

Note: the corner cases should be covered:

```sql
SELECT 
       CASE a
              WHEN 1 THEN 'one'
              WHEN 1 THEN 'oneone'
              ELSE 'other',
       CASE a::decimal 
              WHEN 1.0 THEN 'one'
              WHEN 1 THEN 'oneone'
              ELSE 'other'
       END
    FROM test;
```

title: Support VARIADIC function arguments
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

While looking for a workaround for https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/14704 to parse ISO 8601 intervals, I thought to try regular expressions to parse an ISO 8601 string myself.  This seemed easy enough, especially since my source (Debezium) always outputs the intervals in a very rigid format.  A regexp that captures each ISO 8601 interval element, and then uses it in a format string:

**PostgreSQL SQL**

```
users=# select format('%s year %s month %s day %s:%s:%s', variadic regexp_match('P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.15S', 'P(\d+)Y(\d+)M(\d+)DT(\d+)H(\d+)M([\d\.]+)S'));
            format
-------------------------------
 1 year 2 month 3 day 4:5:6.15
```

**RisingWave SQL**

```
thumbtack=> select format('%s year %s month %s day %s:%s:%s', variadic regexp_match('P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.15S', 'P(\d+)Y(\d+)M(\d+)DT(\d+)H(\d+)M([\d\.]+)S'));
ERROR:  Failed to run the query

Caused by:
  sql parser error: syntax error at or near variadic at line:1, column:57
```

It seems that RisingWave does not understand the VARIADIC keyword used by PostgreSQL for unpacking an array into function arguments, as described at https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/xfunc-sql.html#XFUNC-SQL-VARIADIC-FUNCTIONS

It seems there was a special case recently added for some JSON functions at https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/13016 but I think it was not generalized for any variadic function support?

### Describe the solution you'd like

PostgreSQL-compatible support of the `VARIADIC` keyword when calling functions with variadic parameters.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I can't think of a cleaner-looking alternative than what PostgreSQL is doing.

For my immediate problem, this, um... finally does the trick.... 😞 

```
thumbtack=> select replace(
                replace(
                    replace(
                        replace(
                            regexp_replace(
                                replace(
                                    replace(
                                        'P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.15S', 'P', ''
                                    ), 'Y', ' year '
                                ), 'M', ' month '
                            ), 'DT', ' day '
                        ), 'H', ':'
                    ), 'M', ':'
                ), 'S', ''
            )::interval;
             replace
----------------------------------
 1 year 2 mons 3 days 04:05:06.15
```

### Additional context

_No response_

title: PG-incompatibility: parentheses after GROUP BY shall not be row constructor
body:
When used in SELECT list, a pair of parentheses is treated as [simplified version of row constructor](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rowtypes.html#:~:text=The%20ROW%20keyword%20is%20actually%20optional%20as%20long%20as%20you%20have%20more%20than%20one%20field%20in%20the%20expression):

```
test=# create table t (id int, cat varchar, at timestamptz);
CREATE TABLE
test=# insert into tt values (1, 'foo', now()), (2, 'foo', now());
INSERT 0 2

test=# select id, cat from t;
 id | cat 
----+-----
  1 | foo
  2 | foo
(2 rows)

test=# select (id, cat) from t;
   row   
---------
 (1,foo)
 (2,foo)
(2 rows)

test=# select row(id, cat) from t;
   row   
---------
 (1,foo)
 (2,foo)
(2 rows)
```

However, this shall not be the case after GROUP BY:
```
test=# select id from t group by 3+2, (id, cat);
 id 
----
  2
  1
(2 rows)

test=# select id from t group by 3+2, row(id, cat);
ERROR:  column "t.id" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
LINE 1: select id from t group by 3+2, row(id, cat);
               ^
```

As of now, RisingWave reports the same error in both cases, treating parentheses same as row constructor.

title: feat(meta): make complete barrier non-async in worker loop
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

Previously after we collect a barrier, we call `complete_barrier` to commit the a new hummock snapshot and also do some post-collection work to update the catalog metadata. The `complete_barrier` is an async method, which involves works like doing IO to meta store backend, and acquiring async lock. The `complete_barrier` call will in-place block the global barrier manager worker loop, which may block the handling of other events. 

In this PR, we change to spawn a task a do the `complete_barrier` work, so that the call on it will be non-blocking. We also refactor the method to split it into two parts, one called `update_snapshot`, which updates the hummock snapshot, and the other called `update_tracking_jobs`, which updates the information of tracked create streaming jobs.

title: feat(connector): Add mqtt connector
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?
MQTT is a popular protocol for receiving data from multiple IoT devices, it’s a lightweight pub-sub protocol with some features such as retaining the latest message and some delivering guarantees (QoS). The main use case for me is to trigger alerts when certain events happen over a period of time (which I think can be fully implemented using Rising wave).

This PR Implements the following features using the [rumqtt](https://github.com/bytebeamio/rumqtt) library (A rust native library for MQTT).

 - [x] MQTT v5
 - [x] [QoS](https://www.hivemq.com/blog/mqtt-essentials-part-6-mqtt-quality-of-service-levels/) settings using 0 (At most once) by default
 - [x] Support for plain TCP and SSL, including client authentication
 - [x] Retain option for sinks
 - [x] Data splits when using [wildcards](https://subscription.packtpub.com/book/iot-and-hardware/9781787287815/1/ch01lvl1sec18/understanding-wildcards). Since it’s not supported by default, the way is achieved is by subscribing to the topics using the wildcard and for each new message received will check if the topic was added to include it on the splits.

Since the protocol doesn’t keep track of the offsets when a new consumer subscribes, it will receive the messages from the moment it subscribes plus the retained messages if any it doesn’t make sense to save the state or implement checkpoints

body:

https://arc.net/l/quote/hktvlmzf

> When a query involves multiple window functions, it is possible to write out each one with a separate OVER clause, but this is duplicative and error-prone if the same windowing behavior is wanted for several functions. Instead, each windowing behavior can be named in a WINDOW clause and then referenced in OVER. For example:

```sql
SELECT sum(salary) OVER w, avg(salary) OVER w
  FROM empsalary
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC);

title: Support creating table for CDC connectors with the * syntax
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

When using a mysql cdc source after crfeating a source with 
```
CREATE SOURCE test WITH (
  connector = 'mysql-cdc',
  hostname = 'xxx,
  port = '3306',
  username = 'xxx',
  password = 'xxx',
  database.name = 'auto',
  server.id = 5888
);

```
To create a table from the data base you have to specify all the columns explicitly in table creation

```
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS my_products (
    id STRING,
    -- name of the product
    -- format: <group> <type> (<import/domestic>)
    -- e.g. KNOT Type III (import)
    name STRING, 
    price DECIMAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
) FROM test TABLE 'auto.products'

```

### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like to able to create the table using a select * syntax to automatically detect the columns in the table and create downstream tables

```
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS my_products (
    PRIMARY KEY (id),
    *
) FROM test TABLE 'auto.products'
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context

This is is that when we have a huge number of tables with 100+ columns we can avoid the tedium of write scripts to auto generate schema for create table syntax

body:
### Describe the bug

Groupby date columns are serialized to pulsar as integers and no longer as date strings.

For example if date being grouped by is  '2024-04-25'

Then on pulsar it is emitted as number 739002 but in a sql select query the value is correct as '2024-04-25;

This only seems to happen when sinking MVs that have been grouped by. Non group by MVs emit the date to pulsar correctly as a string.

sometable has column dt as type date

```
create materialized view abc_mv as

with ... pulsar

title: feat: a general commit back framework for source
body:
Hi all, I am revisiting the issue for implementing a general ack mechanism in source, thanks @xxchan for mentioning this. 

My major questions are:
1) for a mq with ack, it has a timeout for the staging queue. If a message fails to ack within the timeout, it will go back to the deliver queue and be delivered again to the clients. Then we can get a message twice in some cases, for example, an mq's timeout is 30min and at that time rw is experiencing heavy load, and it takes 35min to finish one epoch. Then all data in the epoch will be delivered twice (fails to achieve exactly-once semantic, and makes future traffic heavier). Is it desired or we gonna trigger a rollback in advance proactively for the promise? 
2) unlike a cdc-spec one, a general framework gonna retains all messages' ack-id. Considering a 30min sliding time window, we may have to persist millions of records. Shall we introducing a log store for it?

> BTW, this situation is also true for persisted pulsar source with 0 retention.

@yuhao-su can you share more about the case? IIRC, a non-persistent pulsar topic cannot seek to spec position and I think it is expected.

_Originally posted by @tabVersion in https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/15464#issuecomment-2108646007_

title: Proposal: A simple approach towards Stateless UDAF
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Share some ideas about UDAF during our discussion with @wangrunji0408 

Stateless UDAF and Stateful UDAF are very different in both implementation and use cases

- Stateful UDAF usually implements init(), accumulate(), retract() i.e. a incremental implementation
   - The PR is under review: https://github.com/risingwavelabs/arrow-udf/pull/23
- Stateless UDAF is as simple as a normal UDF, except that it accepts multiple rows at a time


### Describe the solution you'd like


We don’t really need to offer a framework for stateless UDAF. Instead, **we can reuse the interface of UDF and accept an `ARRAY` as input argument.**

For example, supposing the user have provided such a UDF:

```python3
def my_simple_udaf(values: list[int]):
    ...
```

or 

```python3
class MyEvent:
    def __init__(self, ts, attr1, attr2):
        self.ts = ts
        self.attr1 = attr1
        self.attr2 = attr2

def my_fancy_udaf(rows: list[MyEvent]):
    ...
```

Then they can no only use it as normal UDFs but also as a UDAF in agg or window agg 

```sql
select my_udaf(a, [b, ...]) from t
select my_udaf(a, [b, ...]) over (...) from t
```

A trivial approach is using `array_agg()` and then call the UDF with the result array. However, in this way, both the result array and the input rows are persisted, resulting in 2 copies of data in the state table. Besides, the `array_agg()` is written by users, which looks very  unfriendly.

To make it more efficient and to make the syntax above just works, we need a special code path to handle these use cases.

set operation SQL syntax `query1 UNION/EXPECT/INTERSECT query2` requires query1 and query2 return the same number of columns and match the columns in left-to-right order (by column index). 

With corresponding specification, the set operation matches columns by the column names. Only columns that are in both side will be overlayed. It will suppress columns that are not in both side of the set operation. Columns are considered in both side if they have the same name or alias

You can specify the columns need to be overlayed in the set operation by putting the column names in  `<corresponding column list>`. Only columns that are in both side and the corresponding column list will be overlayed.


`<corresponding spec> ` can be used after `UNION/EXPECT/INTERSECT [ALL]`
`<corresponding spec> ::=
              CORRESPONDING [ BY <left paren> <corresponding column list> <right parent> ]`

title: feat(storage): adjust base compaction limitation
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

In some scenarios, I found that CN generates small ssts, some ssts will be trivial-moved to base level, and the small files may destroy the efficiency of base level compaction, I want to adjust the strategy to reject some trivial-move and base level compaction tasks for some small ssts, so as to achieve better batching and reduce the small sst.

Notes: however, that this PR is not intended to significantly increase compaction capacity, but rather is a safeguard to minimise the number of small files compacting to the base level. 

This PR changed:

1. Reject to base trivial move tasks that are less than the threshold when validator is turned on
2. Decrease the priority of base level compaction tasks that are less than the threshold (unexpected)

title: refactor(source): handle `INCLUDE header` data type properly
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

To follow better coding practices, and reuse existing utilities rather than creating new feature-limited implementation.

Before:
* `str` -> `Token` by tokenizer
* `Token` -> `ast::DataType` by sqlparser
* `ast::DataType` -> `str` by `handle_addition_columns` using `Debug`
* `str` -> `DataType` & `PbDataType` by `build_header_catalog` using match

After:
* `str` -> `Token` by tokenizer
* `Token` -> `ast::DataType` by sqlparser
* `ast::DataType` -> `DataType` by `handle_addition_columns` using `bind_data_type`
* `DataType` -> `PbDataType` by `build_header_catalog` using `to_protobuf`

Additional benefits:
* Less `match`es to update when extending supported types. Sqlparser shall be agnostic of latter business logic.
* The non-standard `Debug` of data type is limited to `gen_default_addition_col_name` with less usage.
* Support parsing multi-word data types, e.g. `character varying`, `timestamp with time zone`

title: refactor(meta): reorganize global barrier manager field
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://gist.github.com/TennyZhuang/f00be7f16996ea48effb049aa7be4d66#file-rw_cla).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

This PR includes some general refactors on the global barrier manager.

First, currently we have `GlobalBarrierManager` and `GlobalBarrierManagerContext`. `GlobalBarrierManager` is actually a owned worker that works in a loop to handle different async barrier event, and `GlobalBarrierManagerContext` holds some shared structs and is used by both the `GlobalBarrierManager` worker and other external usages (e.g. DdlController and etc). In this PR, the `GlobalBarrierManager` worker is renamed to `GlobalBarrierWorker`, and `GlobalBarrierManagerContext` is renamed to `GlobalBarrierWorkerContext`, and will be used by only `GlobalBarrierWorker`. The external usages will only use a new `GlobalBarrierManager`, which contains only the fields used by the external usages. With this refactor, only the `GlobalBarrierManager` has the `pub` visibility, and the `GlobalBarrierWorker` and the `GlobalBarrierWorkerContext` will only be visible within the crate.

Second, in the code of barrier manager, the tuple `(prev_epoch, curr_epoch, barrier_kind)` appears together in many codes. In this PR, we extract them to a new struct `BarrierInfo` that holds the 3 fields, and some related code can be less verbose.

Third, the `BarrierWorkerState` will be moved from `GlobalBarrierWorker` to `CheckpointControl`, and the logic of `handle_new_barrier` in `GlobalBarrierWorker` is narrowed down to only within `CheckpointControl`, so that it becomes a method of `CheckpointControl` only. Besides, previously in `GlobalBarrierWorker`, we have a separate field `pending_non_checkpoint_barriers`, which tracks the inflight non-checkpoint barrier before the next checkpoint barrier. In this PR, the field is moved to `BarrierWorkerState`, and we introduce a method `next_barrier_info` to generate a `BarrierInfo` of the next barrier in a single method call. In `handle_new_barrier`, the `BarrierWorkerState` becomes immutable after `apply_command`.

Fourth, the `CompletingTask` is moved out of `CheckpointControl` to `GlobalBarrierWorker`, which decouples the logical `CheckpointControl` from the physical join handle that calls `commit_epoch`. In the future PR that supports database isolation, we will have a `CheckpointControl` per database, but still a single global `CompletingTask`.

title: frontend: Support `ORDER BY` arbitrary column

**Describe the bug**

Currently only `ORDER BY` can only apply to output columns. But actually, it should work with arbitrary columns, take the example from PostgreSQL's document. Column `c` is not `SELECT`ed, but we can still `ORDER BY c`.

``` SQL
/* this SHOULD work */
SELECT a, b FROM table1 ORDER BY a + b, c;
```

**To Reproduce**

```SQL
create table t(a int, b int);
dev=> explain select a from t order by b;
ERROR:  Item not found: output column "b"
```

**Expected behavior**
Should produce correct execution plan rather than errors.

### Describe the bug

The following 3 queries shall be equivalent in PostgreSQL, when `t`'s only column is `a`:
* `select 1, (select a from t);`
* `select 1, (select * from t);`
* `select 1, ((select * from t));`

But RisingWave fails to parse the one in the middle.

### Error message/log

```text
ERROR:  Failed to run the query

Caused by:
  sql parser error: syntax error at or near from at line 1, column 21
LINE 1: select 1, (select * from t);
                                 ^
```

### To Reproduce

See description above

### Expected behavior

All 3 queries shall give the same output.

### How did you deploy RisingWave?

_No response_

### The version of RisingWave

As early as 1.5, maybe since the day we supported struct syntax `(st).*` #1079 #7024

### Additional context

In PostgreSQL, `(st).*` or `t.*` can be part of an expr (see #10847), but `*` cannot (thus cannot be parenthesized):
```
test=# select (*) from t;
ERROR:  syntax error at or near "*"
LINE 1: select (*) from t;
                ^
```

But seems RisingWave consider `(st).*` closer to `*` rather than normal exprs, and the special treatment consumed 1 extra parenthesis (thus using 2 pairs made the parsing successful).

https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/blob/9edf3895c7194242d834376c4174c6bf53ea4e97/src/sqlparser/src/parser.rs#L403-L422

title: refactor: migrate actor and fragment metadata from db to in-memory cache
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).



## What's changed and what's your intention?

**Summary**



This PR refactors the actor and fragment models to clearly separate persistent database entities from runtime state, introduces per-fragment parallelism, and simplifies the scaling and rescheduling APIs. Legacy reschedule logic is removed in favor of policy-driven control through the DDL service, and backup/restore is aligned with the new model boundaries. These changes enhance maintainability and scalability, laying groundwork for more flexible resource management.

- Rewrite the entire reschedule process, no longer based on the original actor-vnode rebalance model. Instead, use rerender_jobs/fragments to completely rerender the whole graph.  
- During the online scaling phase, compare the newly rendered graph with the actor info inside the barrier system, generate the diff commands, and push them through the barrier system.  
- Deprecate offline scaling. During recovery, rerender using the provided database_id or rerender all jobs; no longer need separate scale_actors.  
- Native support for database isolation.  
- After rescheduling, post-apply is no longer needed, but the serving mapping still requires a post notification.  
- Rewrite the shared source reschedule process: no manual alignment of no shuffle/splits is needed. When rerendering, realign and reassign shared source splits directly based on the ensemble.  
- Actor split management is now handled in the fragment_split table and splits are reassigned as needed.  
- Actor IDs are reassigned starting from 0 every time meta restarts.

**Details**

- Actor and Fragment Model Refactoring:
  - Introduces distinct runtime (`ActorModel`) and persistent (`Model`) representations for actors, ensuring only persistent fields are stored in the database while runtime state is managed separately.
  - Fragment model gains a JSONB `parallelism` field, enabling fragment-level parallelism configuration. ORM relations between fragments and actors are removed, decoupling the DB schema from runtime topology.

- Reschedule and Scaling API Changes:
  - The legacy ScaleService reschedule API is disabled; scaling logic now flows through explicit policies (`ReschedulePolicy`, `ParallelismPolicy`, `ResourceGroupPolicy`) in the DDL service, supporting fixed/adaptive parallelism and stricter validation.
  - CDC backfill and streaming job scaling require explicit parallelism settings, improving error handling and predictability.

- Meta-model and Backup Adjustments:
  - Unused dependencies (`num-integer`, `num-traits`) are removed to streamline the codebase.
  - Actor records are no longer persisted/restored; backup/restore now focuses on streaming job, fragment, and relation metadata, reflecting runtime/persistence separation.

- Barrier Command Simplifications:
  - The `post_updates` field is removed from reschedule barrier commands, signaling a shift of metadata update responsibilities away from barrier execution toward service/controller logic.

**Architecture impact**
These changes enforce a separation of concerns between runtime state and persistence, making the codebase more maintainable and less error-prone. Decoupling ORM models from runtime logic and fragment-actor relations enables more granular scaling and resource allocation, while disabling legacy APIs clarifies the reschedule pipeline and reduces accidental complexity.

**Technical highlights**
- Runtime and persistent actor data are now strictly separated.
- Per-fragment parallelism is supported, enabling flexible scaling strategies.
- Policy structs encapsulate scaling semantics, improving API robustness and future extensibility.

title: refactor(executor): Decouple barrier alignment and mutation for merge type executor
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt). ## What's changed and what's your intention? Based on https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/pull/23221#issuecomment-3306657966 Decouple barrier mutation from upstream modifications, to eliminate potential dependencies. The original implementation may cause deadlocks in the future: - For the new created table, we must create new executors, then create its corresponding dispatcher for downstream, then we can do `execute()`. - Creating the new dispatcher requires waiting for the downstream job to register the new output. - The `Merge` operator in downstream job must receive a barrier from the old table's fragment-graph before it can obtain the mutation, create a new upstream, and register new output. - This means that the old job must process the barrier and send it to downstream normally before the new job is created. - This means that the upstream job's dispatcher must also be able to send the barrier normally. - The upstream job's dispatcher, when receiving the barrier, must wait for the new downstream table to register its output before sending the barrier to both the old and new downstream tables. So, this becomes: ``` create-new-job -> downstream-receive-barrier -> old-job-process-barrier -> upstream-dispatch-barrier -> create-new-job ``` which will cause deadlocks. See comments in `DispatchBarrierBuffer` for details. Close #23064 ## Checklist - [ ] I have written necessary rustdoc comments. - [ ] I have added necessary unit tests and integration tests. - [ ] I have added test labels as necessary. - [ ] I have added fuzzing tests or opened an issue to track them. - [ ] My PR contains breaking changes. - [ ] My PR changes performance-critical code, so I will run (micro) benchmarks and present the results. - [ ] I have checked the [Release Timeline](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/rw-commits-history/blob/main/release_timeline.md) and [Currently Supported Versions](https://docs.risingwave.com/changelog/release-support-policy#support-end-dates-for-recent-releases) to determine which release branches I need to cherry-pick this PR into. ## Documentation - [ ] My PR needs documentation updates.

title: perf(expr): support writer-style #[function] for array type
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

part of #13263

This PR introduces a "writer pattern" for functions that return `anyarray` or `type[]`, allowing them to write their results directly to a `ArrayBuilder` for total data chunk.

This approach **avoids the overhead of unnecessary memory allocation (`malloc`) and copying (`memcpy`)** when building the return value, significantly improving performance for these functions.

For example, `array_distinct` can now be implemented efficiently without creating an intermediate `ListValue`:

```rust
#[function("array_distinct(anyarray) -> anyarray")]
pub fn array_distinct(list: ListRef<'_>, writer: &mut impl risingwave_common::array::ListWrite) {
    writer.write_iter(list.iter().unique());
}
```

### Benchmark Enhancement

Expression benchmarks now include array support:
- Functions with `int32[]`, `float32[]`, `varchar[]`, `bytea[]` arguments are able to bench.
- Functions with `any`/`anyarray` argument types are benchmarked against four concrete types: `int32`, `float32`, `varchar`, `bytea`.

title: feat(streaming): decouple synced log store progress from downstream backpressure
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt). ## What's changed and what's your intention? A dedicated dispatcher is introduced when a fragment terminates with a synced log store. The synced log store executor is decoupled and colocated with the dispatcher, allowing it to receive and process messages from upstream executors independently of downstream polling. This PR is raised to solve #23953. I added support for colocating a synchronous KV log store with the dispatch executor by introducing SyncLogStoreDispatchExecutor. title: refactor(meta): split hummock timer task into per-handler loops
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt). ## What's changed and what's your intention? Fixes https://github.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/issues/24675. This PR refactors the Hummock timer task to avoid head-of-line blocking in the previous single-loop implementation. On `main`, all periodic triggers were driven by one `select_all(triggers)` loop and each selected handler was awaited inline. A slow handler such as statistics reporting could therefore delay the 1s compaction heartbeat expiration check and cause false worker liveness issues. The new structure keeps the behavior aligned with the original timer logic, but splits the work into semantic lanes: - `heartbeat`: runs `handle_timer_compaction_heartbeat_expired_check` independently, so liveness detection is not blocked by slower background work. - `report`: runs statistics reporting independently. The reporting path now snapshots in-memory state while holding locks and emits metrics outside those locks. - `scheduling`: a single serialized lane for all compaction scheduling related timers: - dynamic compaction, - space reclaim compaction plus vnode watermark compaction, - TTL reclaim compaction, - tombstone reclaim compaction, - compaction group split scheduling, - compaction group merge scheduling. - `maintenance`: a serialized lane for low-frequency maintenance such as dead task checking and full GC. The `scheduling` lane intentionally serializes compaction triggers and group split/merge scheduling together. This preserves the old main-loop mutual exclusion semantics for scheduling-related handlers and avoids introducing additional timer-vs-timer lock contention on `versioning` / `compaction_group_manager`. At the same time, the heartbeat and report lanes are isolated from that scheduling lane, which addresses the starvation issue from #24675. Tests were also updated to cover the periodic-loop behavior and to assert that a serial timer lane does not run handlers concurrently. Local validation: ```text rustfmt --edition 2021 src/meta/src/hummock/manager/timer_task.rs src/meta/src/hummock/manager/compaction/compaction_group_manager.rs git diff --check cargo test -p risingwave_meta hummock::manager::timer_task --lib cargo check -p risingwave_meta --lib ``` ## Checklist - [x] I have written necessary rustdoc comments, or no new rustdoc is needed for this internal refactor. - [x] I have added/updated necessary unit tests. ## Documentation No user-facing documentation update is needed. title: fix(sink): truncate barriers in batching log sink during idle periods
body:
## Summary

- **Problem**: When no data flows through the file sink, barriers accumulate in the log store. This happens because `try_commit()` always returns `false` when there is no active writer (`sink_writer` is `None`), so the barrier branch never truncates.
- **Fix**: In the barrier branch of `BatchingLogSinker`, also truncate the barrier when there is no pending data (no active multipart upload). This is safe because if no writer is active, there is nothing to commit across barriers.
- **State machine update**: Added a `truncated` flag to `BarrierReceived` state so that the `BarrierReceived → EpochBegun` transition correctly sets `max_uncommitted_epoch = None` when the barrier was already truncated, avoiding redundant truncation.

## Changes

- `OpenDalSinkWriter::has_pending_data()` — new read-only method that checks `sink_writer.is_some()`
- `LogConsumerState::BarrierReceived` — added `truncated: bool` field
- Barrier handling — truncate when `try_commit() == true || !has_pending_data()`
- State transition — use `truncated` to decide `max_uncommitted_epoch`

## Test plan

- [ ] Existing file sink e2e tests pass (S3/GCS/Azure sink)
- [ ] Verify with idle file sink scenario: barriers should not accumulate in log store when no data is flowing
- [ ] Verify with normal data flow: behavior unchanged, files still written and committed correctly

title: chore(toolchain): bump nightly 2025-10-10 → 2026-06-11
body:
## TL;DR

Bumps `ci/rust-toolchain` from `nightly-2025-10-10` → **`nightly-2026-06-11`** (rustc ~1.93-nightly → 1.98.0-nightly, ~8 months of nightly churn). Adapts the source for compiler/stdlib/itertools/clippy changes across that window, plus a few CI hardenings. The `lints/` crate (RW's custom dylint rules, including `format_error`) is **kept** and updated alongside the main toolchain.

**All Buildkite gates ✅ green, including `check-dylint`.** The `BUILD_ENV_VERSION` bump in `ci/.env` was auto-detected by the `check-ci-image-rebuild` step, which triggered the `ci-build-images` job to rebuild `rw-build-env` with the bumped `cargo-dylint`/`dylint-link` install — no maintainer-side action required. See "Notes for reviewers" below for the accuracy correction on this gate (a prior version of this PR description incorrectly claimed `dylint` was upstream-blocked on rustc 1.98; that was wrong — the actual block was a stale binary in the CI Docker image, fixed in this PR via the `BUILD_ENV_VERSION` bump).

Behavior-preservation has been empirically confirmed end-to-end: `cargo build` clean on 1.98 (codegen + HRTB), `integration-test-deterministic-simulation` ✅ (runtime exact-output gate on the new toolchain — directly proves the hashbrown 0.16 Copy-clone fast-path drop has zero observable impact), and the full e2e/sim/unit/regress suites all green.

## Why 06-11 specifically

`2026-06-11` is the latest nightly that was reachable without unsafe-allocator surgery. The dominant historical blocker was `hashbrown-0.15.5`'s `RawTableClone` Copy-specialization, which rustc 1.95+'s `min_specialization` soundness tightening rejects. The clean unlock turned out to be **bumping the workspace's `hashbrown0_15` alias to `hashbrown 0.16.1`** (which removed the offending Copy specialization upstream — hashbrown CHANGELOG #662), with the `nightly` feature kept on. That avoided the alternative — migrating `src/common/src/lru.rs` off `std::alloc::Allocator` to `allocator-api2` (~600 lines of unsafe allocator code) — entirely. RW's `lru.rs` only uses `HashTable` / `hash_table::Entry`, so the 0.15→0.16 API churn (e.g. `get_many_mut`→`get_disjoint_mut`, `DefaultHashBuilder` newtype) didn't bite RW.

## Change-set (all behavior-preserving, mechanical only — no semantic changes)

### Toolchain & dependencies
- `ci/rust-toolchain` → `nightly-2026-06-11`.
- Workspace `hashbrown0_15` alias → `hashbrown0_16` = `0.16.1` (`nightly` feature kept on).
- `Cargo.lock`: `ethnum` 1.5.0 → 1.5.3 (fixes E0512 transmute-size on 2026 nightlies).
- **`lints/` kept** with its `clippy_utils` source pin updated to track `nightly-2026-06-11` and `dylint_linting` bumped to `6.0.1`. The custom `format_error` rule (flags `format!("{e}")` over `e.to_report_string()`) is preserved.
- **`ci/Dockerfile`**: `cargo install --locked cargo-dylint dylint-link` bumped 4.1.0 → **6.0.1**. The 4.1.0 binaries baked into `rw-build-env` were the actual cause of `check-dylint`'s `ParseSess.env_depinfo` E0609 on rustc 1.98 — `dylint_driver` 6.0.1's `#[rustversion::since(2026-03-18)]` branch handles the new API.
- **`ci/.env`**: `BUILD_ENV_VERSION` bumped (forces `rw-build-env` rebuild via the `build-docker-image` pipeline so the new binaries take effect).

### Source adaptations (mechanical, behavior-preserving)
- `usize::checked_exact_div` (removed 2025-11-12) → exactness-preserving `is_multiple_of` check; drop now-unused `#![feature(exact_div)]`. (`vector_array.rs`)
- `ArrayChunks::into_remainder` `Option<_>` → direct iterator. (`bitmap.rs`, `expr/impl/.../case.rs`)
- `exactly_one` → UFCS `Itertools::exactly_one(..)` at **45 iterator call sites** (44 from the original sweep + 1 picked up from main's gap_fill merge). Avoids `unstable_name_collisions` future-incompat with std's upcoming `Iterator::exactly_one` (rust#48919). `pending_sink_state` rows leaked on `DROP SINK`. The model declares `on_delete = "Cascade"`, but the original migration never created the DB foreign key, so the cascade from `Object::delete_many` never reached the table. title: S3 streaming multipart uploads can be leaked when a cancelled uploader is dropped after multipart upload starts
body:
### Describe the bug

RisingWave's S3 streaming uploader can lose its only cleanup handle for an in-progress multipart upload when the uploader is cancelled or dropped after `CreateMultipartUpload` has succeeded.

The concrete issue is in the cancellation boundary around `S3StreamingUploader`. Once `upload_next_part()` lazily creates an S3 multipart upload, the uploader stores the returned `upload_id` locally and may also spawn upload-part tasks. The async cleanup operation, `abort_multipart_upload().await`, is only called from the `finish()` error path after `flush_multipart_and_complete().await` returns an error. If the owning future is cancelled or the `S3StreamingUploader` is dropped before `finish()` reaches that error branch, no `AbortMultipartUpload` request is issued.

This matters for compaction because compaction tasks are explicitly cancellable. A `CancelCompactTask` event can make `compactor_runner` stop waiting for unfinished split workers and abort them. Those workers can be in the middle of building/uploading SST files through `StreamingUploadWriter`, which awaits `ObjectStreamingUploader::write_bytes`. If that worker is aborted after S3 multipart upload creation, RisingWave can drop the uploader while S3 still has an incomplete multipart upload and uploaded parts.

The state-machine shape is:

```text
SST streaming upload starts
  -> S3 CreateMultipartUpload succeeds and upload_id is stored in S3StreamingUploader
  -> at least one UploadPart request is issued or in flight
  -> compaction cancellation / task abort / future drop drops the uploader
  -> finish() is not reached, so its error-path abort_multipart_upload() is not run
  -> the S3 multipart upload is left for external lifecycle cleanup, if any
```

The practical impact is bounded by object-store lifecycle configuration, but not eliminated by it. Until lifecycle cleanup runs, incomplete multipart uploads and uploaded parts can consume bucket capacity and incur storage cost. On S3-compatible backends where lifecycle rules are unavailable, disabled, rejected, or delayed, the leak can persist indefinitely.

Relevant code paths:

- `src/object_store/src/object/s3.rs`
  - `S3StreamingUploader::upload_next_part()` creates the multipart upload and stores `upload_id`.
  - `S3StreamingUploader::flush_multipart_and_complete()` joins part uploads and completes the multipart upload.
  - `S3StreamingUploader::abort_multipart_upload()` exists but is async.
  - `impl StreamingUploader for S3StreamingUploader::finish()` calls `abort_multipart_upload()` only when `flush_multipart_and_complete().await` returns `Err`.
- `src/storage/src/hummock/compactor/compactor_runner.rs`
  - compaction races worker completion against `shutdown_rx`;
  - on cancellation it aborts unfinished split worker tasks.
- `src/storage/src/hummock/sstable/writer.rs`
  - `StreamingUploadWriter::write_block`, `write_block_bytes`, and early `finish` logic await `object_uploader.write_bytes(...)` while still owning the uploader.

### Error message/log

```text
There is no user-visible error message in the normal case. The bad state is an external object-store side effect: an incomplete multipart upload can remain after RisingWave reports the compaction task as cancelled and drops the local uploader state.

The whitebox reproduction below records S3 requests issued by `S3StreamingUploader`. It proves that after a multipart upload has started, dropping the uploader does not issue `AbortMultipartUpload`.
```

### To Reproduce

This is easiest to reproduce as a focused whitebox unit test at the object-store layer. The test uses an in-process fake S3 HTTP client, so it does not require real AWS S3 or MinIO.

The test intentionally passes on the current buggy code by asserting the current bad behavior. It is a bug-existence validation test, not a post-fix regression test. After a fix, the final assertion should be inverted or replaced with a stronger invariant such as "abort is issued or cleanup ownership i

title: SELECT on a covering-indexed MV crashes the session
body:
### Describe the bug

A `SELECT` on a materialized view that has a **covering index** (`CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (...)`) crashes the session (`server closed the connection unexpectedly`) when the `WHERE` clause filters the **index key column** together with a column that is **not in the index** (neither the key nor an `INCLUDE` column).

The query is valid SQL and returns correctly when:
- the index is plain (no `INCLUDE`), or
- there is no index, or
- the predicate stays within the index (key only, or key + an `INCLUDE`d column).

A bare `SELECT` is enough — no join, subquery, or `EXISTS` needed. It is deterministic, and the server accepts new connections after the session is dropped.


### Error message/log

```text
server closed the connection unexpectedly
```

### To Reproduce

On a fresh RisingWave, in `psql`:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mc AS SELECT 1 AS id, 'a' AS val, 'x' AS tag;
CREATE INDEX mc_idx ON mc (id) INCLUDE (val);

-- crashes: "server closed the connection unexpectedly"
SELECT 1 FROM mc WHERE id = 1 AND tag = 'x';
```

The crash needs all three: a covering (INCLUDE) index, a predicate on the index key (id), and a predicate on a column outside the index (tag), combined with AND.

[python MVP](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30046114/rw_index_crash_repro.py)

### Expected behavior

I expected the query to return its result (one row).

Instead, the session was terminated (`server closed the connection unexpectedly`). A valid query should never crash the server.

### How did you deploy RisingWave?

Docker, single-node: image `ghcr.io/risingwavelabs/risingwave:latest`, started with `command: single_node`. Reproduced from a client connecting to that service over the Postgres port (4566).


### The version of RisingWave

PostgreSQL 13.14.0-RisingWave-3.0.1 (7f2a49c16fe3bd16df25c2c1ff31fd02497ddb7e)


### Additional context

Boundary — same MV `mc (id, val, tag)`, only the first case crashes:

| Index | WHERE clause | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `(id) include (val)` | `id = 1 and tag = 'x'` | **CRASH** |
| `(id) include (val)` | `id = 1` | ok |
| `(id) include (val)` | `tag = 'x'` | ok |
| `(id) include (val)` | `id = 1 and val = 'a'` (both covered) | ok |
| `(id)` (plain, no INCLUDE) | `id = 1 and tag = 'x'` | ok |
| no index | `id = 1 and tag = 'x'` | ok |

title: Multi-row correlated `VALUES` escapes decorrelation — `PlanCorrelatedIdFinder` never inspects `LogicalValues` rows
body:
### Describe the bug

Follow-up to #12231, which was closed by #13182 (`ValuesExtractProjectRule`). That fix bails on `old_values.rows().len() != 1` (`values_extract_project_rule.rs:31`), so it only rescues **single-row** correlated `VALUES`. The underlying cause was never addressed and multi-row `VALUES` still escapes.

Root cause: `PlanCorrelatedIdFinder` (`src/frontend/src/optimizer/plan_visitor/plan_correlated_id_finder.rs`) overrides `visit_logical_join`, `visit_logical_filter`, `visit_logical_project`, `visit_logical_agg`, `visit_logical_project_set` and `visit_logical_table_function`, but **not** `visit_logical_values`, and its `default_behavior()` is `DefaultValue`. For a leaf `LogicalValues` it therefore never inspects `rows()` and always reports "no correlated id".

`ApplyEliminateRule`'s only correlation gate is `find_correlated_id(right, &correlated_id)` (`apply_eliminate_rule.rs:68`). It gets `false`, skips its bail-out, and rewrites the `LogicalApply` into a plain join — orphaning the `CorrelatedInputRef`s still sitting inside the Values rows. `check_apply_elimination` does not catch this because it only looks for surviving `LogicalApply` nodes.

The binder's own guard doesn't stop it either: `binder/values.rs:153` tests `is_correlated_by_depth(1)`, an exact-depth match. A derived table pushes an extra subquery context, so the reference binds at **depth 2** and slips past.

Corroborating detail: the guard at `pull_up_correlated_project_value_rule.rs:108-113` was written specifically to catch a correlated id inside `LogicalValues` rows — it is dead code for the same reason and can never fire.

### Error message/log

```
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/frontend/src/expr/mod.rs:117:14:
failed to serialize expression to protobuf: "CorrelatedInputRef CorrelatedInputRef { index: 1, correlated_id: 1 } has not been decorrelated"

  frame 4: <ExprImpl as Expr>::to_expr_proto        at src/frontend/src/expr/mod.rs:117:14
  frame 5: BatchValues::row_to_protobuf::{closure#0} at src/frontend/src/optimizer/plan_node/batch_values.rs:59:42
```

Worth noting for whoever writes the regression test: **planning itself succeeds.** The optimizer happily emits a physical plan carrying the un-decorrelated reference, and it only blows up at proto serialization:

```
└─BatchNestedLoopJoin { type: Inner, predicate: true, output: all }
  ├─ ...
  └─BatchValues { rows: [[CorrelatedInputRef { index: 1, correlated_id: 1 }],
                         [CorrelatedInputRef { index: 2, correlated_id: 1 }]] }
```

So a planner test asserting `batch_plan` will pass and hide this; the test must assert `batch_plan_proto`.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(a int, b int, c int);
SELECT * FROM t WHERE t.a IN (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (t.b), (t.c)) v);
```

Control — the single-row form is correctly decorrelated (rescued by `ValuesExtractProjectRule`), producing `BatchValues { rows: [[]] }`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t2(a int, b int);
SELECT * FROM t2 WHERE t2.a IN (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (t2.b)) v);
```

### Expected behavior

Either full decorrelation, or a clean `Not supported` bind error. Not a panic with "This is a bug" and a dropped connection.

### How did you deploy RisingWave?

RiseDev, planner test (`./risedev run-planner-test`), debug build. No running instance needed.

### The version of RisingWave

`main` @ `d881145900` (2026-07-22).

### Additional context

Suggested fix: add `visit_logical_values` to `PlanCorrelatedIdFinder`, delegating to the `LogicalValues` expression walk. That makes `ApplyEliminateRule` and `ApplyJoinTransposeRule` see the correlation and bail correctly, and it also revives the currently-dead guard in `pull_up_correlated_project_value_rule.rs`. Widening the binder's depth-1 check to any depth would be a complementary defence.

Unrelated cleanup spotted nearby: the `FIXME` at `src/frontend/planner_test/tests/testdata/input/with_ordinality.yaml:85` still points at #12231, but that case now yields `Not supported: streaming

title: ArrangementBackfill degrades to one-row-per-barrier under high upstream rate, causing iceberg-engine tables to miss backfill data
body:
## Describe the bug

`ArrangementBackfill` can degrade to processing **one row per barrier** when the upstream keeps delivering data, starving the snapshot read. For an iceberg-engine table (`CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = ICEBERG`), whose internal `__iceberg_sink` uses `ArrangementBackfill` (`SINK` + `STREAM_SCAN`) to backfill the materialized view's historical data into iceberg, this causes the backfill to produce **one single-row data file per barrier** and effectively never finish for actively-written tables. The result: the sink commits only the post-backfill CDC increments, and the historical snapshot rows are missing from the iceberg table (and thus invisible to downstream readers like Doris/Spark), even though the data is fully present in hummock.

## Root cause

In `src/stream/src/executor/backfill/arrangement_backfill.rs`, the main backfill loop uses:

```rust
let mut backfill_stream =
    select_with_strategy(left_upstream, right_snapshot, |_: &mut ()| {
        stream::PollNext::Left   // always prefer upstream
    });
```

When the upstream MV keeps producing chunks/barriers (e.g. a table under active CDC ingestion while other large tables are still backfilling and holding the global barrier cadence high), `left_upstream` is always ready, so the `right_snapshot` branch never gets polled and `has_snapshot_read` stays `false`.

Every loop iteration then falls into the "read at least one row" fallback block:

```rust
if !has_snapshot_read && !paused && rate_limit_ready {
    ...
    for msg in snapshot {
        ...
        Some((vnode, row)) => {
            let builder = builders.get_mut(&vnode).unwrap();
            if let Some(chunk) = builder.append_one_row(row) {
                ... yield Message::Chunk(chunk);
            }
            break;   // <-- reads exactly ONE row then breaks, every barrier
        }
    }
}
```

The `break` exits after a **single row**, so each barrier period advances the backfill by only one row. Under a high barrier rate this is orders of magnitude too slow, and each row is flushed as its own tiny data file.

## Reproduction & evidence (tracing)

Built a `v3.0.1`-based image with `tracing::info!` added at the fallback branch and at the barrier-flush point (logging `snapshot_rows_this_barrier`, `has_snapshot_read`, `upstream_buffer_len`). Created 48 iceberg-engine tables concurrently from a MySQL CDC source (mixed table sizes, so large-table backfills keep barriers frequent).

Observed for the small, actively-written tables:

```
sinkbf_debug_barrier_flush has_snapshot_read=false snapshot_rows_this_barrier=1 upstream_buffer_len=4  total_snapshot_processed_rows=1
sinkbf_debug_barrier_flush has_snapshot_read=false snapshot_rows_this_barrier=1 upstream_buffer_len=10 total_snapshot_processed_rows=2
sinkbf_debug_barrier_flush has_snapshot_read=false snapshot_rows_this_barrier=1 upstream_buffer_len=0  total_snapshot_processed_rows=3
```

Every barrier processes exactly **1** snapshot row, with `has_snapshot_read=false` (main snapshot loop never ran) and the fallback branch hit repeatedly.

On the storage side, the affected tables' iceberg `data/` directories contained dozens of **single-row parquet files** (~8 KB each, one row per file), and none of them were ever added to a snapshot manifest — the table's `total-records` stayed at the tiny post-backfill increment count. In contrast, a static (non-actively-written) table produced normal batched files (~20 KB+, hundreds of rows each) and committed its full backfill in one append.

## Impact

- Iceberg-engine tables built while the cluster is under load can silently miss their historical (backfill) data in the committed iceberg table.
- Data is not lost from hummock, but downstream iceberg consumers see only a fraction of the rows.
- Recovery requires DROP + recreate of the affected table.

## Environment

- RisingWave v3.0.1 (fork build)
- Iceberg engine tables, MySQL CDC upstream, high-concurrency table creation.

In the fallb

title: fix(backfill): avoid one-row-per-barrier starvation in ArrangementBackfill
body:
## What's changed

Fixes the one-row-per-barrier starvation in `ArrangementBackfill` described in #26421.

The backfill loop uses `select_with_strategy(left_upstream, right_snapshot, |_| PollNext::Left)`, always preferring upstream. When the upstream keeps producing data/barriers (e.g. an iceberg-engine `__iceberg_sink` backfilling a table under active CDC ingestion, while other large tables keep the global barrier rate high), the `right_snapshot` branch is never polled, so `has_snapshot_read` stays `false` and every barrier period enters the "read at least one row" fallback block.

That fallback used to `break` after a **single row**:

```rust
Some((vnode, row)) => {
    let builder = builders.get_mut(&vnode).unwrap();
    if let Some(chunk) = builder.append_one_row(row) {
        ... yield Message::Chunk(chunk);
    }
    break;   // <-- one row per barrier
}
```

so the backfill advanced by one row per barrier, flushing each row as its own tiny data file and effectively never finishing for actively-written tables. For iceberg-engine tables this means the historical (backfill) rows silently never make it into the committed iceberg table.

This PR moves the `break` inside the `if let Some(chunk)` branch, so the fallback only exits once a full chunk has been produced — advancing a whole chunk per pass instead of a single row.

## Verification

Built a v3.0.1-based image and created 48 iceberg-engine tables concurrently from a MySQL CDC source (mixed sizes, so large-table backfills keep barriers frequent).

- **Before the fix:** `snapshot_rows_this_barrier` was a constant `1` for actively-written small tables; their iceberg `data/` dirs filled with single-row (~8 KB) parquet files that were never added to a snapshot; iceberg `total-records` stayed at the tiny post-backfill increment count.
- **After the fix:** `snapshot_rows_this_barrier` = `50 / 119 / 1189 / 4712 / 6268 ...`; the 3 previously-truncated tables backfilled completely — iceberg `total-records` = full counts `1481 / 903 / 10058`, matching hummock and the upstream, confirmed via Doris reads.

## Checklist

- [x] Reproduced the bug and verified the fix end-to-end
- [ ] I have written necessary rustdoc comments (inline comment added explaining the invariant)
- [ ] I have added necessary unit tests and integration tests

Closes #26421

title: bug(optimizer): general subquery decorrelation on non-deterministic (eg `random`) outer query
body:
### Describe the bug

RisingWave can return **systematically wrong / NULL** values for correlated scalar aggregates:

```sql
(SELECT SUM(h.amount) FROM hourly_facts h WHERE h.user_id = s.user_id)
```

when `s` is produced by a derived table such as:

```sql
(SELECT user_id FROM windows ORDER BY random() LIMIT 50)
```

On a synthetic dataset with a known lifetime `SUM` per `user_id`, many sampled rows get **`NULL` from the scalar** (not a wrong number). Example on `v3.0.3`:

- [CI run 34492721666](https://github.com/tsekityam/rw-correlated-scalar-repro/actions/runs/34492721666) (`main` @ `74a895cd`): Query A `sample_random_limit_scalar` → **22/50 NULL** (`match_true=28`, `match_null=22`); Query B **50/50**.
- [CI run 34492099604](https://github.com/tsekityam/rw-correlated-scalar-repro/actions/runs/34492099604) (documented example): **19/50 NULL**.

If the caller coalesces NULL to 0, the “source” side looks like ~0.

The **same** `user_id`s computed via a fixed `VALUES` list + `WHERE user_id IN (...)` + `GROUP BY` + `JOIN` match the MV exactly.

A single-row probe `FROM windows w WHERE user_id = '<literal>'` plus the same correlated `SUM` is correct. The failure is tied to the sample / derived-table outer relation.

**Root cause (from `EXPLAIN` on the repro):** decorrelation re-runs `BatchTopN { order: [Random], limit: 50 }` (or `Limit 50`) independently on the aggregate side, then `LeftOuter`/`FullOuter` joins on `user_id`. Two independent `random()` samples do not share the same keys, so the scalar `SUM` is NULL.

`LATERAL (SELECT SUM(...) ...)` over the same sample matches in CI (hash-join to a full agg, no re-sample).

### To Reproduce

Public repro (merged on `main`): https://github.com/tsekityam/rw-correlated-scalar-repro  
Latest intended failure on `main`: https://github.com/tsekityam/rw-correlated-scalar-repro/actions/runs/34492721666  
Harness history: https://github.com/tsekityam/rw-correlated-scalar-repro/pull/1

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tsekityam/rw-correlated-scalar-repro
cd rw-correlated-scalar-repro
docker compose up -d --wait risingwave
export PGHOST=127.0.0.1 PGPORT=4566 PGDATABASE=dev PGUSER=root
bash scripts/run-repro.sh
```

Pinned image: `risingwavelabs/risingwave:v3.0.3` (`single_node --in-memory`). CI runs the same compose stack; exit **1** = `BUG REPRODUCED` (Query A wrong, Query B correct).

Schema (synthetic):

- `hourly_facts(user_id varchar, hour_utc timestamp, amount numeric)` — 80 users × 48 hours, deterministic amounts.
- `windows` = `SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS lifetime_sum FROM hourly_facts GROUP BY user_id`.

**Query A (wrong / NULLs):**

```sql
SELECT
  q.user_id,
  q.expected_sum,
  q.scalar_sum,
  abs(q.expected_sum - q.scalar_sum) < 0.000000000001 AS match
FROM (
  SELECT
    s.user_id,
    w.lifetime_sum AS expected_sum,
    (SELECT SUM(h.amount) FROM hourly_facts h WHERE h.user_id = s.user_id) AS scalar_sum
  FROM (SELECT user_id FROM windows ORDER BY random() LIMIT 50) s
  JOIN windows w ON w.user_id = s.user_id
) q;
```

`match` must be derived from that **same** `scalar_sum` (do not write a second `(SELECT SUM …)` in the select list — RisingWave decorrelates each one independently).

**Query B (correct workaround):**

```sql
WITH ids(user_id) AS (VALUES
  ('aaaaaaaa-bbbb-4ccc-8ddd-000000000001')
  -- …fixed list…
)
SELECT i.user_id, w.lifetime_sum, a.agg_sum
FROM ids i
JOIN windows w ON w.user_id = i.user_id
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS agg_sum
  FROM hourly_facts
  WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM ids)
  GROUP BY user_id
) a ON a.user_id = i.user_id;
```

The repro script also tries `LATERAL`, multiple scalars, `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`, and a client-side `BOOL_AND` over the sample.

### Expected behavior

For every sampled `user_id`, the correlated scalar `SUM` equals `windows.lifetime_sum` (and Query B). No NULLs when matching rows exist in `hourly_facts`.

title: fix(storage): bound SST scans and point gets by table ID
body:
I hereby agree to the terms of the [RisingWave Labs, Inc. Contributor License Agreement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/risingwavelabs/risingwave/17af8a747593ebdbfa826691daf75bdab7d14fa0/.github/contributor-license-agreement.txt).

## What's changed and what's your intention?

When an SST contains multiple tables, a scan or point get can read blocks belonging to another table. Bound SST iterators to the requested table ID so these reads avoid unrelated blocks. For example, a point get before the first key in table 2 now reads only the table-2 block instead of first visiting the preceding table-1 block.
